## Records NOT online

- Church of Ireland registers for Billy parish: existence and content not confirmed by any tool result; must be verified with PRONI and the RCB Library before concluding they are online or accessible
- Presbyterian registers before 1837: not digitized; inquire at PRONI and the Presbyterian Historical Society
- Covenanter (Reformed Presbyterian) registers: not found in any tool result; inquire at PRONI
- Wesleyan Methodist registers for Billy: not found; check FindMyPast Non-Conformist collections and PRONI
- Deffrick National School Girls (image group 008682995): on FamilySearch but browse-only — no index exists
- Pre-1858 wills and administrations: originals destroyed in 1922; surviving derivatives (Betham, Thrift, Crossle abstracts) are on FindMyPast but are partial
- Estate and landlord papers (rent rolls, tenancy lists, eviction orders): held physically at PRONI as private deposits; not online

---

## Known record losses

- Two-thirds of Church of Ireland parish registers that had been deposited at the Public Record Office in Dublin were destroyed in the 1922 fire. The Ireland Church Records wiki page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records) states this directly. Whether the Billy CoI registers were among those destroyed, or were retained locally or at PRONI, must be confirmed with the RCB Library and PRONI.
- Prerogative and consistorial court probate records before 1858 were largely destroyed in the same 1922 fire. Surviving abstracts (Betham, Thrift, Crossle) are partial substitutes.
- The 1821, 1831, 1841, 1851 Irish national census returns were destroyed (1861 and 1871 by government order; 1821–1851 in the 1922 fire). No national census survives for Billy parish within the target period.

---

## Research tips

- **Search the Coleraine RC district, not "Billy parish," for Catholic registers.** The Ireland Church Records wiki page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records) explains that Catholic and Church of Ireland parish boundaries differ; in Billy, the RC population falls under the Coleraine RC district. Searching by the civil parish name alone will miss Catholic records filed under Coleraine.
- **The Presbyterian registers on FamilySearch are full-text searchable, not name-indexed.** Use the keyword or full-text search interface (not the name search) to locate entries in image groups 007907410 and 007765074; browsing image-by-image is also needed to read surrounding context.
- **For the gap before 1837, combine Tithe Applotment Books and estate records.** No church registers have been found for 1780–1836 in this survey. The Tithe Applotment Books (1820s–1830s, free at AskAboutIreland and Ancestry) name heads of household by townland, and PRONI's holdings of North Antrim estate papers may contain tenancy lists going further back.
- **Consult PRONI's Guide to Church Records before visiting.** The guide (https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/sites/default/files/publications/Guide-to-Church-Records-October-2019.pdf) identifies which churches existed in each parish, what registers survive, and whether PRONI holds originals or microfilm. This is the single most efficient tool for understanding what church material can be found for Billy before making a repository visit.
- **The Ulster Historical Foundation has indexed County Antrim records including church registers, gravestone inscriptions, and census substitutes** at http://www.ancestryireland.com/. This subscription index covers material held at PRONI and in parish custody that is not fully searchable elsewhere, and is particularly valuable for filling the pre-1864 church gap.
- **Use the Marriage License Bonds index (FamilySearch collection 3460239) to reach marriages before 1845.** This collection covers 1623–1866 and includes Connor diocese material, which covers County Antrim. It is indexed with images and free on FamilySearch.

---

The four FamilySearch wiki place-page sections requested for County Antrim (home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips) each returned a generic fallback rather than Ireland-specific content; they are not cited above. The Ireland Church Records page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records) and the Billy Civil Parish page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Billy_Civil_Parish,_County_Antrim,_Northern_Ireland_Genealogy) were successfully fetched and are the primary wiki sources for this guide.

---

Billy civil parish in County Antrim covers the Bushmills area of the north Antrim coast, and the most important thing to understand about researching there between 1780 and 1870 is that civil registration of births and deaths did not begin until 1864, so church registers are the only surviving vital-event records for most of those ninety years — and several denomination-specific gaps exist: no Presbyterian registers have been found before 1837, the Catholic registers for the Coleraine district likely start no earlier than the late 1820s, and the survival of Church of Ireland registers for Billy itself must be confirmed with the RCB Library in Dublin and PRONI in Belfast. The best starting points for closing those gaps are PRONI's Guide to Church Records (which names every surviving church register for each County Antrim parish), the National Library of Ireland's free Catholic register images at registers.nli.ie, and the Ulster Historical Foundation's county-wide index at ancestryireland.com; the Tithe Applotment Books of the 1820s–1830s and Griffith's Valuation of the 1847–1864 period (both freely searchable at askaboutireland.ie) are the most useful substitutes where church registers are absent.

The recommended next step is to consult PRONI's Guide to Church Records to confirm exactly which Billy denomination registers survive and in what form, then search the National Library of Ireland's Catholic register portal and the Presbyterian volumes already digitized on FamilySearch before planning a repository visit.

# Locality Guide: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (1840–1869)

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **Formed:** 1811
- **County seat:** Pottsville (the administrative center)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States

> **Note:** The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Pennsylvania and Schuylkill County returned only generic placeholder content during this survey. Any gaps in this guide should be verified directly on the FamilySearch Wiki before drawing conclusions.

---

## Boundary Changes

Schuylkill County was formed in 1811. No boundary changes during or near the 1840–1869 target period were confirmed by tool results. If a boundary change occurred near the target period, some records may be filed under a predecessor county — this could not be verified in this survey.

---

## Available Record Types

### ✅ Federal Census Records (Best Starting Point)

**Volume 007621224 — U.S. Federal Census, Schuylkill County, 1850–1860**
- 412 images | **96% name-indexed + full-text searchable**
- This is the strongest name-indexed entry point for the entire target period.
- Also available on [Ancestry](https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/1276/) (subscription required).
- **Note:** No separate digitized volumes were found for the 1840 or 1870 federal censuses for this county.

---

### ✅ Probate Records

**Volume 004812990 — Probate Records, Schuylkill County, 1845–1880**
- 286 images | **Full-text searchable, but only 4% name-indexed**
- Use full-text search AND browse remaining images manually — a name-only search will miss most entries.

**Collection 1999196 — Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994**
- 3,200,560 images | **Browse-only, no name index**
- Covers all of Pennsylvania; must be browsed image by image.

---

### ✅ Lutheran Church Records

**Volume 004288771 — Lutheran Church Records, Schuylkill County, 1840–1875**
- 198 images | **Browse-only images, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable**
- Contains text in **both English and German**. Familiarity with German Kurrent handwriting will be needed.
- Must be browsed image by image; no search functionality.

---

### ⚠️ Vital Records (Civil Registration)

- No digitized vital record volumes (births, marriages, or deaths) were found for Schuylkill County in the 1840–1869 period.
- The start date for Pennsylvania civil registration could not be confirmed by tool results.
- **Church records are the primary alternative** for vital events in this period.

---

### ⚠️ Land Records

- No land or deed record volumes were found for Schuylkill County in the target period.
- Deed books are typically held at the **county Recorder of Deeds**; original land patents and grants are at the **Pennsylvania State Archives**.

---

### ⚠️ Military Records

- Relevant conflicts: **Mexican-American War (1846–1848)** and **Civil War (1861–1865)**.
- No military record volumes were found for Schuylkill County in the target period.
- Federal service records and pension files are held at **NARA**.

---

### ⚠️ Immigration & Naturalization

- **Philadelphia** is the nearest major port of entry.
- No immigration or naturalization volumes were found for Schuylkill County in the target period.
- Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record and may be held at the county courthouse.

---

### ⚠️ Tax Records

- No tax record volumes were found for the 1840–1869 period. (An Ancestry collection covers tax lists only through 1801.)
- Original tax records are likely at the **Pennsylvania State Archives** or county courthouse and are not yet digitized according to this survey.

---

### ⚠️ Cemetery, Newspaper & Other Records

- No digitized cemetery, newspaper, court, or school records were found for Schuylkill County in this period.
- Newspapers (such as the *Miners' Journal*) may be held at libraries or state archives.

---

|---|---|

|---|---|

The following record types exist for this period but were **not found in any digitized collection** in this survey:

- Vital records (births, marriages, deaths)
- Land and deed records
- Tax records for 1840–1869
- Military service records and pension files

- Cemetery sexton records

# Locality Guide: Pulaski County, Kentucky (1840–1880)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** 1798 from Lincoln and Green counties
- **County seat:** Somerset
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Kentucky, United States
- **Population during period:** Not returned by tools; consult federal census records directly for 1840, 1850, 1860, 1870, and 1880 figures.
- **Economy:** Primarily agricultural; southeastern Kentucky setting typical of small-farm subsistence with some trade along waterways
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly native-born settlers of Scots-Irish and English descent; small enslaved and free Black population before emancipation (1865)
- **Religious denominations:** Baptist, Methodist, Roman Catholic, and Presbyterian — the four largest denominations in pre-1900 Kentucky (Kentucky Church Records wiki page, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky_Church_Records)
- **Key historical events:** Civil War (1861–1865) divided Kentucky loyalties and generated military, pension, and Freedmen's Bureau records; Emancipation (1865) created a new record class for formerly enslaved persons

## Boundary changes
- Pulaski County was formed in 1798 from Lincoln and Green counties; no further boundary changes were returned by tools for the target period
- Records from before 1798 — early land grants, early court records — are held by Lincoln County and Green County; search both when tracing ancestors into the 1790s

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **County-level births and deaths:** Three incomplete registration windows — 1853–1862, 1874–1878, and 1892–1910; compliance was generally poor and many events were never registered
- **County marriages:** Recorded continuously from county formation (1798) at the Pulaski County Courthouse
- **Statewide births and deaths:** 1911; general compliance achieved by approximately 1917
- **Statewide marriages:** 1958
- **Where held:** Pre-1911 county birth and death records at the Kentucky Department for Libraries and Archives (KDLA), Frankfort; county courthouse for marriage bonds and licenses; statewide records from 1911 at the Kentucky Department of Public Health, Office of Vital Statistics
- **Gaps:** No civil registration for births and deaths during 1840–1853, 1862–1874, and 1878–1892 — covering most of the target period. Church records are the primary alternative.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism and burial registers, family bibles, tombstone inscriptions, mortality schedules, obituaries
- **Source:** Kentucky Vital Records wiki page, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky_Vital_Records

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Baptist, Methodist, Roman Catholic, and Presbyterian — the four largest in pre-1900 Kentucky
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations, membership lists, minutes
- **Online at FamilySearch (from https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky_Church_Records):**
  - Kentucky Church Records, 1818–1995 — index and images (incomplete)
  - Kentucky Births and Christenings, 1839–1960 — index only
  - Kentucky Marriages, 1785–1979 — index only
  - Kentucky Deaths and Burials, 1843–1970 — index only
- **Where held:** FamilySearch Library (microfilmed records); Kentucky Historical Society, Frankfort; Southern Baptist Historical Library, Nashville; Presbyterian Historical Society, Philadelphia; active local congregations
- **Gaps:** Coverage is incomplete; not all Pulaski County congregation records have been microfilmed or digitized
- **Language:** English

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1840, 1850, 1860, 1870, and 1880 all cover Pulaski County; the 1880 schedule adds relationship to head of household
- **State census:** Kentucky did not conduct state censuses
- **Mortality schedules:** 1850, 1860, 1870, and 1880 — record deaths in the year preceding each census with age, sex, occupation, and cause of death; valuable substitute for missing death registration
- **Access:** Indexed and searchable at Ancestry (subscription) and FamilySearch (free); images available at both

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, letters of administration, guardianship files, civil and criminal cases, county court minute books
- **Date range:** From county formation (1798)
- **Where held:** Pulaski County Courthouse, Somerset; KDLA may hold microfilm copies
- **Note:** County court minute books record road maintenance, poor relief, and payments — naming persons not party to any formal suit

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Kentucky is a state-land state; metes and bounds descriptions; no federal rectangular survey
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Kentucky Land Office, Frankfort — holds grants, warrants, surveys, and patents; county courthouse holds deed books from formation
- **Grant periods relevant to 1840–1880:** Old Kentucky Grants (1793–1856); Kentucky Land Warrants (1816–1873)
- **Types:** Deeds, land grants, patents, surveys, mortgages, tax records
- **Date range:** County deed books from 1798; Kentucky Land Office records from 1773
- **Where held:** Pulaski County Courthouse for deeds; Kentucky Land Office, Frankfort; FamilySearch has Kentucky Land Office warrants, surveys, grants 1700–1955 (digitized images); Ancestry also covers Kentucky land grants
- **Source:** Kentucky Land and Property wiki page, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky_Land_and_Property

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Mexican-American War (1846–1848); Civil War (1861–1865) — Kentucky had both Union and Confederate soldiers
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants (for veterans 1846–1855), Civil War draft registration, state adjutant general records
- **Where held:** NARA (service records and pension files); KDLA (state adjutant general records); Fold3 (subscription) for digitized military records at https://www.fold3.com/

### Cemetery records
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave.com covers many Pulaski County cemeteries — https://www.findagrave.com/
- **Physical records:** Sexton records vary by cemetery; local historical and genealogical societies may hold transcriptions

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Somerset was the county seat; local newspapers were published there during the period, though specific titles and date ranges were not returned by tools
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (subscription) for digitized papers at https://www.newspapers.com/; Kentucky Historical Society may hold microfilm
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, estate sale notices, legal notices, sheriff's sale advertisements

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Pulaski County is inland (southeastern Kentucky); immigrants who settled here typically arrived via East Coast ports (Baltimore, New York, Philadelphia) or overland through Cumberland Gap via the Wilderness Road
- **Record types:** Passenger lists at NARA and Ancestry/FamilySearch for port arrivals; naturalization records at the Pulaski County Circuit Court (pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record)
- **Where held:** NARA, https://www.archives.gov/; Ancestry (subscription)
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents; examine the full manifest when researching a family

### Tax records
- **Types:** Property tax lists, personal property tax
- **Date range:** From county formation; tax lists exist throughout 1840–1880 and serve as annual substitutes for census records between enumerations
- **Where held:** County courthouse; KDLA; some microfilm at the FamilySearch Library
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists fill gaps between census years and may identify men who do not appear elsewhere in surviving records

### Other record types
- **Freedmen's Bureau records (1865–1872):** Cover formerly enslaved persons and freedpeople in Pulaski County; held at NARA; searchable at FamilySearch

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Kentucky Church Records 1818–1995; Kentucky Births and Christenings 1839–1960; Kentucky Marriages 1785–1979; Kentucky Deaths and Burials 1843–1970; Kentucky Land Office records 1700–1955 | Pre-registration vital events; land grants; church records | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection; Kentucky land grants | Census records 1840–1880; land records | Subscription — https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/ |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records for Pulaski County | Burial dates and places not in civil death records | Free — https://www.findagrave.com/ |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers | Obituaries, marriage notices, legal notices not in vital records | Subscription — https://www.newspapers.com/ |
| Fold3 | Military records | Civil War service and pension; Mexican-American War records | Subscription — https://www.fold3.com/ |
| NARA | National Archives holdings | Passenger lists, military records, naturalizations, Freedmen's Bureau | In-person / online request — https://www.archives.gov/ |

**Coverage of this survey:** FamilySearch volume and collection search tools returned 0 results for both Pulaski County and the state of Kentucky, and the FamilySearch catalog returned 0 hits at both levels. This likely reflects an authentication limitation rather than a genuine absence of digitized records. Researchers should log into FamilySearch directly to search its full holdings.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Pulaski County Courthouse, Somerset, KY | Marriage bonds and licenses from 1798; deed books; probate and court records | In-person / mail |
| Kentucky Dept. for Libraries and Archives (KDLA), Frankfort | Pre-1911 county vital records; microfilmed county records | In-person / online catalog |
| Kentucky Historical Society, Frankfort | Manuscripts, newspapers, genealogical collections, church records | In-person / online catalog |
| Kentucky Land Office, Frankfort | Land grants, warrants, surveys, patents from 1773 | In-person / some online |
| University of Kentucky Special Collections, Lexington | Manuscript collections, local histories | In-person |

## Records NOT online
- County marriage bonds and licenses (the physical originals remain at the Pulaski County Courthouse; FamilySearch's marriage index is partial)
- County deed books
- County court minute books
- Probate estate files and inventories
- Tax lists (not confirmed as digitized online for Pulaski County by any tool result)
- Local newspaper runs (physical holdings at Kentucky Historical Society or Pulaski County Public Library)

## Known record losses
No tool result returned specific information about courthouse fires or record losses for Pulaski County. Researchers should contact the Pulaski County Courthouse and KDLA to verify what survives; Kentucky Civil War–era county records are sometimes incomplete.

## Research tips
- Kentucky's civil vital registration was sporadic and poorly complied with before 1911; the three registration windows (1853–1862, 1874–1878, 1892–1910) cover only parts of the 1840–1880 target period, and many events were simply never registered. Treat church records, census records, and obituaries as the primary sources for births and deaths. (Kentucky Vital Records wiki page, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky_Vital_Records)
- Records predating 1798 are held by Lincoln and Green counties — search both parent counties if tracing ancestors back before Pulaski County's formation.
- Kentucky is a state-land state: there are no BLM General Land Office patents here; instead search the Kentucky Land Office (Frankfort) and FamilySearch's Kentucky Land Office collection (1700–1955). (Kentucky Land and Property wiki page, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky_Land_and_Property)
- The largest denominations in pre-1900 Kentucky were Baptist, Methodist, Roman Catholic, and Presbyterian; begin with Baptist and Methodist registers for rural southeastern Kentucky ancestors whose church affiliation is unknown. (Kentucky Church Records wiki page, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky_Church_Records)
- The 1880 federal census records each person's relationship to the head of household — use it to reconstruct families before working backward through 1870, 1860, and 1850.
- Mortality schedules (1850–1880) can confirm a death year just before each census date, filling gaps left by Kentucky's incomplete death registration.

## Original Christ Church Marriage Register, Philadelphia, 1734

**Where the original is held:**

Christ Church remains an active congregation, and the FamilySearch Wiki on Pennsylvania Church Records states clearly that for active Episcopal parishes, the original registers stay with the church itself. The original 1734 marriage register is therefore held by **Christ Church**, located at:

> **20 N. American Street, Philadelphia, PA 19106**

---

Contact the church's archive staff directly. As one of colonial America's most historically prominent churches, Christ Church has long maintained its own archives and regularly assists researchers. You would need to inquire about:
- Whether the 1734 register survives and its condition
- Visiting hours and appointment requirements for in-person viewing

---

**What to avoid confusing with the original:**

The **Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP)** holds abstracts drawn from various Pennsylvania church records — including Christ Church — but those are derivative transcriptions, not the original registers. FamilySearch's indexed collection "Pennsylvania, HSP, Marriages (1512–1989)" draws on those same abstracts. These can help you identify the specific entry you want, but they are not the document you're asking about.

---

**Bottom line:** To see the original 1734 marriage register in the hand it was written, contact Christ Church Philadelphia directly to arrange access.

Here is the locality guide for pre-statehood Alabama (~1800):

---

## Alabama Region, ca. 1800 — Locality & Repository Guide

### Jurisdictional Context
Researching an ancestor in what is now Alabama around 1800 means working under the **Mississippi Territory** (established 1798). Alabama did not become its own territory until 1817 or a state until December 1819. The **Mobile coastal zone** was under **Spanish colonial administration** until 1813, so records for anyone there before that date may be held in Seville, Spain or Paris, with copies at the Library of Congress. For the interior settler population, the records landscape is quite different.

---

### Key Record Types and Repositories

| Record Type | Availability | Repository |
|---|---|---|
| Territorial census lists | 1801, 1805, 1808, 1810 | Alabama Dept. of Archives and History (ADAH); FamilySearch images |
| County marriage records | From 1809 onward | ADAH; county courthouses |
| Church records | From ca. 1803 onward | ADAH; denominational archives |
| County probate & deed books | Early territorial period | ADAH; county probate courts |
| Federal land patents | Territorial period onward | Bureau of Land Management (BLM) GLO Records |
| Spanish colonial records (Mobile) | Pre-1813 | Archivo General de Indias (Seville); Library of Congress |

> **Note:** No civil registration of births or deaths existed in this period. Vital events must be inferred from church registers, estate inventories, census lists, and family bibles.

---

### Primary Archives & Finding Resources

1. **Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH), Montgomery**
   The central repository for Alabama territorial and early statehood records. Holds county deed books, probate records, early census transcripts, and military records for the territorial militia.

2. **FamilySearch.org**
   Digitized images of many Alabama county records are available, though many early records are unindexed and must be browsed image by image. Start with the [Alabama Genealogy wiki page](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy) for current collection guidance.

3. **Bureau of Land Management – GLO Records (glorecords.blm.gov)**
   Federal land patents issued to early settlers in the Mississippi Territory / Alabama Territory are searchable here and are often the first documentary trace of a settler family.

4. **Library of Congress**
   Holds transcribed copies of Spanish colonial records for the Mobile district.

5. **Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain**
   Original Spanish colonial records for the Mobile/Gulf Coast zone predating 1813.

# Locality Guide: Alabama Region (Pre-Statehood, ca. 1795–1820)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** The Alabama Territory was formed in 1817 from the eastern half of the Mississippi Territory, which was itself established in 1798. Alabama achieved statehood on December 14, 1819.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Territorial capital: St. Stephens (Washington County). First state capital: Huntsville, then Cahaba.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Mississippi Territory (1798–1817) → Alabama Territory (1817–1819) → State of Alabama (1819–)
- **Population during period:** No population data returned by tools for this period; the 1810 federal census is the first to enumerate present-day Alabama counties.
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, hunting, early cotton cultivation in river valleys; trade with Native American nations (Creek, Cherokee).
- **Ethnic composition:** Anglo-American settlers from the Carolinas, Virginia, and Georgia arriving after c. 1800; Creek and Cherokee populations throughout the interior; French/Spanish/African Creole community in the Mobile area.
- **Religious denominations:** Methodist circuit riders, Baptist congregations in settler areas; Roman Catholic parishes centered in Mobile from French colonial founding c. 1702.
- **Key historical events:** Creek War of 1813–1814 disrupted settlement and opened vast new territory; Mobile seized from Spain by U.S. forces in 1813; cotton boom after 1814 brought rapid in-migration.

## Boundary changes
- Before 1798: The northern interior was not under U.S. administration; the Mobile area was part of Spanish West Florida.
- 1798: The Mississippi Territory was established from land ceded by Georgia and Spain, covering a narrow strip, expanded in 1804 and again in 1812 to the full area of present-day Mississippi and Alabama.
- 1813: Mobile and the coastal zone were seized from Spain and incorporated into the U.S.
- 1817: The Mississippi Territory was divided — the western half became the state of Mississippi; the eastern half was organized as the Alabama Territory.
- 1819: Alabama became a state (December 14).
- Records created before 1817 were generated under the Mississippi Territory; before 1813 in the Mobile area, under Spanish colonial administration. Search under 'Mississippi Territory' in pre-1817 indexes.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No statewide civil registration of vital events existed during this period. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Alabama vital records returned only generic content and do not state an Alabama-specific registration start year for this survey; consult the Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH) directly.
- **What exists:** The earliest county marriage records in FamilySearch collection 1598408 ('Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950,' 612,345 records, 1,224,690 persons, 306,172 images) begin in 1809, covering only counties organized by that date.
- **Where held:** County courthouses for post-1809 marriage bonds and licenses; FamilySearch collection 1598408 (free, indexed + images from 1809).
- **Gaps:** No civil birth or death registration in this period. Marriage records before 1809 are absent from digital collections or held only in physical repositories.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism, marriage, and burial registers; estate inventories naming heirs; territorial census enumerations; tax lists.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (Mobile area, continuous since French colonial founding c. 1702); Methodist and Baptist circuit congregations emerging in settler areas after c. 1800.
- **Record types:** Catholic baptisms, marriages, and burials from Mobile parishes; Protestant congregational records (scattered and sparse before 1810).
- **Where held:** Catholic records held at the Archdiocese of Mobile and partially at the Mobile Municipal Archives; FamilySearch collection 1986396 ('Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950,' 156,789 records, 78,394 images) covers Protestant and some Catholic records from 1803 — indexed + images.
- **Gaps:** Protestant church records in rural settler areas before c. 1810 are sparse or non-surviving. Mobile Catholic registers from the Spanish period (pre-1813) may be in Seville (see Colonial records below).
- **Language:** Mobile-area colonial church records may be in French (pre-1763) or Spanish (1780–1813).

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** The 1810 federal census is the earliest to enumerate settlers in present-day Alabama counties. No federal census covered the Alabama region in 1800.
- **Territorial censuses:** The Mississippi Territory conducted enumerations in 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810 covering the present-day Alabama area. These are held at the Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH) in Montgomery (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records). Physical access only for pre-1810 enumerations.
- **State/provincial census:** None during the territorial period.
- **Other enumerations:** Tax lists (see Tax records) function as annual substitutes.
- **Access:** FamilySearch collection 2016756 ('Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890,' 287,634 records, index only, no images) covers substitutes from 1810 onward — name-indexed, no images. Pre-1810 territorial censuses at ADAH are physical only.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, petitions; territorial court records.
- **Date range:** From county formation; Washington County (formed 1800) is the earliest organized county. FamilySearch collection 1537764 ('Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985,' 438,210 records, 219,105 images) starts in 1809.
- **Where held:** County courthouses; FamilySearch collection 1537764 (indexed + images from 1809); FamilySearch volume 004512889 (214 images, territorial court and land records 1808–1819, browse-only); volume 004512890 (96 images, Washington County deed and probate records 1803–1820, browse-only).
- **Access:** Collection 1537764 — indexed + images. Volumes 004512889 and 004512890 — browse-only images; must be examined image by image with no name search.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Rectangular survey (federal public-land state). Land was distributed under federal authority after U.S. acquisition from Native nations through treaties.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The federal General Land Office issued original patents; records are at the Bureau of Land Management GLO website (glorecords.blm.gov, free, online). The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Alabama land records returned only generic content and do not confirm specific land district names for this survey.
- **Types:** Federal land patents/grants; county deed books (after county formation); Spanish and British colonial grants in the Mobile area (pre-1813).
- **Date range:** Federal land sales in Alabama began in earnest after Creek cessions, chiefly post-1805 and especially post-1814. FamilySearch volume 004512889 covers territorial court and land records 1808–1819.
- **Where held:** Federal patents: BLM GLO website (free, online). County deeds: county courthouses and FamilySearch volume 004512890 (Washington County, 1803–1820, browse-only). Colonial grants: see Colonial records below.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Creek War of 1813–1814 (U.S. Army and Tennessee militia); War of 1812 (Battle of Mobile, 1813); territorial militia rolls from before 1813.
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty-land warrants at NARA; militia muster rolls at ADAH; some records on Fold3.com.
- **Where held:** NARA (archives.gov, some free online); Fold3 (fold3.com, subscription); ADAH (Montgomery, in-person).

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Church graveyards attached to early Methodist and Baptist congregations; Catholic cemeteries in Mobile (continuous from colonial period).
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (findagrave.com) covers many Alabama cemeteries; coverage for rural pre-1820 burials is limited.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records for rural early 19th-century cemeteries are sparse; gravestone transcription projects through the Alabama Genealogical Society may supplement.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Mobile area had early newspapers in the territorial period; interior Alabama had little press before the 1810s.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (subscription) covers some Alabama titles; ADAH holds physical microfilm.
- **Content value:** Legal notices (estate settlements, land sales), migration notices; formal obituaries are uncommon in this period.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Mobile (Gulf Coast) was the main entry for maritime arrivals. Most settlers arrived overland from the Carolinas, Georgia, and Virginia and left no immigration record.
- **Record types:** No formal immigration records for most overland settlers. Pre-1906 naturalizations for foreign-born residents can appear in any court of record — check territorial and early county court minutes (volume 004512889).
- **Where held:** NARA (archives.gov) holds passenger lists for Mobile port arrivals. FamilySearch volume 004512889 (territorial court records 1808–1819) may include early naturalization proceedings.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Territorial and county property and poll tax lists.
- **Date range:** From county formation; some territorial tax records survive from before 1817.
- **Where held:** ADAH; county courthouses; FamilySearch collection 2016756 ('Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890') includes some tax-list substitutes.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists substitute for missing census years and document presence year by year — particularly valuable for the 1800–1810 gap before the first federal census.

### Colonial records (pre-American period)
- **Mobile area (French 1702–1763; British 1763–1780; Spanish 1780–1813):** French colonial records are at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer in Aix-en-Provence (France), with microfilm copies at the Mobile Municipal Archives. Spanish records of the Mobile District include census returns, church registers, and land grants held at the Archivo General de Indias in Seville (Spain), with copies at the Library of Congress (Washington, D.C.). Source: FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records).
- **Language:** French (pre-1763) and Spanish (1780–1813).

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (familysearch.org) | Collection 1598408 (County Marriages 1809–1950); Collection 1537764 (Probate Records 1809–1985); Collection 2016756 (Census Substitutes 1810–1890); Collection 1986396 (Church Records 1803–1950); Volumes 004512889 and 004512890 (browse-only territorial/county records 1803–1820) | County marriages, probate, church records, census substitutes, territorial land/court records | Free |
| BLM GLO (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents for Alabama | Original federal land grants; no county deed equivalent online | Free |
| Ancestry.com (ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | U.S. Federal Census Collection | 1810 and later federal census for Alabama | Subscription |
| Fold3 (fold3.com) | Military Records | Creek War and War of 1812 service records, pension files | Subscription |
| Find A Grave (findagrave.com) | Cemetery Records | Gravestone transcriptions for Alabama cemeteries | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | National Archives holdings | Mobile port passenger lists; federal military/pension records; pre-1906 naturalizations | Free / In-person |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned a total of 2 digitized volumes matching Alabama, 1780–1820; both are shown above. This is the complete set returned for the period.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH), Montgomery | Mississippi Territory censuses 1801, 1805, 1808, 1810; territorial legislative records; colonial record copies; militia rolls; newspapers | In-person; some holdings online at adah.alabama.gov |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence, France | French colonial records for the Mobile area (1702–1763) | In-person or written inquiry; microfilm copies at Mobile Municipal Archives |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Spanish colonial records for the Mobile District (1780–1813): census, church registers, land grants | In-person or written inquiry; copies at Library of Congress |
| Library of Congress, Washington, D.C. | Copies of Spanish colonial records for the Mobile District | In-person; some digitized holdings online |
| Mobile Municipal Archives, Mobile, AL | Microfilm of French colonial records; local Mobile city records | In-person |
| County courthouses (Washington County org. 1800; Madison, Baldwin, etc. organized shortly after) | Deed books, probate files, court minutes from county formation | In-person; some volumes on FamilySearch |

## Records NOT online
- Mississippi Territory censuses for 1801, 1805, and 1808 — held only at ADAH.
- Spanish and French colonial church registers and land grants (original documents) — held in Seville and Aix-en-Provence; Library of Congress has some copies.
- County court minutes and territorial legislative records other than what appears in FamilySearch volume 004512889.
- Early Baptist and Methodist congregational registers (rural areas, pre-1810) — held by individual churches or the Alabama Baptist State Convention archives if they survive.

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey states that specific record sets for pre-statehood Alabama were destroyed or lost. The sparse digitization and near-absence of indexed records for this period reflect low settlement density, limited government record-keeping, and incomplete digitization — not necessarily destruction. For any specific county or record type, contact ADAH directly to confirm survival and location.

## Research tips
- For events before 1817, search under 'Mississippi Territory' — many indexes and catalogs file these records under that name rather than 'Alabama.' (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records)
- The Mississippi Territory censuses of 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810 at ADAH are the closest equivalent to census records for this period; FamilySearch collection 2016756 provides an index from 1810 onward.
- If the ancestor was near Mobile, look first at the colonial record series (Spain and France) and the Mobile Municipal Archives before assuming no records exist.
- Alabama is a federal land state: search the BLM GLO site (glorecords.blm.gov) for original patents before searching county deed books.
- The two browse-only FamilySearch volumes covering 1803–1820 (004512889 and 004512890) must be examined image by image — there is no name index.
- The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Alabama (all four research-guide sections and several topic pages) returned only generic content during this survey; consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy directly for the latest Alabama-specific guidance.
- A negative online search result does not mean the record does not exist — much of this period's material is undigitized and held only at ADAH, county courthouses, or European archives.

---

**Arkansas (Spanish Louisiana), Pre-1800 — Locality Research Guide**

The area that is now Arkansas was part of the **Spanish Province of Louisiana** from 1763 to 1800, administered from New Orleans, with **Arkansas Post** as the only permanent European settlement in the region. The records that survive fall into three main categories:

### Available Record Types

1. **Catholic Sacramental Registers** (baptisms, marriages, burials)
   - FamilySearch has digitized one volume of Arkansas Post sacramental registers covering **1763–1800** (image group 008814402, 64 images). These are in Spanish, unindexed, and must be browsed page by page.

2. **Spanish Colonial Household Census Lists (Padrones)**
   - Physical copies held at the **Arkansas History Commission** (Little Rock) and the **Archivo General de Indias** (Seville, Spain), which is the primary archive for Spanish colonial records worldwide.
   - The **Library of Congress** holds microfilm copies of some colonial Louisiana material.

3. **Land Concession Documents**
   - Also held at the Arkansas History Commission and the Archivo General de Indias.

### An Important Secondary Source: US Land Claims

After 1803, families with pre-existing Spanish land claims filed petitions with US land commissioners. Those **NARA claim files** often name earlier family members and document colonial-era residence — making them a valuable indirect source for pre-1800 research.

### Language Note

All records from this period are in **French, Spanish, or Latin**, so translation will be a necessary step in your research.

---

### Recommended Next Steps

1. **Browse the FamilySearch digitized volume** (image group 008814402) for Arkansas Post sacramental registers (1763–1800).
2. **Contact the Arkansas History Commission** to inquire about colonial padrones and land concessions that may name your ancestors.
3. Consider searching **NARA post-1803 Spanish land claim files** for family mentions that reach back into the colonial period.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Arkansas (Spanish Colonial Period, 1763–1800)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** The area that is now Arkansas was not a distinct jurisdiction before 1800. Under the Treaty of Paris (1763), France ceded the territory west of the Mississippi to Spain. It was administered as part of the Province of Louisiana (Luisiana), a dependency of the Captaincy General of Cuba under the Viceroyalty of New Spain.
- **Administrative center:** New Orleans (provincial seat); Arkansas Post served as the local military and civil outpost for the region
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Province of Louisiana, Viceroyalty of New Spain
- **Population during period:** Very sparse European settlement, concentrated at Arkansas Post; no population figures for this period were returned from tools
- **Economy:** Fur trade, subsistence farming, military garrison supply
- **Ethnic composition:** French Creole settlers, Spanish soldiers and officials, and Native American tribes — principally the Quapaw, with Osage and others in the broader region
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic; French Franciscan missionaries and later secular clergy served Arkansas Post from 1686 onward
- **Key historical events:** Spain took formal possession of Louisiana in 1769; Arkansas Post was briefly threatened during the American Revolutionary War (1783); Spain secretly retroceded Louisiana to France in 1800; the United States acquired the territory via the Louisiana Purchase in 1803

## Boundary changes
- Before 1763: French La Louisiane
- 1763–1800: Spanish Province of Louisiana (Luisiana) — the target period
- 1800–1803: French Louisiana (brief retrocession before the Purchase)
- 1803: Louisiana Purchase; the region entered the District of Louisiana, then Missouri Territory (1812), then Arkansas Territory (1819), and finally statehood in 1836
- **Records from the 1763–1800 period belong to the Spanish Province of Louisiana's administrative chain, not to any Arkansas civil jurisdiction. County-level searching will not locate them.**

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil registration existed in this region during the Spanish colonial period. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Arkansas Vital Records returned only generic content and gave no jurisdiction-specific start date for Arkansas.
- **What exists:** None for 1763–1800
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Catholic sacramental registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) are the primary and in most cases sole source for vital events before civil registration

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (French Franciscan missionaries and later secular clergy; the only Christian denomination with a documented presence at Arkansas Post during this period)
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, and burials of European settlers and Native Americans; sacramental forms in Latin, registers in Spanish and French
- **Where held:** FamilySearch holds 1 digitized volume (image group 008814402, 64 images) covering Arkansas Post sacramental registers, date range 1763–1800 — browse-only images, 0% name-indexed, records in Spanish. Per the [Arkansas Genealogy — Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Church_Records) article on the FamilySearch Wiki, the Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock and the Arkansas History Commission also hold surviving registers.
- **Gaps:** Records from the French period before 1763 and gaps within the Spanish period reflect both losses and the small size of the European population

### Census records
- **Spanish colonial padrones:** Spanish administrators conducted periodic household censuses (padrones) of colonial settlements, listing heads of household and family members. Per the [Arkansas Genealogy — Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records) article, surviving padrones for the Arkansas Post area are held at the Arkansas History Commission, the Archivo General de Indias in Seville, Spain, and in microfilm at the Library of Congress. No FamilySearch digitized collection covers Arkansas padrones for 1763–1800.
- **Post-1800 coverage:** The earliest FamilySearch census collection for Arkansas is "Arkansas, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1819-1870" (collection 2085124), beginning with territorial-era enumerations after 1819 — outside the Spanish period.
- **Access:** Padrones are microfilm or physical only; contact the Arkansas History Commission or the Library of Congress Manuscript Division

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Informal civil proceedings and military court matters at Arkansas Post under Spanish colonial law
- **Date range:** 1763–1800
- **Where held:** Any surviving records would be at the Arkansas History Commission (Little Rock) or in the Spanish colonial archives at the Archivo General de Indias. No FamilySearch digitized collection covers this record type for this period.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Spanish land concessions (grants issued by the Governor of Louisiana in New Orleans on behalf of the Spanish Crown)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Spanish Crown, administered through the Governor of Louisiana. The FamilySearch Wiki page for Arkansas Land and Property returned only generic content and named no specific Arkansas repository for originals.
- **Types:** Land concessions (colonial grants) and post-1803 US adjudication files for Spanish-era claims
- **Where held:** Per the [Arkansas Genealogy — Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records) article, land concession records are at the Arkansas History Commission. After 1803, Spanish land claims were submitted to US land commissioners; those claim files are at NARA and frequently document pre-1803 family relationships and residence.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** American Revolutionary War (Spain allied with France; Arkansas Post area affected 1779–1783); general garrison duty throughout the Spanish period
- **Record types:** Garrison muster rolls, officer correspondence, and service records for the Arkansas Post garrison
- **Where held:** Spanish military records for Louisiana are primarily at the Archivo General de Indias, Seville. Some microfilm copies may be at the Library of Congress. NARA holds post-1803 US territorial military records.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Catholic burial grounds at Arkansas Post (present-day Arkansas Post National Memorial, Arkansas County)
- **Online coverage:** No specific indexed coverage for this period was returned from tools. Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) may carry later transcriptions of some markers.
- **Physical records:** Burial entries appear in the sacramental registers rather than in separate sexton books for this period

### Newspaper records
- No newspapers were published in the Arkansas region during the Spanish colonial period. This record type does not apply to 1763–1800.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant routes:** French and Spanish settlers arrived via the Mississippi River from New Orleans and from Illinois country to the north; some from the Caribbean
- **Record types:** No formal passenger manifests or immigration registers exist for internal colonial movement during this period. Movement of settlers was tracked in military correspondence and land concession applications.
- **Where held:** Archivo General de Indias and the Arkansas History Commission, per the Colonial Records article cited above

### Tax records
- **Types:** Spanish colonial taxation (alcabala and related levies)
- **Date range:** 1763–1800
- **Where held:** Any surviving tax records for the Province of Louisiana would be in the Archivo General de Indias. No FamilySearch collection or digitized volume was returned for this record type and period.
- **Substitute value:** Padrones (census lists) partially substitute for tax records as proof of residence and household composition

### Other record types
- **Trade and commercial records:** Fur trade licenses and trading post records were maintained by Spanish colonial officials. Look in the Archivo General de Indias under the Louisiana (Luisiana) colonial series.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | 1 digitized volume (image group 008814402): Arkansas Post sacramental registers 1763–1800, 64 images, browse-only, in Spanish | The only digitized church records for the Spanish colonial period | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Post-1803 territorial records; Spanish land claim adjudication files | Documents pre-1803 residence and family for land claimants | Free catalog; some in-person |

**Coverage of this survey:** 1 digitized volume matches Arkansas for the 1763–1800 period; this was the complete result set returned by the volume search.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Arkansas History Commission, Little Rock | Colonial records including padrones, land concessions, and surviving post records | In-person or mail request; arkansasheritage.com |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Primary Spanish colonial records for Louisiana: military, civil, ecclesiastical | In-person; partial online catalog at culturaydeporte.gob.es |
| Library of Congress, Washington DC | Microfilm copies of colonial Louisiana records | In-person; some via loc.gov |
| Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock | Sacramental registers not held by FamilySearch | Contact diocese archives directly |

## Records NOT online
- Spanish colonial padrones (census lists) for Arkansas Post, 1763–1800
- Spanish land concession records
- Spanish military garrison records (muster rolls, officer correspondence)
- Civil proceedings and court records from the Arkansas Post era
- Pre-1803 trade and fur-trade licenses

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey specified the destruction or confirmed loss of any particular Arkansas colonial record set. The Arkansas History Commission is the first point of contact to determine which records survive; a gap in FamilySearch or other online databases is a coverage gap, not evidence of destruction.

## Research tips
- Arkansas Post is the focal point of all pre-1800 research in this region. The [Arkansas Genealogy — Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records) article states that surviving colonial records are at the Arkansas History Commission, the Archivo General de Indias in Seville, and in microfilm at the Library of Congress.
- The administrative chain ran from Arkansas Post → New Orleans (provincial capital) → Havana (Captaincy General) → Spain. When local records are missing, search the next level up — Louisiana colonial records in New Orleans repositories (such as the Louisiana State Archives) often document Arkansas Post inhabitants.
- Records from the 1763–1800 period are in French and Spanish; sacramental forms use Latin. A translator or reading knowledge of those languages is required before you can use the original registers.
- After the Louisiana Purchase (1803), families with pre-1803 land claims filed petitions with US land commissioners. These claim files at NARA often name earlier generations and document pre-1803 residence, making them a productive bridge between colonial and American-era records.
- The single FamilySearch digitized volume of Arkansas Post sacramental registers (image group 008814402, 1763–1800) must be browsed image by image with no name index and no full-text search — allow extra time and work through the register sequentially.
- All four Arkansas-specific FamilySearch Wiki place pages returned only generic content during this survey. For the most current Arkansas-specific guidance, consult the Arkansas Genealogy article directly at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy.

added.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Arkansas (Spanish Colonial Period, 1763–1800)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** The area that is now Arkansas was not a distinct jurisdiction before 1800. Under the Treaty of Paris (1763), France ceded the territory west of the Mississippi to Spain. It was administered as part of the Province of Louisiana (Luisiana), a dependency of the Captaincy General of Cuba under the Viceroyalty of New Spain.
- **Administrative center:** New Orleans (provincial seat); Arkansas Post served as the local military and civil outpost for the region
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Province of Louisiana, Viceroyalty of New Spain
- **Population during period:** Very sparse European settlement, concentrated at Arkansas Post; no population figures for this period were returned from tools
- **Economy:** Fur trade, subsistence farming, military garrison supply
- **Ethnic composition:** French Creole settlers, Spanish soldiers and officials, and Native American tribes — principally the Quapaw, with Osage and others in the broader region
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic; French Franciscan missionaries and later secular clergy served Arkansas Post from 1686 onward
- **Key historical events:** Spain took formal possession of Louisiana in 1769; Arkansas Post was briefly threatened during the American Revolutionary War (1783); Spain secretly retroceded Louisiana to France in 1800; the United States acquired the territory via the Louisiana Purchase in 1803

## Boundary changes
- Before 1763: French La Louisiane
- 1763–1800: Spanish Province of Louisiana (Luisiana) — the target period
- 1800–1803: French Louisiana (brief retrocession before the Purchase)
- 1803: Louisiana Purchase; the region entered the District of Louisiana, then Missouri Territory (1812), then Arkansas Territory (1819), and finally statehood in 1836
- **Records from the 1763–1800 period belong to the Spanish Province of Louisiana's administrative chain, not to any Arkansas civil jurisdiction. County-level searching will not locate them.**

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil registration existed in this region during the Spanish colonial period. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Arkansas Vital Records returned only generic content and gave no jurisdiction-specific start date for Arkansas.
- **What exists:** None for 1763–1800
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Catholic sacramental registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) are the primary and in most cases sole source for vital events before civil registration

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (French Franciscan missionaries and later secular clergy; the only Christian denomination with a documented presence at Arkansas Post during this period)
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, and burials of European settlers and Native Americans; sacramental forms in Latin, registers in Spanish and French
- **Where held:** FamilySearch holds 1 digitized volume (image group 008814402, 64 images) covering Arkansas Post sacramental registers, date range 1763–1800 — browse-only images, 0% name-indexed, records in Spanish. Per the [Arkansas Genealogy — Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Church_Records) article on the FamilySearch Wiki, the Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock and the Arkansas History Commission also hold surviving registers.
- **Gaps:** Records from the French period before 1763 and gaps within the Spanish period reflect both losses and the small size of the European population

### Census records
- **Spanish colonial padrones:** Spanish administrators conducted periodic household censuses (padrones) of colonial settlements, listing heads of household and family members. Per the [Arkansas Genealogy — Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records) article, surviving padrones for the Arkansas Post area are held at the Arkansas History Commission, the Archivo General de Indias in Seville, Spain, and in microfilm at the Library of Congress. No FamilySearch digitized collection covers Arkansas padrones for 1763–1800.
- **Post-1800 coverage:** The earliest FamilySearch census collection for Arkansas is "Arkansas, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1819-1870" (collection 2085124), beginning with territorial-era enumerations after 1819 — outside the Spanish period.
- **Access:** Padrones are microfilm or physical only; contact the Arkansas History Commission or the Library of Congress Manuscript Division

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Informal civil proceedings and military court matters at Arkansas Post under Spanish colonial law
- **Date range:** 1763–1800
- **Where held:** Any surviving records would be at the Arkansas History Commission (Little Rock) or in the Spanish colonial archives at the Archivo General de Indias. No FamilySearch digitized collection covers this record type for this period.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Spanish land concessions (grants issued by the Governor of Louisiana in New Orleans on behalf of the Spanish Crown)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Spanish Crown, administered through the Governor of Louisiana. The FamilySearch Wiki page for Arkansas Land and Property returned only generic content and named no specific Arkansas repository for originals.
- **Types:** Land concessions (colonial grants) and post-1803 US adjudication files for Spanish-era claims
- **Where held:** Per the [Arkansas Genealogy — Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records) article, land concession records are at the Arkansas History Commission. After 1803, Spanish land claims were submitted to US land commissioners; those claim files are at NARA and frequently document pre-1803 family relationships and residence.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** American Revolutionary War (Spain allied with France; Arkansas Post area affected 1779–1783); general garrison duty throughout the Spanish period
- **Record types:** Garrison muster rolls, officer correspondence, and service records for the Arkansas Post garrison
- **Where held:** Spanish military records for Louisiana are primarily at the Archivo General de Indias, Seville. Some microfilm copies may be at the Library of Congress. NARA holds post-1803 US territorial military records.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Catholic burial grounds at Arkansas Post (present-day Arkansas Post National Memorial, Arkansas County)
- **Online coverage:** No specific indexed coverage for this period was returned from tools. Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) may carry later transcriptions of some markers.
- **Physical records:** Burial entries appear in the sacramental registers rather than in separate sexton books for this period

### Newspaper records
- No newspapers were published in the Arkansas region during the Spanish colonial period. This record type does not apply to 1763–1800.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant routes:** French and Spanish settlers arrived via the Mississippi River from New Orleans and from Illinois country to the north; some from the Caribbean
- **Record types:** No formal passenger manifests or immigration registers exist for internal colonial movement during this period. Movement of settlers was tracked in military correspondence and land concession applications.
- **Where held:** Archivo General de Indias and the Arkansas History Commission, per the Colonial Records article cited above

### Tax records
- **Types:** Spanish colonial taxation (alcabala and related levies)
- **Date range:** 1763–1800
- **Where held:** Any surviving tax records for the Province of Louisiana would be in the Archivo General de Indias. No FamilySearch collection or digitized volume was returned for this record type and period.
- **Substitute value:** Padrones (census lists) partially substitute for tax records as proof of residence and household composition

### Other record types
- **Trade and commercial records:** Fur trade licenses and trading post records were maintained by Spanish colonial officials. Look in the Archivo General de Indias under the Louisiana (Luisiana) colonial series.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | 1 digitized volume (image group 008814402): Arkansas Post sacramental registers 1763–1800, 64 images, browse-only, in Spanish | The only digitized church records for the Spanish colonial period | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Post-1803 territorial records; Spanish land claim adjudication files | Documents pre-1803 residence and family for land claimants | Free catalog; some in-person |

**Coverage of this survey:** 1 digitized volume matches Arkansas for the 1763–1800 period; this was the complete result set returned by the volume search.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Arkansas History Commission, Little Rock | Colonial records including padrones, land concessions, and surviving post records | In-person or mail request; arkansasheritage.com |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Primary Spanish colonial records for Louisiana: military, civil, ecclesiastical | In-person; partial online catalog at culturaydeporte.gob.es |
| Library of Congress, Washington DC | Microfilm copies of colonial Louisiana records | In-person; some via loc.gov |
| Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock | Sacramental registers not held by FamilySearch | Contact diocese archives directly |

## Records NOT online
- Spanish colonial padrones (census lists) for Arkansas Post, 1763–1800
- Spanish land concession records
- Spanish military garrison records (muster rolls, officer correspondence)
- Civil proceedings and court records from the Arkansas Post era
- Pre-1803 trade and fur-trade licenses

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey specified the destruction or confirmed loss of any particular Arkansas colonial record set. The Arkansas History Commission is the first point of contact to determine which records survive; a gap in FamilySearch or other online databases is a coverage gap, not evidence of destruction.

## Research tips
- Arkansas Post is the focal point of all pre-1800 research in this region. The [Arkansas Genealogy — Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records) article states that surviving colonial records are at the Arkansas History Commission, the Archivo General de Indias in Seville, and in microfilm at the Library of Congress.
- The administrative chain ran from Arkansas Post → New Orleans (provincial capital) → Havana (Captaincy General) → Spain. When local records are missing, search the next level up — Louisiana colonial records in New Orleans repositories (such as the Louisiana State Archives) often document Arkansas Post inhabitants.
- Records from the 1763–1800 period are in French and Spanish; sacramental forms use Latin. A translator or reading knowledge of those languages is required before you can use the original registers.
- After the Louisiana Purchase (1803), families with pre-1803 land claims filed petitions with US land commissioners. These claim files at NARA often name earlier generations and document pre-1803 residence, making them a productive bridge between colonial and American-era records.
- The single FamilySearch digitized volume of Arkansas Post sacramental registers (image group 008814402, 1763–1800) must be browsed image by image with no name index and no full-text search — allow extra time and work through the register sequentially.
- All four Arkansas-specific FamilySearch Wiki place pages returned only generic content during this survey. For the most current Arkansas-specific guidance, consult the Arkansas Genealogy article directly at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy.

### Jurisdictional / Boundary History

Two areas of Ohio used *different survey systems* and their records sit in **different repositories**, not Ohio archives:

1. **Virginia Military District** → Records held at the **Virginia State Library**
2. **Connecticut Western Reserve** → Records held at the **Western Reserve Historical Society**

# Locality Guide: Ohio (Northwest Territory Period, ca. 1785–1803)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** The Northwest Territory was established by the Northwest Ordinance of 1787, covering the region north of the Ohio River and east of the Mississippi. Ohio achieved statehood on 1 March 1803 as the 17th state.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Marietta (Washington County seat, est. 1788); Cincinnati (Hamilton County seat, est. 1790)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Northwest Territory (federal, under Congress), 1787–1803
- **Population during period:** Population figures for the territorial period could not be retrieved from the tool query.
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, fur trade, military settlement; early town development at Marietta (1788) and Cincinnati (1788)
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly Anglo-American settlers from Virginia, Pennsylvania, New England, and New Jersey; small numbers of French traders; Native American populations (Shawnee, Delaware, Wyandot, Miami)
- **Religious denominations:** Methodist, Presbyterian, Baptist, Congregationalist (brought by New England settlers to the Connecticut Western Reserve), some German Reformed congregations
- **Key historical events:** Northwest Ordinance (1787); founding of Marietta (1788) as first permanent American settlement; establishment of Washington County (1788) and Hamilton County (1790); Northwest Indian War (1785–1795); Treaty of Greenville (1795) opened interior to safer settlement

## Boundary changes
- **Before 1788:** No formal county government. All territorial administration was at the federal/territorial level from Marietta.
- **1788:** Washington County organized — the first county in the Northwest Territory, covering essentially all settled portions of present-day Ohio.
- **1790:** Hamilton County carved from Washington County, covering the southwestern settlements around Cincinnati. This is a geographic split: which county holds a record depends on where within the territory the event occurred — search both for any 1790 event whose location is uncertain.
- After 1790, additional counties were rapidly carved from Washington and Hamilton. Researchers must determine which county held jurisdiction at the specific time and place of each event. Early court and land records for the territorial period are held at the Ohio History Connection in Columbus ([Ohio Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Northwest_Territory)).

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil vital registration existed in the Northwest Territory in 1790. The FamilySearch Wiki Ohio Vital Records page returned only generic content during this survey — a specific statewide registration start year cannot be confirmed from tool results.
- **What exists:** No government-mandated vital record series for 1790.
- **Where held:** N/A for this period.
- **Gaps:** The entire period before Ohio statehood (1803) lacks civil vital registration.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (baptisms, marriages, burials) are the primary vital substitute. County marriage records begin as early as 1789 — FamilySearch holds indexed collection "Ohio, County Marriages, 1789–2013" (collection 1803785, 1,523,678 records, 3,047,356 persons).

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Methodist, Presbyterian, Baptist, Congregationalist (New England settlers in the Western Reserve), some German Reformed congregations among earliest settlers.
