# Locality Guide: California, United States (1848–1870)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** California gained statehood September 9, 1850, bypassing territorial status entirely (Wikipedia: California Gold Rush)
- **County seat / administrative center:** Sacramento (state capital from 1854)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Mexican territory until 1848 cession; U.S. state from September 1850
- **Population during period:** Approximately 300,000 migrants arrived during the Gold Rush (Wikipedia: California Gold Rush); no structured population table was returned by the population tool for this place
- **Economy:** Gold mining (1848–1855 peak), trade, agriculture; rapid urbanization around San Francisco and Sacramento
- **Ethnic composition:** Extraordinarily diverse — Americans from every state, Chinese, Chilean, Australian, European, and Pacific Islander miners; predominantly male and transient during the peak rush years
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (pre-statehood mission heritage); Protestant denominations (Methodist, Baptist, Presbyterian, Episcopal) arrived with American settlers from 1849
- **Key historical events:** Gold discovery January 24, 1848 at Sutter's Mill (Wikipedia); California statehood September 9, 1850; rapid county formation throughout the 1850s; Civil War (1861–1865) drew California volunteers

## Boundary changes
- California was admitted as a state in 1850, bypassing territorial status; there are no U.S. territorial-era records for the 1848–1850 gap
- Many counties were formed and their boundaries adjusted rapidly during the 1850s as mining camps grew into permanent settlements
- Pre-statehood records (1769–1848) were kept under Spanish colonial and then Mexican authority; mission records run through 1850 as secular parishes assumed record-keeping

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki California Vital Records page was not returned during this survey (the page redirected to generic content); a California-specific statewide registration start date cannot be confirmed from tool results in this run
- **What exists:** County birth records beginning 1850 in collection 2017276 "California, County Births, 1850-1919" (789,456 records); county marriage records beginning 1850 in collection 1452832 "California, County Marriages, 1850-1952" (567,890 records); no statewide death collection for this period was returned
- **Where held:** County courthouses; FamilySearch has indexed collections for births and marriages
- **Gaps:** No indexed death collection for the 1848–1870 period was returned; death records from this era may exist only at county courthouses or as church burial registers
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptismal and burial registers; California Mission Records (collection 1804372) for pre-1850 events

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (Franciscan missions through 1834, then secular parishes); Protestant denominations from 1849
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials (mission era 1769–1834); sacramental registers in secular Catholic parishes post-1834; Protestant congregation registers from the 1850s
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1804372 "California, Mission Records, 1769-1850" (98,765 records); diocese archives; California State Library
- **Gaps:** Protestant Gold Rush–era church records are not represented in the returned FamilySearch collections
- **Language:** Mission-era records are in Spanish

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1850 is the first federal census for California; the FamilySearch Wiki search result (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Pre-Statehood_Records) states the 1850 census was partially destroyed and some county returns are missing; 1860 and 1870 federal censuses follow
- **State census:** California State Census of 1852 is volume 006601001 (88% name-indexed, full-text searchable, 522 images) — the best substitute for missing 1850 county returns
- **Other enumerations:** Federal mortality schedules (1850–1880) record deaths in the census year and name the deceased
- **Access:** 1852 state census: indexed + images; 1850 federal census: varies by surviving county; 1860 and 1870 federal censuses: indexed + images on Ancestry and FamilySearch

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, guardianship files, letters of administration, naturalization petitions, civil suits
- **Date range:** From county formation (most counties 1850–1853)
- **Where held:** County courthouses; pre-1906 naturalizations can appear in any court of record — county, state superior, or federal district court
- **Note:** Naturalization declarations of intention were often filed in the nearest court of record; for Gold Rush immigrants, that was typically the county superior court in the mining county

### Land records
- **Survey system:** California is a public-land (federal land) state; a parallel Spanish/Mexican rancho grant system operated before 1848
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Federal land patents via the Bureau of Land Management General Land Office; Spanish/Mexican land grants confirmed by the U.S. Land Commission (est. 1851)
- **Types:** Federal land patents; Spanish/Mexican rancho grants; county deed books; mining claim registers
- **Date range:** Mining claim registers for San Francisco county 1849–1855 are volume 006601002 (browse-only, 340 images, no name index); county deed books from 1850; BLM GLO patents searchable online
- **Where held:** BLM General Land Office website for federal patents; county courthouses and county recorders' offices for deeds and mining claims per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Mexican-American War (1846–1848); California's Bear Flag Revolt (1846); Civil War (1861–1865) — California furnished volunteer units
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants (at NARA); California state militia and volunteer records (California State Archives)
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/); California State Archives, Sacramento

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Numerous Gold Rush–era cemeteries throughout the Sierra Nevada foothills (El Dorado, Calaveras, Tuolumne, Nevada, Placer counties) and in San Francisco and Sacramento
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/)
- **Physical records:** Sexton records at county level; many early mining camps had informal or no burial registers; Gold Rush deaths were heavily underdocumented

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** San Francisco newspapers were established from 1846; Sacramento papers from 1849; county papers followed mining settlement through the 1850s
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/); California Digital Newspaper Collection (Chronicling America)
- **Content value:** Obituaries, mining news, ship arrival notices, legal notices, name announcements — especially valuable for the 1848–1860 period when other vital records are sparse

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** San Francisco was the primary port of entry for sea arrivals via Cape Horn or via Panama overland; Sacramento received river traffic; overland routes from Missouri also brought large numbers
- **Record types:** Ship passenger manifests at San Francisco (held at NARA San Bruno, per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records); Sacramento Port Arrival Registers 1849–1858 as volume 006601003 (298 images, browse-only, no name index)
- **Where held:** NARA Pacific Region, San Bruno, California (ship manifests); NARA main (https://www.archives.gov/)
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** County property tax, personal property tax; California also levied a Foreign Miners' Tax (1850, re-enacted 1852) targeting non-citizen miners
- **Date range:** From county formation (1850–1853 for most mining counties)
- **Where held:** County courthouses; California State Archives
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists name adult male property-holders and can substitute for missing census returns; the Foreign Miners' Tax rolls specifically name immigrant miners

### Other record types
- **Great Registers (voter registration):** Collection 1923340 "California, Great Registers, 1866-1910" (1,345,678 records) — these detailed voter registration records list name, age, birthplace, occupation, and physical description and are among the richest name indexes for adult males who remained in California
- **Mining claim records:** County recorders' offices hold original claim registers; volume 006601002 covers San Francisco county 1849–1855 as browse-only only; county-level records for Sierra Nevada mining counties are physical
- **Overland trail records:** Diaries, journals, and trail registers at the California State Library and Bancroft Library at UC Berkeley per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | California, County Births, 1850-1919 (2017276); California, Great Registers, 1866-1910 (1923340); California, County Marriages, 1850-1952 (1452832); California, Mission Records, 1769-1850 (1804372) | County births and marriages; voter registration; mission-era baptisms and burials | Free |
| Ancestry.com (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | U.S. Federal Census Collection | 1850, 1860, 1870 federal census for California | Subscription |
| FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Cemetery Records | Gold Rush-era burials | Free |
| Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) | Historical Newspapers | Obituaries, arrivals, legal notices 1848–1870 | Subscription |
| Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) | Military Records | Civil War and Mexican-American War service | Subscription |
| NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) | Ship passenger manifests; federal land records | Sea arrivals at San Francisco; federal land patents | Free/request |

**Coverage of this survey:** 14 digitized volumes match this place and period; only the first 3 are detailed above. The remaining 11 volumes were not examined — further volume details are available on request. No volume summary counts by record type were returned by the tool.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| NARA Pacific Region, San Bruno, CA | Ship passenger manifests for San Francisco port arrivals | In-person or written request |
| California State Archives, Sacramento | State census, land commission records, state militia and volunteer records | In-person or online request |
| County courthouses (mining counties) | Deed books, probate files, marriage registers, mining claim registers | In-person or mail |
| California State Library, Sacramento | Gold Rush manuscripts, overland trail journals | In-person; some digitized |
| Bancroft Library, UC Berkeley | Gold Rush–era manuscript collections | In-person; appointment required |

## Records NOT online
- Mining claim registers for Sierra Nevada counties beyond San Francisco county (physical at individual county recorders' offices)
- Overland trail journals and diaries (manuscript collections at California State Library and Bancroft Library)
- Full runs of county probate files from the 1850s
- California state militia and volunteer records for the Civil War period (California State Archives, physical)
- County-level death records for the 1848–1870 period (not represented in returned FamilySearch collections)

## Known record losses
- The FamilySearch Wiki search result (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Pre-Statehood_Records) states the 1850 federal census for California was partially destroyed and some county returns are missing. The 1852 California State Census (volume 006601001, 88% name-indexed) is the best substitute for the affected counties.

## Research tips
- Mining claim records are held at county recorders' offices throughout the Sierra Nevada foothills; search the specific mining county (El Dorado, Calaveras, Tuolumne, Nevada, Placer, etc.), not just San Francisco. Per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records
- The 1852 California State Census (volume 006601001, 88% name-indexed, full-text searchable) predates the missing 1850 federal census county returns and is often the first reliable name-search for Gold Rush arrivals.
- Great Registers (collection 1923340, beginning 1866) are among the richest biographical indexes for adult males — they record name, age, birthplace, occupation, and physical description and are free on FamilySearch.
- The Sacramento Port Arrival Registers 1849–1858 (volume 006601003) must be browsed image by image with no name index; ship manifests for San Francisco sea arrivals are at NARA San Bruno.
- California became a state in 1850 without territorial status, so there are no U.S. territorial-era records for 1848–1850; for that two-year window look to newspaper arrivals notices, early county records, and ship passenger manifests.
- The Foreign Miners' Tax (1850, re-enacted 1852) generated county-level tax rolls that name immigrant miners by name and origin — these can be found at county courthouses and the California State Archives.

- **Where held:** NARA Pacific Region, San Bruno, California (ship manifests); NARA main (https://www.archives.gov/)
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** County property tax, personal property tax; California also levied a Foreign Miners' Tax (1850, re-enacted 1852) targeting non-citizen miners
- **Date range:** From county formation (1850–1853 for most mining counties)
- **Where held:** County courthouses; California State Archives
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists name adult male property-holders and can substitute for missing census returns; the Foreign Miners' Tax rolls specifically name immigrant miners

### Other record types
- **Great Registers (voter registration):** Collection 1923340 "California, Great Registers, 1866-1910" (1,345,678 records) — these detailed voter registration records list name, age, birthplace, occupation, and physical description and are among the richest name indexes for adult males who remained in California
- **Mining claim records:** County recorders' offices hold original claim registers; volume 006601002 covers San Francisco county 1849–1855 as browse-only only; county-level records for Sierra Nevada mining counties are physical
- **Overland trail records:** Diaries, journals, and trail registers at the California State Library and Bancroft Library at UC Berkeley per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | California, County Births, 1850-1919 (2017276); California, Great Registers, 1866-1910 (1923340); California, County Marriages, 1850-1952 (1452832); California, Mission Records, 1769-1850 (1804372) | County births and marriages; voter registration; mission-era baptisms and burials | Free |
| Ancestry.com (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | U.S. Federal Census Collection | 1850, 1860, 1870 federal census for California | Subscription |
| FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Cemetery Records | Gold Rush-era burials | Free |
| Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) | Historical Newspapers | Obituaries, arrivals, legal notices 1848–1870 | Subscription |
| Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) | Military Records | Civil War and Mexican-American War service | Subscription |
| NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) | Ship passenger manifests; federal land records | Sea arrivals at San Francisco; federal land patents | Free/request |

**Coverage of this survey:** 14 digitized volumes match this place and period; only the first 3 are detailed above. The remaining 11 volumes were not examined — further volume details are available on request. No volume summary counts by record type were returned by the tool.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| NARA Pacific Region, San Bruno, CA | Ship passenger manifests for San Francisco port arrivals | In-person or written request |
| California State Archives, Sacramento | State census, land commission records, state militia and volunteer records | In-person or online request |
| County courthouses (mining counties) | Deed books, probate files, marriage registers, mining claim registers | In-person or mail |
| California State Library, Sacramento | Gold Rush manuscripts, overland trail journals | In-person; some digitized |
| Bancroft Library, UC Berkeley | Gold Rush–era manuscript collections | In-person; appointment required |

## Records NOT online
- Mining claim registers for Sierra Nevada counties beyond San Francisco county (physical at individual county recorders' offices)
- Overland trail journals and diaries (manuscript collections at California State Library and Bancroft Library)
- Full runs of county probate files from the 1850s
- California state militia and volunteer records for the Civil War period (California State Archives, physical)
- County-level death records for the 1848–1870 period (not represented in returned FamilySearch collections)

## Known record losses
- The FamilySearch Wiki search result (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Pre-Statehood_Records) states the 1850 federal census for California was partially destroyed and some county returns are missing. The 1852 California State Census (volume 006601001, 88% name-indexed) is the best substitute for the affected counties.

## Research tips
- Mining claim records are held at county recorders' offices throughout the Sierra Nevada foothills; search the specific mining county (El Dorado, Calaveras, Tuolumne, Nevada, Placer, etc.), not just San Francisco. Per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records
- The 1852 California State Census (volume 006601001, 88% name-indexed, full-text searchable) predates the missing 1850 federal census county returns and is often the first reliable name-search for Gold Rush arrivals.
- Great Registers (collection 1923340, beginning 1866) are among the richest biographical indexes for adult males — they record name, age, birthplace, occupation, and physical description and are free on FamilySearch.
- The Sacramento Port Arrival Registers 1849–1858 (volume 006601003) must be browsed image by image with no name index; ship manifests for San Francisco sea arrivals are at NARA San Bruno.
- California became a state in 1850 without territorial status, so there are no U.S. territorial-era records for 1848–1850; for that two-year window look to newspaper arrivals notices, early county records, and ship passenger manifests.
- The Foreign Miners' Tax (1850, re-enacted 1852) generated county-level tax rolls that name immigrant miners by name and origin — these can be found at county courthouses and the California State Archives.

Here is the locality guide for New York City in the 1700s colonial period:

---

**New York City, 1700s Colonial Period — Locality Research Guide**

**Background**
New York City was a British colonial city throughout the 1700s (and was Dutch before 1664). There was **no civil registration** of births, marriages, or deaths during this era — the only contemporary records of those vital events are **church registers**.

---

**Key Record Types & Where to Find Them**

**Church Records**
The most important source for vital events:
- **Dutch Reformed Church** — oldest series goes back to **1639**, records are in Dutch; FamilySearch holds indexed collections of New York church records from 1640; a digitized volume covering 1700–1776 is available at FamilySearch but must be browsed image by image (no search index)
- **Trinity Church (Anglican)** — registers from **1697**
- **Presbyterian and Jewish congregations** — a handful of earlier congregations also survive

**Land & Probate Records**
- FamilySearch holds **New York land records from 1630** and **probate records from 1629**, all free online
- The **New-York Historical Society** published *Abstracts of Wills* for the colonial-era Prerogative Court — an important printed finding aid

**Court & Colonial Government Records**
- **New York Colonial Manuscripts** at the New York State Archives in Albany — the central provincial record series covering court, land, and military matters

**Municipal Records**
- **Mayor's Court records** at the **New York City Municipal Archives**

**Census Substitutes** *(no federal census until 1790)*
- **Ward-level tax assessment rolls** and **militia rolls** are the closest equivalent to a census for the 1700s

---

**Key Repositories**
| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** (free online) | Church records (1640+), land records (1630+), probate (1629+) |
| **New York State Archives, Albany** | New York Colonial Manuscripts |
| **New York City Municipal Archives** | Mayor's Court records |
| **New-York Historical Society** | Published Abstracts of Wills |

---

**Important Caveats**
- The FamilySearch Wiki pages for New York and New York City returned only generic content during this survey, so some registration dates and record locations could not be fully confirmed from that source. Re-running this guide when those pages are more accessible is recommended.
- Dutch-language records will require translation assistance.

---

**Recommended Next Step**
Build a research plan that stages searches through these record types in sequence, beginning with the church registers and probate collections that have the best colonial-era online coverage.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: New York City, New York (1700–1800)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Originally founded as New Amsterdam (Dutch, 1626); seized by England in 1664 and renamed New York City, becoming the colonial capital of New York Province
- **County seat / administrative center:** New York City (Manhattan, New York County)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** New York Province (British colony) until 1783; New York State from 1788
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the survey tools; the city was a major commercial port and one of the largest urban centers in colonial North America
- **Economy:** Major commercial port and trading hub; provincial administrative center
- **Ethnic composition:** Dutch, English, and other European settlers; enslaved African population; small indigenous presence
- **Religious denominations:** Dutch Reformed (oldest continuous church registers, beginning 1639), Anglican/Episcopal (Trinity Church, records from 1697), Presbyterian, Quaker, Jewish (Shearith Israel, founded 1654), Lutheran
- **Key historical events:** Dutch-to-English transition (1664); Queen Anne's War (1702–1713); French and Indian War (1754–1763); Revolutionary War (1776–1783) during which the city was British-occupied; city served as first U.S. capital 1785–1790

## Boundary changes
- Dutch colonial period: 1626–1664 (New Amsterdam, under Dutch West India Company)
- British colonial period: 1664–1783 (New York Province); records administered at the provincial level
- State period: 1788, when New York ratified the Constitution; city remained within New York County
- Records before 1664 are in Dutch; for the 1700s the city was entirely under British administration

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Civil registration did not exist during the colonial period. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for New York Vital Records returned only generic content during this survey; specific start dates cannot be confirmed from the returned pages.
- **What exists:** No civil births, marriages, or deaths for the 1700s — church registers are the only contemporary record of these events for most families
- **Where held:** Church registers (see below); civil-era records begin after 1800
- **Gaps:** Complete absence of civil vital registration for the entire colonial period
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptismal, marriage, and burial registers are the primary vital record substitute for the 1700s

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Dutch Reformed (registers from 1639, the oldest continuous series); Anglican/Episcopal (Trinity Church); Presbyterian; Quaker; Jewish (Shearith Israel); Lutheran
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations, membership lists
- **FamilySearch collection:** "New York, Church Records, 1640–1940" (collection 1469062, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1469062) — 2,345,678 records with images, covering the entire colonial period
- **Digitized volume:** Image group 007733180 — Dutch Reformed Church registers, 211 images, covering 1700–1776, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable: **browse-only**; all content is in Dutch
- **Gaps:** Indexing is uneven across the colonial era; many volumes are browse-only. Denominations other than Dutch Reformed and Anglican may have sparse or no surviving registers for the 1700s
- **Language:** Dutch Reformed records in Dutch; Anglican records in English

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** The first U.S. federal census is 1790, covering the very end of this period. No federal or colonial census existed before that date
- **Colonial-era substitutes:** Tax assessment lists, militia rolls, and church membership lists substitute for census records during the 1700s
- **State census:** New York conducted state censuses from 1825 onward — none during the colonial period
- **Access:** The 1790 census is indexed and available online; colonial-era substitutes are primarily physical or browse-only

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, inventories, guardianships
- **Prerogative Court:** Colonial-era wills in New York Province were proved before the Prerogative Court of New York. The Abstracts of Wills series published by the New-York Historical Society is the main finding aid for this court series. (Source: wiki_search, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records)
- **FamilySearch collection:** "New York, Probate Records, 1629–1971" (collection 1542780, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1542780) — 987,654 records, the most directly relevant indexed collection for the 1700s
- **Court records:** Mayor's Court records exist for the colonial period and are held at the New York City Municipal Archives and New York State Archives as physical holdings
- **Where held:** New York State Archives (Albany) holds New York Colonial Manuscripts; New York County Surrogate's Court holds probate originals; New York City Municipal Archives holds municipal records

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (colonial-era grants)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Land patents during the British period were granted by the colonial governor. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for New York Land and Property returned only generic content during this survey; the specific granting office cannot be confirmed from the returned pages.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "New York, Land Records, 1630–1975" (collection 2078654, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078654) — 1,567,890 records spanning the full colonial period
- **Types:** Deeds, grants, patents, and conveyances
- **Where held:** New York State Archives holds colonial land patents; New York County Clerk's office holds deed books

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Queen Anne's War (1702–1713), King George's War (1744–1748), French and Indian War (1754–1763), Revolutionary War (1775–1783)
- **Record types:** Colonial militia rolls (useful for identifying residents — list men of military age); Revolutionary War service and pension records. (Source: wiki_search, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records)
- **Where held:** Revolutionary War pension files at NARA (Fold3, https://www.fold3.com/); colonial militia rolls at the New York State Archives; New York Colonial Manuscripts contain military-related documents

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Trinity Church burial ground (Anglican, Manhattan, records from 1697); Dutch Reformed churchyards; Shearith Israel cemetery (oldest Jewish cemetery in the US, records from 1656)
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) carries transcriptions of colonial-era NYC gravestone inscriptions
- **Physical records:** Sexton's burial registers, where they survive, are held by the respective church or the New York City Municipal Archives

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** New York Gazette (founded 1725), New York Weekly Journal (1733), and others from the 1700s. Wikipedia identified the New York Gazette as the city's first colonial newspaper
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) holds digitized historical newspapers; colonial-era NYC papers may have limited online coverage. The New-York Historical Society and New York Public Library hold physical or microfilm runs
- **Content value:** Marriage notices, death notices, legal notices, estate advertisements — primary source for vital events not in church registers

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** New York Harbor was the principal port of entry throughout the colonial period
- **Record types:** Colonial-era passenger manifests survive for some voyages; no systematic passenger list series existed before 1820. Pre-1906 naturalizations were filed in any court of record — Mayor's Court, Court of Common Pleas — many within the New York Colonial Manuscripts
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) holds post-1820 federal passenger lists; colonial-era manifests are scattered across British and American archives

# Locality Guide: New York City, New York (1700–1800)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Originally founded as New Amsterdam (Dutch, 1626); seized by England in 1664 and renamed New York City, becoming the colonial capital of New York Province
- **County seat / administrative center:** New York City (Manhattan, New York County)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** New York Province (British colony) until 1783; New York State from 1788
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the survey tools; the city was a major commercial port and one of the largest urban centers in colonial North America
- **Economy:** Major commercial port and trading hub; provincial administrative center
- **Ethnic composition:** Dutch, English, and other European settlers; enslaved African population; small indigenous presence
- **Religious denominations:** Dutch Reformed (oldest continuous church registers, beginning 1639), Anglican/Episcopal (Trinity Church, records from 1697), Presbyterian, Quaker, Jewish (Shearith Israel, founded 1654), Lutheran
- **Key historical events:** Dutch-to-English transition (1664); Queen Anne's War (1702–1713); French and Indian War (1754–1763); Revolutionary War (1776–1783) during which the city was British-occupied; city served as first U.S. capital 1785–1790

## Boundary changes
- Dutch colonial period: 1626–1664 (New Amsterdam, under Dutch West India Company)
- British colonial period: 1664–1783 (New York Province); records administered at the provincial level
- State period: 1788, when New York ratified the Constitution; city remained within New York County
- Records before 1664 are in Dutch; for the 1700s the city was entirely under British administration

- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptismal, marriage, and burial registers are the primary vital record substitute for the 1700s

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Dutch Reformed (registers from 1639, the oldest continuous series); Anglican/Episcopal (Trinity Church); Presbyterian; Quaker; Jewish (Shearith Israel); Lutheran

- **FamilySearch collection:** "New York, Church Records, 1640–1940" (collection 1469062, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1469062) — 2,345,678 records with images, covering the entire colonial period

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** The first U.S. federal census is 1790, covering the very end of this period. No federal or colonial census existed before that date

- **State census:** New York conducted state censuses from 1825 onward — none during the colonial period

# Locality Guide: Virginia, United States (1775–1783)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** One of the original thirteen colonies; declared independence from Britain on 29 June 1776, becoming the Commonwealth of Virginia
- **Administrative center:** Richmond (capital from 1780; Williamsburg before that)
- **Population during period:** No population figures were returned by the survey tools for this period
- **Economy:** Tobacco planting, subsistence farming; wartime economy disrupted by British raids and impressment
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English-descended colonists; enslaved African Americans constituted a substantial portion of the population; German and Scots-Irish communities present in western counties
- **Religious denominations:** Anglican (Church of England / later Episcopal) was the legally established church through the early Revolution; Baptist, Presbyterian, Methodist, and Quaker congregations also active
- **Key historical events:** Declaration of Independence (1776); Yorktown campaign (1781) — British raids disrupted county records in some localities

## Boundary changes
- Virginia's county structure expanded westward continuously; the Kentucky District was part of Virginia until Kentucky became a separate state in 1792
- Researchers tracing families in present-day Kentucky for 1775–1783 must search Virginia records filed under the relevant Virginia-era county
- New counties were carved from existing ones throughout this period; always identify the parent county for any Virginia locality before 1800

## Available record types

Virginia had no civil vital registration during 1775–1783. Records are held at the county level for most civil record types; note the county of interest before beginning any search.

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil registration existed in Virginia during 1775–1783; the FamilySearch Wiki returned only generic content and does not state a statewide start date
- **What exists:** No state or county civil vital registration for this period
- **Where held:** N/A
- **Gaps:** The entire research period predates civil registration
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism, marriage, and burial registers — FamilySearch collection 1598230, 'Virginia, Church Records, 1680–1929'

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Anglican/Episcopal (legally established through the colonial era); Baptist, Presbyterian, Methodist, Quaker
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials; vestry records (poor relief, orphan care, parish boundary surveys naming householders)
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1598230, 'Virginia, Church Records, 1680–1929,' holds 1,234,567 person records with images; original Anglican/Episcopal registers are largely at the Library of Virginia and diocesan archives; dissenting congregation records vary
- **Gaps:** Anglican vestry records for some counties were disrupted or lost during British raids
- **Language:** English

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** Virginia's 1790 federal census was destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814 (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands); the first surviving federal census for Virginia is 1800
- **State/provincial census:** No Virginia state census exists for 1775–1783
- **Other enumerations:** Personal property tax lists from 1782 onward are the principal substitute — FamilySearch collection 1456723, 'Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850,' covers 456,789 records; volume 005301449 (87 images, 1782–1799) is full-text searchable but not name-indexed
- **Access:** Tax list volume 005301449: full-text searchable, not name-indexed (browse with text search)

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, administrations, guardianships; county court order books recording wartime supply contracts, militia musters, impressment warrants
- **Date range:** County-level probate dates from the mid-1600s
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 2134567, 'Virginia, County Court Records, 1650–1920,' holds 1,789,012 records; county courthouses and the Library of Virginia hold originals; volume 005301448 (Augusta County court order books, 1775–1795, 158 images) is 61% name-indexed

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Colonial land patents were issued by the colonial government; Revolutionary War bounty land warrants were issued by Virginia to its Continental Line veterans
- **Types:** Deeds, grants, land patents, bounty land warrants — FamilySearch collection 1734285, 'Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900,' covers 2,567,890 records; Revolutionary War land bounty warrant records (volume 005301447, 341 images, 1779–1800) are browse-only images
- **Post-war bounty lands:** Virginia granted bounty lands in the Virginia Military District of Ohio to Continental Line veterans; warrant and survey records connect veterans to their home county and wartime service (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands)
- **Where held:** Library of Virginia; FamilySearch digitized collections; Virginia Military District warrants at the National Archives

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** American Revolutionary War, 1775–1783
- **Record types:**
  - Continental Line service records and muster rolls: NARA Record Group 93
  - Virginia militia records: Library of Virginia, Richmond
  - Pension and bounty-land warrant application files: NARA Record Group 15
  - Virginia State Navy records: Library of Virginia
  - FamilySearch collection 1945678, 'Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783,' covers 345,678 records
  (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War)
- **Where held:** NARA (service records, pension files); Library of Virginia (militia, navy); Fold3 at https://www.fold3.com/ (military records, subscription)

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Family farm burying grounds and churchyard cemeteries predominated; no large public cemeteries existed in this period
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave at https://www.findagrave.com/ covers many Virginia churchyards
- **Physical records:** Churchyard burial registers (where extant) are part of the church records collections noted above

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Virginia Gazette (Williamsburg) published during this period; several wartime papers existed
- **Where held:** Historical newspapers at https://www.newspapers.com/ (subscription); the Library of Virginia and university libraries hold microfilm
- **Content value:** Militia call-ups, estate sale notices, wartime proclamations, runaway servant ads, patriot/Loyalist notices

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Hampton Roads (Norfolk/Hampton); Alexandria
- **Record types:** Pre-Revolution passenger arrival lists documenting earlier migration; wartime British prisoner-of-war records; Loyalist removal records
- **Where held:** NARA at https://www.archives.gov/; Library of Virginia
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Personal property tax (tithables list from 1782 onward substituting for the destroyed 1790 census); land tax records
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection 1456723 begins 1782; volume 005301449 covers 1782–1799
- **Where held:** Library of Virginia; county courthouses; FamilySearch collection 1456723, 'Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850'
- **Substitute value:** 1782 and later personal property tax lists are the best available substitute for the missing 1790 census and for all household enumeration before it

### Other record types
- **Pension declarations:** Veterans' pension application narratives (NARA RG 15) can run several pages and describe military service, home county, family composition, and neighbors who vouched for the applicant — among the most genealogically detailed records of this period
- **Loyalist claims:** British government Loyalist Claims Commission records document families who remained loyal and fled or suffered losses; held at The National Archives (UK) and partially accessible via Fold3

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783 (1945678); Virginia, Church Records, 1680–1929 (1598230); Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850 (1456723); Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900 (1734285); Virginia, County Court Records, 1650–1920 (2134567) | No civil registration during this period; destroyed 1790 census | Free |
| National Archives (NARA) | NARA RG 93 (Continental Line); NARA RG 15 (pensions and bounty lands) | Service records, pension files | Free in-person; partial online via Fold3 — https://www.archives.gov/ |
| Fold3 | Revolutionary War service and pension records | NARA holdings not freely available online | Subscription — https://www.fold3.com/ |
| Find A Grave | Virginia churchyard cemetery records | Churchyard burials for which no register survives | Free — https://www.findagrave.com/ |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Virginia newspapers | Wartime notices, militia call-ups, estate sales | Subscription — https://www.newspapers.com/ |

**Coverage of this survey:** 3 digitized volumes match Virginia for 1775–1800; all 3 are detailed above (the complete result set).

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Library of Virginia, Richmond | Virginia militia records; Virginia State Navy records; original parish registers; land patents; county court originals | In-person; finding aids at lva.virginia.gov |
| National Archives (NARA) | Continental Line service records (RG 93); pension and bounty-land warrants (RG 15) | In-person at NARA Washington; online request; Fold3 subscription |
| County courthouses | Deed books, order books, will books, land tax records | In-person or mail request |
| Episcopal Diocese archives | Anglican/Episcopal parish original registers | In-person; contact the relevant diocese |

## Records NOT online
- Complete Virginia militia service records (Library of Virginia originals; not fully digitized)
- Virginia State Navy records (Library of Virginia)
- Virginia Military District of Ohio bounty land survey records (partial — some at NARA, browse access only via volume 005301447)
- County court order books outside the Augusta County volume 005301448 (most must be viewed at the county courthouse or Library of Virginia)
- Original Episcopal parish registers (many microfilmed by FamilySearch but browse-only)

## Known record losses
- The 1790 Virginia federal census was destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814; the 1782–1800 personal property tax lists (FamilySearch collection 1456723; volume 005301449) are the most comprehensive alternative (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands). Some county court records were lost to British raids and courthouse fires; the Library of Virginia's finding aids identify counties with gaps.

## Research tips
- **Start with pension files, not just service records.** NARA RG 15 pension application narratives frequently include a soldier's age, birthplace, home county, wife's name, and neighbors' affidavits — far more genealogical detail than a bare muster-roll entry (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War).
- **Use 1782–1790 personal property tax lists as the census substitute.** Virginia's personal property tax lists beginning in 1782 are the principal tool for locating individuals in the decade when no federal census survives for Virginia (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands).
- **Search both Continental Line and militia record series separately.** A veteran who served in both will appear in NARA RG 93 (Continental) and separately in Library of Virginia militia records; searching only one series will miss the other (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War).
- **Follow post-war bounty land warrants into Ohio.** Virginia granted land in the Virginia Military District of Ohio to Continental Line veterans; a warrant record there names the veteran and links him to his wartime service and home county (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands).
- **County court order books name non-officers.** Wartime supply contracts, road impressment orders, and militia muster records appear in county court order books (FamilySearch collection 2134567; volume 005301448 for Augusta County, 1775–1795, 61% name-indexed) and name men who left no Continental service record.
- **The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Virginia returned only generic content during this survey.** Visit https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Genealogy directly for Virginia-specific guidance.

Some county court records were lost to British raids and courthouse fires; the Library of Virginia's finding aids identify counties with gaps.

## Research tips
- **Start with pension files, not just service records.** NARA RG 15 pension application narratives frequently include a soldier's age, birthplace, home county, wife's name, and neighbors' affidavits — far more genealogical detail than a bare muster-roll entry (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War).
- **Use 1782–1790 personal property tax lists as the census substitute.** Virginia's personal property tax lists beginning in 1782 are the principal tool for locating individuals in the decade when no federal census survives for Virginia (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands).
- **Search both Continental Line and militia record series separately.** A veteran who served in both will appear in NARA RG 93 (Continental) and separately in Library of Virginia militia records; searching only one series will miss the other (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War).
- **Follow post-war bounty land warrants into Ohio.** Virginia granted land in the Virginia Military District of Ohio to Continental Line veterans; a warrant record there names the veteran and links him to his wartime service and home county (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands).
- **County court order books name non-officers.** Wartime supply contracts, road impressment orders, and militia muster records appear in county court order books (FamilySearch collection 2134567; volume 005301448 for Augusta County, 1775–1795, 61% name-indexed) and name men who left no Continental service record.
- **The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Virginia returned only generic content during this survey.** Visit https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Genealogy directly for Virginia-specific guidance.

The locality guide (**loc_001**) has been saved to your project. Here is what it found:

---

## New Orleans in the Early 1800s — Record Survival & Substitutes

### The Disasters

New Orleans faced two catastrophic fires in **1788** and **1794** that destroyed large portions of the French Quarter and many colonial-era documents. Yellow fever epidemics, hurricanes, and floods added further losses throughout the period. A missing record may reflect destruction rather than the event never having been recorded.

### What Survived

Despite the disasters, three important record classes came through with only survivable gaps:

1. **St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers** — Catholic baptisms, marriages, and burials from **1731**; these are your primary substitute for civil vital records in this era.
2. **Notarial acts** — Legal documents (property transfers, contracts, wills, successions) held by the **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** from **1733**. This is the Louisiana equivalent of deeds and probate.
3. **Records of the Cabildo** — Spanish colonial governing body records that survived.

### A Critical Louisiana Warning

Louisiana uses **civil law, not common law**, so there are no deed books or probate files in the usual sense. Everything runs through **notarial acts** and **successions**, organized by *notary name and date* — not by family name. Plan your searches accordingly.

---

## Where to Look

### Online (FamilySearch — free)
| Collection | Coverage |
|---|---|
| Louisiana church records | 1718–1925 |
| Louisiana probate/succession records | 1756–1984 |
| Louisiana death index | from 1819 |
| Notarial acts (browse-only, not name-indexed) | 1803–1820 |

### Physical Repositories
- **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** — the main repository for notarial acts
- **Louisiana Historical Center** — French- and Spanish-era colonial records
- **Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives** — sacramental registers not yet digitized
- **Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge** — state-level records

---

### Next Steps

The guide recommends building a **research plan** to sequence searches in the right order for your specific ancestor. If you share the person's name and approximate dates, we can proceed to planning.

Colonial-era notarial records from the French period (1718–1769) and Spanish period (1769–1803) are held at the Louisiana Historical Center in the Old U.S. Mint building, not at the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: New Orleans, Orleans Parish, Louisiana (1800–1860)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** City of New Orleans founded 1718 by French colonizers; Spanish control 1763–1800; briefly returned to France 1800–1803; incorporated into the United States by the Louisiana Purchase in 1803; Louisiana became a state in 1812.
- **Administrative center:** New Orleans is both the city and the seat of Orleans Parish.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Orleans Parish, Louisiana, United States.
- **Population during period:** Population figures were not returned by tools during this survey.
- **Economy:** Major port city; cotton, sugar, and slave trade dominated commerce; river trade made New Orleans the largest port in the South.
- **Ethnic composition:** Highly diverse — French Creoles, Spanish Creoles, free people of color (gens de couleur libres), enslaved African Americans, Anglo-Americans arriving after 1803, German and Irish immigrants from the 1820s onward, and a substantial Caribbean immigrant population.
- **Religious denominations:** Predominantly Roman Catholic (the dominant denomination throughout), with Protestant congregations (Episcopal, Methodist, Presbyterian) appearing after 1803 and Jewish congregations also present.
- **Key historical events:** 1788 and 1794 fires destroyed most of the French Quarter and large numbers of colonial records; yellow fever epidemics killed thousands throughout the period and created surges in death records; the Louisiana Purchase (1803) changed the governing legal system; the Battle of New Orleans (1815) during the War of 1812.

## Boundary changes
- Orleans Parish boundaries were largely stable during this period.
- Louisiana was an organized territory (Orleans Territory) from 1804 until statehood in 1812; territorial-era records are distinct from later state records and are held at the Louisiana State Archives in Baton Rouge.
- Louisiana uses a civil law tradition (Napoleonic Code) inherited from France and Spain — it is the only US state that does not use common law. This fundamentally changes record types, terminology, and repositories compared to other states.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil registration start date was confirmed from any tool result during this survey — the FamilySearch Wiki pages for Louisiana were unreachable. Do not assume a statewide civil registration series existed for the early 1800s; check the Louisiana Vital Records wiki page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Vital_Records) before searching.
- **What exists:** The FamilySearch collection "Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819-1964" (collection 1543892) is an index with 2,345,678 entries and no attached images — it covers deaths from 1819 onward at the index level.
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Archives (Baton Rouge) holds territorial and early state records; local records were also kept at the parish level.
- **Gaps:** Fires of 1788 and 1794 destroyed many pre-1803 records. Yellow fever epidemics, hurricanes, and floods created additional gaps throughout the period. The absence of a statewide civil registration requirement during this period means church records (see below) are the primary substitute.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers (Catholic baptisms, marriages, burials from 1731 with gaps) are the main vital-record substitute for the early 1800s. Notarial records also document births, deaths, and marriages indirectly through succession and marriage contract filings.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic is the dominant denomination and the one with surviving registers from the colonial era. Protestant congregations (Episcopal, Methodist, Presbyterian) arrived after 1803 but had no comparable early-period coverage.
- **Record types:** Baptisms (which name parents and often godparents), marriages (which may include marriage contracts filed with a notary), and burials; also confirmations.
- **Where held:** The Archdiocese of New Orleans holds baptism, marriage, and burial registers from St. Louis Cathedral (1731–present) and other parish churches. Many have been microfilmed by FamilySearch. The FamilySearch collection "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925" (collection 1612905, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905) has 987,654 records and 493,827 images and is the primary online access point.
- **Gaps:** The fires of 1788 and 1794 created gaps in the St. Louis Cathedral registers; some pre-1788 entries do not survive. The Diocese of Baton Rouge and Diocese of Lafayette hold significant collections for parishes outside New Orleans.
- **Language:** French (1718–1769), Spanish (1769–1803), and English (after 1803). Catholic sacramental records continued partly in French after 1803. Researchers must be able to read the original language for records in the relevant period (Spanish for events 1769–1803, French for the French colonial period and some Catholic entries after 1803).
- **Digitization level:** Indexed + images (collection 1612905 covers the period).

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** Federal census enumerations are available from 1810 onward for New Orleans (Orleans Territory in 1810; Louisiana became a state in 1812). The 1800 census covers Orleans Territory. The 1820, 1830, 1840, 1850, and 1860 censuses all include New Orleans.
- **State/provincial census:** Louisiana conducted some state-level enumerations; check the Louisiana State Archives for territorial censuses.
- **Other enumerations:** The Cabildo (Spanish colonial governing body) conducted enumerations during the Spanish period; those records are held at the Louisiana Historical Center.
- **Access:** Federal census records are indexed and available online through Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) and FamilySearch.

### Probate and court records
- **Louisiana-specific terminology:** Louisiana does not use "probate" — the equivalent is "successions" (estates of deceased persons). "Tutorships" are guardianships. "Interdictions" are incompetency proceedings. Search these terms, not common-law equivalents.
- **Types:** Successions (wills and intestate administrations), tutorships, interdictions, inventories of estates, emancipation records.
- **Where held:** The FamilySearch collection "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756-1984" (collection 2078341, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341) has 456,789 records and images and covers the target period. Originals are held by the Civil District Court for Orleans Parish and the Louisiana State Archives.
- **Notarial link:** Successions were often processed through notarial acts; the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds succession records from 1733 onward, organized by notary name and date.
- **Date range:** From 1756 (collection coverage); territorial records from 1804 are at the Louisiana State Archives.
- **Digitization level:** Indexed + images (collection 2078341).

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (French/Spanish arpent system) — Louisiana did not use the rectangular township-and-range system common to other states.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Louisiana is a federal land state; the Bureau of Land Management's General Land Office website (glorecords.blm.gov) holds federal patents. Spanish and French land grants from before 1803 were adjudicated by the US government after the Louisiana Purchase.
- **Types:** Notarial acts for property transfers (deeds in Louisiana's civil law system), land grants and patents, mortgage acts, donation acts.
- **Where held:** The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center (records from 1733, organized by notary name and date) is the primary repository for property transfers. Colonial-era records (French 1718–1769, Spanish 1769–1803) are at the Louisiana Historical Center in the Old U.S. Mint building. The Louisiana State Archives holds territorial-era land records.

# Locality Guide: New Orleans, Orleans Parish, Louisiana (1800–1860)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** City of New Orleans founded 1718 by French colonizers; Spanish control 1763–1800; briefly returned to France 1800–1803; incorporated into the United States by the Louisiana Purchase in 1803; Louisiana became a state in 1812.
- **Administrative center:** New Orleans is both the city and the seat of Orleans Parish.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Orleans Parish, Louisiana, United States.
- **Population during period:** Population figures were not returned by tools during this survey.
- **Economy:** Major port city; cotton, sugar, and slave trade dominated commerce; river trade made New Orleans the largest port in the South.
- **Ethnic composition:** Highly diverse — French Creoles, Spanish Creoles, free people of color (gens de couleur libres), enslaved African Americans, Anglo-Americans arriving after 1803, German and Irish immigrants from the 1820s onward, and a substantial Caribbean immigrant population.
- **Religious denominations:** Predominantly Roman Catholic (the dominant denomination throughout), with Protestant congregations (Episcopal, Methodist, Presbyterian) appearing after 1803 and Jewish congregations also present.
- **Key historical events:** 1788 and 1794 fires destroyed most of the French Quarter and large numbers of colonial records; yellow fever epidemics killed thousands throughout the period and created surges in death records; the Louisiana Purchase (1803) changed the governing legal system; the Battle of New Orleans (1815) during the War of 1812.

## Boundary changes
- Orleans Parish boundaries were largely stable during this period.
- Louisiana was an organized territory (Orleans Territory) from 1804 until statehood in 1812; territorial-era records are distinct from later state records and are held at the Louisiana State Archives in Baton Rouge.
- Louisiana uses a civil law tradition (Napoleonic Code) inherited from France and Spain — it is the only US state that does not use common law. This fundamentally changes record types, terminology, and repositories compared to other states.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil registration start date was confirmed from any tool result during this survey — the FamilySearch Wiki pages for Louisiana were unreachable. Do not assume a statewide civil registration series existed for the early 1800s; check the Louisiana Vital Records wiki page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Vital_Records) before searching.
- **What exists:** The FamilySearch collection "Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819-1964" (collection 1543892) is an index with 2,345,678 entries and no attached images — it covers deaths from 1819 onward at the index level.
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Archives (Baton Rouge) holds territorial and early state records; local records were also kept at the parish level.
- **Gaps:** Fires of 1788 and 1794 destroyed many pre-1803 records. Yellow fever epidemics, hurricanes, and floods created additional gaps throughout the period. The absence of a statewide civil registration requirement during this period means church records (see below) are the primary substitute.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers (Catholic baptisms, marriages, burials from 1731 with gaps) are the main vital-record substitute for the early 1800s. - **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic is the dominant denomination and the one with surviving registers from the colonial era. Protestant congregations (Episcopal, Methodist, Presbyterian) arrived after 1803 but had no comparable early-period coverage.

- **Where held:** The Archdiocese of New Orleans holds baptism, marriage, and burial registers from St. Louis Cathedral (1731–present) and other parish churches. - **Gaps:** The fires of 1788 and 1794 created gaps in the St. Louis Cathedral registers; some pre-1788 entries do not survive. The Diocese of Baton Rouge and Diocese of Lafayette hold significant collections for parishes outside New Orleans.
- **Language:** French (1718–1769), Spanish (1769–1803), and English (after 1803). Catholic sacramental records continued partly in French after 1803. Researchers must be able to read the original language for records in the relevant period (Spanish for events 1769–1803, French for the French colonial period and some Catholic entries after 1803).
- **Digitization level:** Indexed + images (collection 1612905 covers the period).

Here is the locality guide for tracing immigrants entering through Boston in the 1840s:

---

**Boston Port Records, 1840s — Locality Guide**

Boston in the 1840s was one of the five major American ports of entry. Records that document arriving immigrants fall into two main streams:

### Key Record Types & Repositories

**1. Customs Passenger Lists**
- Held by the **National Archives at Boston (Waltham, Massachusetts)**, Record Group 36
- Originals for every ship that cleared the port
- **FamilySearch** holds a digitized collection: *Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891* (over 1.2 million records) — collection **1784312**
- One specific digitized volume covers 1840–1850 Boston port arrivals (389 images), but it is only **3% name-indexed** — full-text keyword search is the practical route in, not a standard name search

> ⚠️ **Important limitation:** 1840s customs lists record only name, age, sex, occupation, and country of origin — no hometown or American contacts. The passenger list is a starting point, not a complete answer.

**2. Naturalization Records**
- FamilySearch collection **1459213** (Naturalization Records, 1790–1906)
- Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in *any court* — federal, state, or local — so all three series must be searched

**3. Catholic Parish Registers**
- Kept by the **Archdiocese of Boston**
- Often the *only* source of family detail for Irish Famine-era arrivals, especially those who moved on before any census was taken
- FamilySearch collection **1921657** covers church records through 1920

**4. Additional FamilySearch Collections**
- Town vital records through 1890
- Probate records extending to 1991

---

### Recommended Next Steps

1. Search FamilySearch **collection 1784312** (*Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891*) using **full-text search** for surname variants of your arriving ancestor
2. Follow any match into **collection 1459213** (Naturalization Records)
3. Search **collection 1921657** (Catholic parish registers) to establish post-arrival vital events such as baptisms, marriages, and burials

---

*Note: The FamilySearch Wiki pages for both Boston and Massachusetts returned only generic content during this survey. The Massachusetts-specific details on those pages (registration start dates, coverage details) should be consulted directly before drawing final conclusions about what exists.*

# Locality Guide: Boston, Massachusetts — Port of Entry (1840–1850)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Boston founded 1630; incorporated as a city 1822
- **County seat / administrative center:** Suffolk County seat; also the Massachusetts state capital
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Suffolk County, Massachusetts, United States
- **Population during period:** By 1850 over a quarter of Boston's residents were Irish-born (Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston); population figures by census year were not returned by the place_population tool for this location.
- **Economy:** Major Atlantic seaport; trade, manufacturing, and maritime commerce drove substantial immigrant labor demand
- **Ethnic composition:** Large Irish immigration in the 1840s driven by the Great Famine (1845–1852); immigrants settled in the North End and Fort Hill neighborhoods (Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston)
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic (Cathedral of the Holy Cross, St. Patrick's); Congregational, Episcopal, Methodist, Baptist
- **Key historical events:** Boston was one of the five major U.S. ports of entry receiving tens of thousands of Irish Famine immigrants in the 1840s; customs passenger lists document these arrivals (wiki_search result: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration#Port_of_Boston)

## Boundary changes
- place_search_all returned no historical boundary changes for Boston during the 1840s target period.
- If your ancestor may have settled outside the city limits, also search Suffolk County records more broadly.

## Available record types

For each record type below the jurisdictional level (city, county, or state) at which records were created is noted where the tools confirmed it.

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki page for Massachusetts Vital Records returned only generic content during this survey and no specific Massachusetts registration start date can be confirmed from tool results. The FamilySearch Wiki should be consulted directly for Massachusetts registration dates before assuming a civil record exists for the 1840s.
- **What exists:** FamilySearch collection 2061550 "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620-1890" (3,456,789 records) covers births, marriages, and deaths at the town level through 1890, encompassing the 1840s.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550 (indexed + images)
- **Gaps:** Specific coverage gaps not stated in tool results; gap details require consulting the FamilySearch Wiki Massachusetts Vital Records page directly.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Catholic and Protestant church records are the primary alternative source for 1840s immigrants.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Catholic (Cathedral of the Holy Cross, St. Patrick's); various Protestant denominations
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials — Catholic parish registers dating from the 1840s onward document Irish Famine immigrants (wiki_search result: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Boston)
- **Where held:** Archdiocese of Boston archives holds Catholic parish registers (wiki_search result: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Boston); FamilySearch collection 1921657 "Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630-1920" (987,654 records) — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657 (indexed + images)
- **Gaps:** Specific per-parish gaps not stated in tool results
- **Language:** English; Catholic records commonly also in Latin

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** 1840 and 1850 federal censuses cover Boston. Note: the 1840 census lists heads of household only, not all members by name; the 1850 census is the first to list all household members by name.
- **State/provincial census:** None confirmed by tool results for Massachusetts in this period.
- **Other enumerations:** Not confirmed by tool results.
- **Access:** Accessible via FamilySearch and Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/, subscription)

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, estate petitions
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection 1678901 "Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635-1991" covers this period
- **Where held:** FamilySearch — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901 (indexed + images); originals at Suffolk County Probate Court

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Massachusetts is not a federal public-land state)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Town clerk and county registry of deeds levels; the FamilySearch Wiki Massachusetts Land and Property page was not specifically fetched during this survey
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, tax records
- **Date range:** Colonial era onward
- **Where held:** Suffolk County Registry of Deeds; Massachusetts State Archives

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Mexican-American War (1846-1848); pre-Civil War era
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants, draft registrations
- **Where held:** National Archives and Records Administration — https://www.archives.gov/; Fold3 — https://www.fold3.com/ (subscription)

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Catholic and Protestant cemeteries throughout Boston; specific names not returned by tools
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave — https://www.findagrave.com/ (free)
- **Physical records:** Sexton records at individual cemeteries or the City of Boston archives

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Pilot (Boston's Irish Catholic newspaper) published arrival notices and a missing-persons column for Irish immigrants from the 1840s onward (Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston)
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com — https://www.newspapers.com/ (subscription); physical copies and microfilm at Boston Public Library
- **Content value:** The Pilot's missing-persons column is especially valuable for tracing Irish Famine-era immigrants who passed through Boston

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Port of Boston (primary port for the 1840s target period)
- **Record types:**
  - Customs passenger lists (NARA Record Group 36): FamilySearch collection 1784312 "Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820-1891" (1,234,567 records) — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1784312
  - 1 digitized volume covers 1840-1850 specifically (image group 003345210, 389 images): 3% name-indexed, full-text searchable — use full-text search, not name-only search
  - Naturalization petitions and declarations of intention: FamilySearch collection 1459213 "Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790-1906" (345,678 records) — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1459213
- **Where held:** Originals of customs passenger lists held at the National Archives at Boston (Waltham, MA), Record Group 36 (wiki_search result: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration#Port_of_Boston)
- **Content note:** 1840s customs passenger lists record only name, age, sex, occupation, and country of origin — they do not give hometown, last residence, or names of contacts in America, unlike post-1890 manifests. Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents; when researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Property tax, poll tax
- **Date range:** Pre-statehood onward; specific digitized holdings not confirmed by tool results for the 1840s period
- **Where held:** City of Boston archives; Massachusetts State Archives
- **Substitute value:** Tax records can substitute for missing census years to establish residence

### Other record types
- **City directories:** Boston city directories for the 1840s-1850s are valuable for locating immigrant residents between census years; physical copies at Boston Public Library and Massachusetts Historical Society (not confirmed online in tool results)
- **Naming conventions:** The FamilySearch Wiki Massachusetts Naming Customs page was not specifically fetched during this survey; naming patterns unconfirmed from tool results.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1784312 | Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820-1891 (1,234,567 records) | Primary port arrival records for the 1840s | Free |
| FamilySearch — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1459213 | Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790-1906 (345,678 records) | Pre-1906 naturalizations not in federal courts only | Free |
| FamilySearch — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550 | Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620-1890 (3,456,789 records) | Births, marriages, deaths during and after arrival | Free |
| FamilySearch — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657 | Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630-1920 (987,654 records) | Church-based vital records for the 1840s | Free |
| FamilySearch — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901 | Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635-1991 (567,890 records) | Estate and relationship evidence | Free |
| Ancestry — https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/ | U.S. Federal Census Collection | 1840 and 1850 census access | Subscription |
| FindAGrave — https://www.findagrave.com/ | Cemetery records | Burial locations and death dates | Free |
| Newspapers.com — https://www.newspapers.com/ | Historical newspapers including The Pilot | Arrival notices and missing-persons column for Irish immigrants | Subscription |
| Fold3 — https://www.fold3.com/ | Military records | Service records and pension files | Subscription |
| NARA — https://www.archives.gov/ | Passenger list originals (Record Group 36) | Volumes not yet digitized by FamilySearch | Free (in-person at Waltham, MA) |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned 1 digitized volume matching this place and period (image group 003345210, 389 images, 1840-1850, complete: true). Additional years within the 1820-1891 range of FamilySearch collection 1784312 may hold further digitized passenger list volumes not captured by this survey scope.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| National Archives at Boston (Waltham, MA) | Customs passenger lists, Record Group 36 (originals) | In-person research; records request via archives.gov |
| Archdiocese of Boston Archives | Catholic parish registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) from 1840s onward | Contact Archdiocese directly; some records on FamilySearch collection 1921657 |
| Massachusetts State Archives | State vital records, court records, naturalization records | In-person / online request |
| Boston Public Library | City directories, The Pilot newspaper, local histories | In-person; some materials digitized |
| Suffolk County Registry of Deeds | Deeds, mortgages | In-person / online search |
| Suffolk County Probate Court | Probate records (wills, administrations) | In-person; records on FamilySearch collection 1678901 |

## Records NOT online
- Original NARA Record Group 36 customs passenger list volumes beyond what FamilySearch has digitized must be consulted in person at the National Archives at Boston (Waltham, MA)
- Boston city directories from the 1840s-1850s are not confirmed as fully digitized online
- Archdiocese of Boston Catholic parish registers not covered by FamilySearch collection 1921657 require contacting the Archdiocese directly

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey states a specific loss of Boston or Massachusetts immigrant records for the 1840s period. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Massachusetts were not available in specific form during this survey — consult the Massachusetts State Archives and the National Archives at Boston (Waltham, MA) for confirmation of any losses.

## Research tips
- The 1840s customs passenger lists at the Port of Boston record only name, age, sex, occupation, and country of origin — search by surname variant spellings and check the full manifest for entire families traveling together (wiki_search result: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration#Port_of_Boston).
