# Locality Guide: Boston, Massachusetts — Port of Entry (1840–1850)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Boston founded 1630; incorporated as a city 1822
- **County seat / administrative center:** Suffolk County seat; also the Massachusetts state capital
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Suffolk County, Massachusetts, United States
- **Population during period:** By 1850 over a quarter of Boston's residents were Irish-born (Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston); population figures by census year were not returned by the place_population tool for this location.
- **Economy:** Major Atlantic seaport; trade, manufacturing, and maritime commerce drove substantial immigrant labor demand
- **Ethnic composition:** Large Irish immigration in the 1840s driven by the Great Famine (1845–1852); immigrants settled in the North End and Fort Hill neighborhoods (Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston)
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic (Cathedral of the Holy Cross, St. Patrick's); Congregational, Episcopal, Methodist, Baptist
- **Key historical events:** Boston was one of the five major U.S. ports of entry receiving tens of thousands of Irish Famine immigrants in the 1840s; customs passenger lists document these arrivals (wiki_search result: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration#Port_of_Boston)

## Boundary changes
- place_search_all returned no historical boundary changes for Boston during the 1840s target period.
- If your ancestor may have settled outside the city limits, also search Suffolk County records more broadly.

## Available record types

For each record type below the jurisdictional level (city, county, or state) at which records were created is noted where the tools confirmed it.

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki page for Massachusetts Vital Records returned only generic content during this survey and no specific Massachusetts registration start date can be confirmed from tool results. The FamilySearch Wiki should be consulted directly for Massachusetts registration dates before assuming a civil record exists for the 1840s.
- **What exists:** FamilySearch collection 2061550 "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620-1890" (3,456,789 records) covers births, marriages, and deaths at the town level through 1890, encompassing the 1840s.

- **Gaps:** Specific coverage gaps not stated in tool results; gap details require consulting the FamilySearch Wiki Massachusetts Vital Records page directly.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Catholic and Protestant church records are the primary alternative source for 1840s immigrants.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Catholic (Cathedral of the Holy Cross, St. Patrick's); various Protestant denominations
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials — Catholic parish registers dating from the 1840s onward document Irish Famine immigrants (wiki_search result: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Boston)
- **Where held:** Archdiocese of Boston archives holds Catholic parish registers (wiki_search result: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Boston); FamilySearch collection 1921657 "Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630-1920" (987,654 records) — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657 (indexed + images)
- **Gaps:** Specific per-parish gaps not stated in tool results
- **Language:** English; Catholic records commonly also in Latin

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** 1840 and 1850 federal censuses cover Boston. Note: the 1840 census lists heads of household only, not all members by name; the 1850 census is the first to list all household members by name.
- **State/provincial census:** None confirmed by tool results for Massachusetts in this period.
- **Other enumerations:** Not confirmed by tool results.

- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Massachusetts is not a federal public-land state)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Town clerk and county registry of deeds levels; the FamilySearch Wiki Massachusetts Land and Property page was not specifically fetched during this survey

Locality guide written to your project as **loc_001**. Here is the full response:

---

This survey covers **Indian Territory** — the region that became Oklahoma in 1907 — from the period when the Five Civilized Tribes (Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek, and Seminole) were relocated there in the 1830s and 1840s.

## Why This Region Is Different

No county-level civil government and no statewide birth, marriage, or death registration existed in Indian Territory during the mid-1800s. As a result, the records that trace families here are fundamentally different from those in eastern states:

- **Tribal membership rolls and annuity payment lists** compiled by federal Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) agents serve as the census and vital record equivalents.
- **Missionary church registers** from Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, and Moravian congregations fill the role of baptism and burial records.
- **Treaty documents and BIA correspondence** at the National Archives at Fort Worth are where land and citizenship questions were settled.

---

## Key Record Types and Repositories

### 1. Tribal Enrollment Rolls
- **Dawes Rolls (1898–1914)** — The most widely searched tribal enrollment. Most useful as a bridge *backward* to mid-1800s rolls; not a direct source for that period.
- **1851 and 1852 tribal rolls** (tribe-specific) — Available on FamilySearch, partially indexed. These are the primary mid-century population lists.
- **FamilySearch collection: Oklahoma Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959** — The best online starting point.

### 2. Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) Annuity Rolls
- Compiled annually by BIA agents; functioned as census substitutes.
- Held at the **National Archives at Fort Worth (NARA Southwest Region)** — only partially indexed; much requires in-person research or a written request to NARA Fort Worth.

### 3. Missionary Church Records
- Baptism, marriage, and burial registers from Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, and Moravian missions operating in Indian Territory.
- Survival varies by congregation; check FamilySearch and denominational archives.

### 4. Treaty Documents and BIA Correspondence
- National Archives at Fort Worth holds the core collection of federal agency correspondence, land records, and citizenship decisions for Indian Territory.

- **Administrative center:** No single territorial capital; each of the Five Civilized Tribes maintained its own capital (Tahlequah — Cherokee; Tishomingo — Chickasaw; Tuskahoma — Choctaw; Okmulgee — Creek; Wewoka — Seminole)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** United States federal government administered through the Bureau of Indian Affairs
- **Population during period:** Population data were not returned by place tools for Indian Territory; no county-level civil government existed during the mid-1800s
- **Economy:** Subsistence agriculture, ranching, trade with non-Native settlers; some plantation-style farming among slaveholding tribal members
- **Ethnic composition:** Five Civilized Tribes (Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek/Muscogee, Seminole); freedmen brought by tribal members; intermarried white citizens; other tribal nations in western sections
- **Religious denominations:** Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, and Moravian missionaries established congregations and kept records from the 1820s onward (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Missionary_Records)
- **Key historical events:** Trail of Tears relocation (1830s–1840s); U.S. Civil War disrupted tribal governments and BIA record-keeping; post-war Reconstruction treaties; Dawes Act (1887) prepared for allotment

## Boundary changes
- 1830: Indian Removal Act designated Indian Territory covering present-day Oklahoma
- 1890: Oklahoma Territory created from the western portion; eastern portion retained the name Indian Territory
- 1907: Both territories merged at Oklahoma statehood — county-level civil government replaced tribal authority
- For the mid-1800s target period, virtually all of present-day Oklahoma was Indian Territory with no U.S.-style county government

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Oklahoma statehood was November 16, 1907; the FamilySearch Wiki returned only generic content and did not state a year for statewide civil registration. No civil vital registration existed in Indian Territory during the mid-1800s.
- **What exists:** No uniform birth, marriage, or death registration existed before 1907; each tribe maintained citizenship and membership records
- **Where held:** Tribal archives; National Archives at Fort Worth (Record Group 75)

- **Dawes Rolls (1898–1914):** Most widely used tribal enrollment for the Five Civilized Tribes; list name, age, sex, blood quantum, and tribal affiliation; held at NARA Fort Worth and indexed at FamilySearch and Ancestry — note these postdate the mid-1800s target period but are used to work backward (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Tribal_Rolls)
- **Annuity payment rolls:** Compiled annually by BIA agents from the 1830s; list heads of household and sometimes all family members; at NARA RG 75, M234, partially indexed on FamilySearch and Fold3 (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Five_Civilized_Tribes_Records#Annuity_Rolls)

- **Record types:** Registers of converts, students, and community members; baptisms, marriages, burials
- **FamilySearch collection 1654321:** "Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965" — 123,456 records, 61,728 images at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1654321
- **Where held:** NARA holds BIA-related missionary records; denominational archives hold originals
- **Language:** English

### Census records
- **Federal census:** Indian Territory was not routinely enumerated in standard decennial federal censuses during the mid-1800s; special BIA-administered Indian censuses were taken
- **BIA agency records:** Annuity rolls serve as the census equivalent for the tribal period; at NARA RG 75 (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Five_Civilized_Tribes_Records#Annuity_Rolls)
- **Access:** Collection 1987432 on FamilySearch is indexed and searchable; bulk NARA holdings require in-person or written request

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Each tribal nation maintained its own courts handling wills, administrations, guardianships; federal courts in Indian Territory handled non-Indian matters
- **Where held:** NARA at Fort Worth (RG 75); Oklahoma Historical Society
- **Digitization:** No digitized mid-1800s probate or tribal court series was identified in this survey

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Indian Territory lands were tribal communal holdings — the standard U.S. rectangular survey system did not apply until allotment under the Dawes Act (1887+)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Federal government through BIA and treaty process; allotment administered by the Dawes Commission beginning in the 1890s
- **Types:** Treaty records, BIA land registers, allotment records
- **FamilySearch collection 1541872:** "Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907" — 234,567 records, 117,283 images at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1541872
- **Where held:** NARA; BLM General Land Office (for post-allotment patents)

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** U.S.-tribal conflicts; Civil War (tribal units fought on both sides); Indian Wars of the late 19th century
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, draft registrations at NARA; Fold3 hosts indexed military records
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/)

### Cemetery records
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) is the primary online index
- **Physical records:** Mission and tribal burial records held at denominational archives and tribal archives; sexton records where they survive

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Five Civilized Tribes published tribal newspapers (e.g., the Cherokee Phoenix); Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) holds territorial-period papers

---

**Pennsylvania Quaker Records — Late 1700s**

Pennsylvania had **no statewide civil registration** for births or deaths until 1906, which makes Quaker meeting records the functional equivalent of a vital records system for this population. Monthly meetings recorded:

- Births, marriages, and deaths
- **Disownments** (a key record type unique to Friends)
- **Certificates of Removal** — documents issued when a family transferred from one meeting to another, invaluable for tracking migration

Quaker **marriage certificates** were signed by all witnesses present — sometimes 20 or more names — making them an excellent source for identifying extended family and neighbors.

---

| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|

---

- **County probate records** (Register of Wills) — 3.2 million browse-only images on FamilySearch
- **County tax assessment lists** — a census substitute before the first federal census in 1790

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Pennsylvania, United States (1750–1800)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** 1681 as a proprietary colony under William Penn; statehood 1787
- **Administrative center:** Philadelphia (colonial and early state capital)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** British Crown (pre-1776); United States (post-1776)
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned for this period by the survey tool
- **Economy:** Agriculture, trade, iron manufacturing; Philadelphia was the largest city in British North America
- **Ethnic composition:** English Quakers predominated in the founding era; Welsh, Scots-Irish, German, and other settlers were numerous by mid-1700s; Quakers were concentrated in Philadelphia, Chester, Bucks, and Delaware counties (Wikipedia)
- **Religious denominations:** Quakers (Friends), Anglican/Episcopal, German Lutheran, German Reformed, Presbyterian, Mennonite, Moravian
- **Key historical events:** French and Indian War (1754–1763); American Revolutionary War (1775–1783), which disrupted some record-keeping and prompted Quaker disownments for bearing arms or paying war taxes

## Boundary changes
- Pennsylvania's county structure expanded considerably in the 18th century; many counties were carved from earlier ones (e.g., York from Lancaster in 1749, Cumberland from Lancaster in 1750)
- For events in areas that became new counties during the target period, records before the county's formation will be under the parent county; confirm the formation date for each county before searching

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Statewide birth and death registration did not begin until 1906 at the state level (Philadelphia began county-level registration from 1860, Allegheny from 1870), per the FamilySearch Wiki at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records
- **What exists for 1750–1800:** No statewide civil vital records; church registers and county marriage records are the primary sources
- **Where held:** County courthouses hold marriage licenses and bonds from the colonial period; FamilySearch collection 1571957 (Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950, 312,045 records) and collection 1502909 (Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900, 198,765 records) cover the target period
- **Gaps:** No statewide birth or death registration for the target period; Quaker meeting records and other church registers must substitute

### Church records — Quaker (Friends) meetings
This is the central record series for tracing Quaker families in this period.

- **Record types:** Monthly meeting minutes recorded births, marriages, deaths, disownments, and certificates of removal (transfers between meetings); Quaker marriage certificates were signed by all witnesses present — often 20 or more names; quarterly and yearly meeting minutes recorded higher-level governance
- **Dense meeting areas:** Philadelphia Yearly Meeting governed Pennsylvania Quakers; monthly meetings in Chester County, Bucks County, Philadelphia County, and Delaware County had particularly dense Quaker populations (Wikipedia; https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records)
- **Where held:**
  - Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore College: the largest collection of American Quaker records (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records)
  - Quaker and Special Collections, Haverford College (Wikipedia)
  - FamilySearch has microfilmed many monthly meeting minutes and registers (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records)
- **Digitized volumes found:** 1 volume — Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes, 1750–1800 (DGS 001188322, 145 images). This volume is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable: it must be browsed image by image
- **Published abstracts:** William Wade Hinshaw's *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy* (6 volumes) abstracts Pennsylvania meeting records; widely held in genealogical libraries (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Published_Quaker_Abstracts)
- **Certificates of removal:** When a Quaker family moved, the sending meeting issued a removal certificate acknowledged by the receiving meeting — evidence exists in two locations and documents migration
- **Disownments:** Disciplinary proceedings name the person and reason; disowned members may have been reinstated, so follow both threads

### Church records — other denominations
- **Present:** Anglican/Episcopal, German Lutheran, German Reformed, Presbyterian, Mennonite, Moravian
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials
- **Where held:** Denominational archives and FamilySearch microfilm
- **Language:** German Lutheran and Reformed registers are often in German

### Census records
- **Federal census:** First federal census taken in 1790; indexed and available online for Pennsylvania
- **Pre-census substitutes:** Pennsylvania tax assessment lists survive from the 1690s in some counties and serve as census substitutes before 1790; the 1693 Chester County tax list is among the earliest surviving colonial records (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_Records)
- **State census:** No Pennsylvania state census is known for the target period

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, inventories, guardianships
- **Date range:** From the colonial period onward at the county Register of Wills (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_Records)
- **Where held:** County Register of Wills; FamilySearch collection 1999196 (Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994, 3,200,560 images) — browse-only, 0 name-indexed records
- **Testate or intestate:** Search wills first (testate); if none found, look for administration bonds and inventories (intestate)

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Penn's proprietary system)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania Land Office; the State Land Office in Harrisburg holds warrant, survey, and patent records from 1681 onward (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_Records)
- **Types:** Warrants, surveys, patents; county deed books from each county's formation onward
- **Date range:** Land grants begin 1681
- **Where held:** Pennsylvania State Archives (Land Office records); county Recorder of Deeds

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** French and Indian War (1754–1763), American Revolution (1775–1783)
- **Record types:** Revolutionary War service records, pension files, bounty land warrants; state militia records
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) for federal records; Pennsylvania State Archives for state militia; Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) for digitized military records
- **Quaker note:** Many Quakers were disowned for participation in the war; disownment proceedings in meeting minutes are a named record source

### Cemetery records
- **Quaker burial grounds:** Quaker meetings maintained their own burial grounds; burial records are part of the meeting's registers, held at Friends Historical Library and Haverford College
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has coverage of some Pennsylvania Quaker burial grounds
- **Physical records:** Meeting burial registers are held at Friends Historical Library and Haverford College

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Philadelphia had active newspapers in the late 1700s (e.g., Pennsylvania Gazette, Pennsylvania Packet)
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) has historical Pennsylvania newspapers; Library of Congress Chronicling America project
- **Content value:** Death notices, marriage announcements, sheriff's sales naming property owners

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia was the primary port of entry for Pennsylvania
- **Record types:** Philadelphia ship passenger lists; naturalization records in county courts (pre-1906, any court of record)
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); FamilySearch and Ancestry
- **Quaker relevance:** Certificates of removal function as internal migration records across the Quaker network; check both sending and receiving meeting records
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Property tax assessment lists, tax duplicates
- **Date range:** From the 1690s in some counties
- **Where held:** County archives and Pennsylvania State Archives
- **Substitute value:** Name heads of household and taxable property; the best census substitute before 1790 (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_Records)

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Collection 1999196 (Probate Records 1683–1994, 3.2M images, browse-only); Collection 1571957 (Civil Marriages 1677–1950); Collection 1502909 (Compiled Marriages 1700–1900); DGS 001188322 (Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes 1750–1800, browse-only) | Probate; colonial marriages; Quaker meeting minutes | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | 1790 census (first federal census) | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery Records (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Quaker burial grounds not otherwise indexed | Free |
| Fold3 | Military Records (https://www.fold3.com/) | Revolutionary War records | Subscription |
| NARA | National Archives (https://www.archives.gov/) | Passenger lists; federal military records | Free/In-person |

**Coverage of this survey:** 1 digitized volume matches the religious record type for Pennsylvania 1750–1800 in the FamilySearch volume search; this is the complete result set returned.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore College | Largest collection of American Quaker records; Pennsylvania monthly meeting minutes, certificates of removal, disownments, burial records | In-person; some records microfilmed by FamilySearch |
| Quaker and Special Collections, Haverford College | Quaker records and manuscripts | In-person |
| Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg | Land Office records, state militia records, tax assessments | In-person / online finding aids |
| County Register of Wills / Recorder of Deeds | Probate, deeds, county marriages | In-person / mail |

## Records NOT online
- Most individual monthly meeting minute books and registers (beyond the one Philadelphia Yearly Meeting volume) are not name-indexed online; FamilySearch microfilm of many meetings must be browsed image by image
- County tax assessment lists (most pre-1800)
- Pennsylvania Land Office warrants and surveys (many require in-person at Pennsylvania State Archives)
- Pre-1906 birth and death records were not registered; church records substitute

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey states that specific Pennsylvania Quaker meeting records were destroyed or lost for the target period. Consult the Pennsylvania State Archives and Friends Historical Library directly regarding any specific county or meeting record losses.

## Research tips
- Quaker meeting records serve as the functional equivalent of civil vital registration for Pennsylvania in 1750–1800; Pennsylvania did not mandate statewide registration until 1906 (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records; https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records).
- Always search for certificates of removal when a family appears to have moved — the sending meeting kept the original and the receiving meeting kept an acknowledgment, giving evidence in two repositories.
- Hinshaw's *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy* (6 volumes) is the standard published abstract of Pennsylvania meeting records; it is widely held in genealogical libraries and is the fastest way to survey a meeting before ordering microfilm.
- The Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes (DGS 001188322, 1750–1800, 145 images) must be browsed image by image — there is no name index and no full-text search capability.
- Tax assessment lists from the 1690s onward are the best census substitute for Pennsylvania before 1790 — search the county archives and Pennsylvania State Archives for the specific county and year (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_Records).
- When a county was formed from a parent county during the target period, search the parent county's probate, deed, and marriage records for dates before the formation.

- **Start date:** Statewide birth and death registration did not begin until 1906 at the state level (Philadelphia began county-level registration from 1860, Allegheny from 1870), per the FamilySearch Wiki at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records
- **What exists for 1750–1800:** No statewide civil vital records; church registers and county marriage records are the primary sources
- **Where held:** County courthouses hold marriage licenses and bonds from the colonial period; FamilySearch collection 1571957 (Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950, 312,045 records) and collection 1502909 (Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900, 198,765 records) cover the target period
- **Gaps:** No statewide birth or death registration for the target period; Quaker meeting records and other church registers must substitute

### Church records — Quaker (Friends) meetings
This is the central record series for tracing Quaker families in this period.

- **Record types:** Monthly meeting minutes recorded births, marriages, deaths, disownments, and certificates of removal (transfers between meetings); Quaker marriage certificates were signed by all witnesses present — often 20 or more names; quarterly and yearly meeting minutes recorded higher-level governance
- **Dense meeting areas:** Philadelphia Yearly Meeting governed Pennsylvania Quakers; monthly meetings in Chester County, Bucks County, Philadelphia County, and Delaware County had particularly dense Quaker populations (Wikipedia; https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records)
- **Where held:**
  - Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore College: the largest collection of American Quaker records (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records)
  - Quaker and Special Collections, Haverford College (Wikipedia)
  - FamilySearch has microfilmed many monthly meeting minutes and registers (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records)
- **Digitized volumes found:** 1 volume — Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes, 1750–1800 (DGS 001188322, 145 images). This volume is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable: it must be browsed image by image
- **Published abstracts:** William Wade Hinshaw's *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy* (6 volumes) abstracts Pennsylvania meeting records; widely held in genealogical libraries (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Published_Quaker_Abstracts)
- **Certificates of removal:** When a Quaker family moved, the sending meeting issued a removal certificate acknowledged by the receiving meeting — evidence exists in two locations and documents migration
- **Disownments:** Disciplinary proceedings name the person and reason; disowned members may have been reinstated, so follow both threads

### Church records — other denominations
- **Present:** Anglican/Episcopal, German Lutheran, German Reformed, Presbyterian, Mennonite, Moravian
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials
- **Where held:** Denominational archives and FamilySearch microfilm
- **Language:** German Lutheran and Reformed registers are often in German

### Census records
- **Federal census:** First federal census taken in 1790; indexed and available online for Pennsylvania
- **Pre-census substitutes:** Pennsylvania tax assessment lists survive from the 1690s in some counties and serve as census substitutes before 1790; the 1693 Chester County tax list is among the earliest surviving colonial records (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_Records)
- **State census:** No Pennsylvania state census is known for the target period

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, inventories, guardianships
- **Date range:** From the colonial period onward at the county Register of Wills (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_Records)
- **Where held:** County Register of Wills; FamilySearch collection 1999196 (Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994, 3,200,560 images) — browse-only, 0 name-indexed records
- **Testate or intestate:** Search wills first (testate); if none found, look for administration bonds and inventories (intestate)

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Penn's proprietary system)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania Land Office; the State Land Office in Harrisburg holds warrant, survey, and patent records from 1681 onward (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_Records)
- **Types:** Warrants, surveys, patents; county deed books from each county's formation onward
- **Date range:** Land grants begin 1681
- **Where held:** Pennsylvania State Archives (Land Office records); county Recorder of Deeds

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** French and Indian War (1754–1763), American Revolution (1775–1783)
- **Record types:** Revolutionary War service records, pension files, bounty land warrants; state militia records
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) for federal records; Pennsylvania State Archives for state militia; Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) for digitized military records
- **Quaker note:** Many Quakers were disowned for participation in the war; disownment proceedings in meeting minutes are a named record source

### Cemetery records
- **Quaker burial grounds:** Quaker meetings maintained their own burial grounds; burial records are part of the meeting's registers, held at Friends Historical Library and Haverford College
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has coverage of some Pennsylvania Quaker burial grounds
- **Physical records:** Meeting burial registers are held at Friends Historical Library and Haverford College

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Philadelphia had active newspapers in the late 1700s (e.g., Pennsylvania Gazette, Pennsylvania Packet)
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) has historical Pennsylvania newspapers; Library of Congress Chronicling America project
- **Content value:** Death notices, marriage announcements, sheriff's sales naming property owners

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia was the primary port of entry for Pennsylvania
- **Record types:** Philadelphia ship passenger lists; naturalization records in county courts (pre-1906, any court of record)
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); FamilySearch and Ancestry
- **Quaker relevance:** Certificates of removal function as internal migration records across the Quaker network; check both sending and receiving meeting records
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Property tax assessment lists, tax duplicates
- **Date range:** From the 1690s in some counties
- **Where held:** County archives and Pennsylvania State Archives
- **Substitute value:** Name heads of household and taxable property; the best census substitute before 1790 (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_Records)

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Collection 1999196 (Probate Records 1683–1994, 3.2M images, browse-only); Collection 1571957 (Civil Marriages 1677–1950); Collection 1502909 (Compiled Marriages 1700–1900); DGS 001188322 (Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes 1750–1800, browse-only) | Probate; colonial marriages; Quaker meeting minutes | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | 1790 census (first federal census) | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery Records (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Quaker burial grounds not otherwise indexed | Free |
| Fold3 | Military Records (https://www.fold3.com/) | Revolutionary War records | Subscription |
| NARA | National Archives (https://www.archives.gov/) | Passenger lists; federal military records | Free/In-person |

**Coverage of this survey:** 1 digitized volume matches the religious record type for Pennsylvania 1750–1800 in the FamilySearch volume search; this is the complete result set returned.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore College | Largest collection of American Quaker records; Pennsylvania monthly meeting minutes, certificates of removal, disownments, burial records | In-person; some records microfilmed by FamilySearch |
| Quaker and Special Collections, Haverford College | Quaker records and manuscripts | In-person |
| Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg | Land Office records, state militia records, tax assessments | In-person / online finding aids |
| County Register of Wills / Recorder of Deeds | Probate, deeds, county marriages | In-person / mail |

## Records NOT online
- Most individual monthly meeting minute books and registers (beyond the one Philadelphia Yearly Meeting volume) are not name-indexed online; FamilySearch microfilm of many meetings must be browsed image by image
- County tax assessment lists (most pre-1800)
- Pennsylvania Land Office warrants and surveys (many require in-person at Pennsylvania State Archives)
- Pre-1906 birth and death records were not registered; church records substitute

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey states that specific Pennsylvania Quaker meeting records were destroyed or lost for the target period. Consult the Pennsylvania State Archives and Friends Historical Library directly regarding any specific county or meeting record losses.

## Research tips
- Quaker meeting records serve as the functional equivalent of civil vital registration for Pennsylvania in 1750–1800; Pennsylvania did not mandate statewide registration until 1906 (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records; https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records).
- Always search for certificates of removal when a family appears to have moved — the sending meeting kept the original and the receiving meeting kept an acknowledgment, giving evidence in two repositories.
- Hinshaw's *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy* (6 volumes) is the standard published abstract of Pennsylvania meeting records; it is widely held in genealogical libraries and is the fastest way to survey a meeting before ordering microfilm.
- The Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes (DGS 001188322, 1750–1800, 145 images) must be browsed image by image — there is no name index and no full-text search capability.
- Tax assessment lists from the 1690s onward are the best census substitute for Pennsylvania before 1790 — search the county archives and Pennsylvania State Archives for the specific county and year (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_Records).
- When a county was formed from a parent county during the target period, search the parent county's probate, deed, and marriage records for dates before the formation.

Locality guide written as **loc_001**. Here is what the survey found:

---

## Pittsburgh, Allegheny County, Pennsylvania — Late 1800s Steel Boom (c. 1870–1900)

### Key Context

Pennsylvania had **no statewide civil registration** for births or deaths during this period. This makes ethnic church registers and other record types essential for vital events.

The **1890 federal census was destroyed by fire**, creating a critical ten-year gap. You must bridge it using:
- **1880 and 1900 federal censuses** (occupation columns are especially useful)
- **Pittsburgh city directories** (annual, held at the Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh)
- **County tax lists**

---

### Occupational & Industrial Records

- **Senator John Heinz History Center** (Pittsburgh) — holds fragmentary but surviving Carnegie Steel and related company records: employment files, payroll ledgers, and accident registers. These are **not online**.
- **Rivers of Steel National Heritage Area archives** (Pittsburgh) — additional industrial-era records. Also **not online**; in-person or correspondence visits required.

---

### Immigration & Naturalization

The steel industry drew large numbers of Polish, Slovak, Croatian, Italian, Irish, and German workers. **Naturalization files** are the single most valuable record for immigrant workers because they frequently name the exact European hometown and ship of arrival.

- **Allegheny County Courthouse** — naturalization records
- **NARA Philadelphia** — naturalization records for the federal courts

---

### Ethnic Church Records

Dozens of ethnic Catholic (and some Protestant and Orthodox) parishes organized specifically to serve mill-worker communities. Baptismal and burial registers from these parishes are the front-line source for vital events. Many are held at:
- Individual parish archives
- Diocesan archives (Diocese of Pittsburgh)
- Some have been microfilmed by FamilySearch

---

### Recommended Research Sequence

1. **Federal censuses (1870, 1880, 1900)** — identify the household, occupation, and birthplace
2. **Naturalization records** — establish European origin and arrival details
3. **Ethnic parish registers** — confirm vital events (birth/baptism, marriage, death/burial)
4. **City directories** — fill the 1890 gap, track residential and occupational mobility
5. **Industrial company records** — Heinz History Center and Rivers of Steel for employment details

---

### Note

The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Allegheny County vital, church, and land records were unreachable during this survey and returned only generic pages. This guide should be revisited once the wiki is accessible to confirm specific FamilySearch collection coverage.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Pittsburgh, Allegheny County, Pennsylvania (1870–1900)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Allegheny County was formed in 1788 from Washington and Westmoreland Counties; Pittsburgh dates from 1758.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Pittsburgh
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the survey tool for this location.
- **Economy:** Pittsburgh was the center of America's steel industry in the late 1800s; Andrew Carnegie's steel empire and other major firms anchored iron and steel production alongside glass, coke, and railroad industries (Wikipedia).
- **Ethnic composition:** Irish, German, Polish, Slovak, Croatian, and Italian immigrant workers poured into Pittsburgh and surrounding mill towns during this period (Wikipedia).
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic parishes organized along ethnic lines (Polish, Slovak, Croatian, Italian, Irish, German); Protestant denominations including Presbyterian, Methodist, Episcopal, Lutheran, and Baptist; Jewish congregations.
- **Key historical events:** Rapid industrial expansion drawing hundreds of thousands of immigrant workers throughout the 1870s–1900s; the Pittsburgh rail hub connected the city's products to national markets (Wikipedia).

## Boundary changes
- Allegheny County was formed in 1788 and its boundaries were stable throughout the 1870–1900 research period.

## Available record types

For each record type below, the jurisdictional level at which it is held is stated. No specific-page result was returned from the FamilySearch Wiki during this survey (see quirks); holding levels are drawn from collections_search and volume_search results supplemented by the wiki_search result for Allegheny County (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy).

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Pennsylvania did not maintain statewide civil registration for births or deaths during 1870–1900. The FamilySearch collection "Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906–1968" (collection 2255317) begins in 1906, confirming that statewide death registration was not in place during the target period. The FamilySearch Wiki vital records page was unreachable during this survey; re-run the locality guide to confirm exact registration levels and dates.
- **What exists:** County-level marriage records are available in two FamilySearch collections: "Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885–1950" (collection 1921317; 524,189 records; indexed + images) and "Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950" (collection 1571957; 312,045 records; indexed + images). A third compiled marriages set, "Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900" (collection 1502909; 198,765 records), covers through 1900 but has no images. No indexed birth or death collections for the 1870–1900 window were found at FamilySearch.
- **Where held:** County-level records at the Allegheny County Courthouse; FamilySearch online for the marriage collections named above.
- **Gaps:** No statewide birth or death registration during 1870–1900; marriage records may be incomplete before 1885.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptismal, marriage, and burial registers are the primary source for births and deaths in this period.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Catholic parishes organized by ethnicity (Polish, Slovak, Croatian, Italian, Irish, German), Protestant denominations, and Jewish congregations (Wikipedia).
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations.
- **Where held:** Individual parish and diocesan archives. The FamilySearch Wiki church records page was unreachable during this survey; consult it directly for which Allegheny County denominations have been microfilmed by FamilySearch.

Here is the locality guide for researching Philadelphia families during the 1793 yellow fever epidemic:

---

## Philadelphia, Pennsylvania — 1793 Yellow Fever Epidemic: Records & Repositories

**Survey period:** 1780–1810, focused on the epidemic year 1793

---

### The Core Challenge

Pennsylvania had **no civil registration in 1793** — statewide vital records didn't begin until 1906. This means epidemic deaths were recorded only church by church, across a diverse denominational landscape. The epidemic killed roughly **one in ten Philadelphia residents**, making this one of the most document-rich single events in early American genealogy — but the records are almost entirely offline.

---

### Key Records for the Epidemic Itself

| Record | What It Contains | Where Held |
|---|---|---|
| **Mathew Carey's published list of the dead** | Names of epidemic victims | Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP); also published in print |
| **Minutes of the Citizen Committee** | Relief and management records for the outbreak | Historical Society of Pennsylvania |
| **Bush Hill Fever Hospital records** | Patients treated at the epidemic hospital | Philadelphia City Archives |
| **Church burial registers** | Death records by congregation | Individual churches; HSP holds many |

> **Action:** Contact the **Historical Society of Pennsylvania** (hsp.org) and the **Philadelphia City Archives** for access to the Committee minutes, Bush Hill records, and Carey's list.

---

### Bracketing the Epidemic: Census & Tax Records

| Record | Years | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Federal Census** | 1790, 1800 | Bracket the epidemic; heads of household only |
| **Federal Direct Tax ("Two-Percent Tax")** | 1798 | Property lists — fills the gap between censuses |
| **Philadelphia City Directories** | Annual, 1785 onward | Names, occupations, addresses year by year |

---

### Church Records

Because vital registration didn't exist, **church records are essential**. Philadelphia's denominational diversity (Quaker, Anglican/Episcopal, Lutheran, German Reformed, Catholic, Presbyterian, Methodist, Jewish) means you must identify the family's congregation.

- **FamilySearch** holds browse-only images of the **Philadelphia Yearly Meeting (Quaker) minutes, 1750–1800** (image group 001188322, ~145 images). No name index — must be browsed page by page. If the family was Quaker, browse the 1792–1794 images.
- Many other church registers are held at **HSP** or at the churches themselves.

---

### Probate Records

- **Pennsylvania probate records from 1683 onward** are on FamilySearch (collection **1999196**) as browse-only images. Deaths from the epidemic would generate wills and administration files in Philadelphia County Orphans' Court, 1793–1795.

---

### Other FamilySearch Collections (Confirmed Available)

- **Pennsylvania civil and compiled marriages** — indexed on FamilySearch
- **1790 and 1800 federal censuses** — indexed on FamilySearch

---

### Recommended Next Steps

1. **If the family was Quaker:** Browse FamilySearch image group **001188322** for the Philadelphia Yearly Meeting minutes, years 1792–1794.
2. **For all other denominations:** Contact the **Historical Society of Pennsylvania** for Mathew Carey's list and the Committee minutes — these are the most direct sources for identifying epidemic victims by name.
3. **Check Philadelphia City Directories** for the family before and after 1793 to track disappearances.
4. **Search probate records** (FamilySearch collection 1999196) for 1793–1795 estate filings.

---

*Note: The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Philadelphia County vital records and church records returned generic results during this survey. Check them directly at familysearch.org/wiki before treating their absence here as definitive.*

# Locality Guide: Philadelphia, Pennsylvania (1780–1810, with focus on the 1793 Yellow Fever Epidemic)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Philadelphia County established 1682; the city of Philadelphia chartered 1701
- **County seat / administrative center:** Philadelphia (city and county seat were the same location until 1854 consolidation)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States
- **Population during period:** Approximately 50,000 in 1793 (Wikipedia: Yellow fever epidemic of 1793, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow_fever_epidemic_of_1793)
- **Economy:** Dominant port city; commerce, shipping, artisan trades, printing; seat of the federal government until 1800
- **Ethnic composition:** English Quaker founding stock, significant German, Scots-Irish, Irish, and free Black communities; city was diverse even by 1793
- **Religious denominations:** Anglican/Episcopal (Christ Church), Lutheran, German Reformed, Presbyterian, Methodist, Catholic, Baptist, Jewish, Quaker (Friends), Swedish Lutheran (Gloria Dei/Old Swedes')
- **Key historical events:** 1793 yellow fever epidemic (August–November) killed approximately 5,000 residents; thousands fled the city; federal government temporarily relocated; Bush Hill established as a fever hospital

## Boundary changes
- In 1793 the city of Philadelphia occupied only the core of Philadelphia County — most of the county was made up of smaller townships (Germantown, Kensington, Northern Liberties, Southwark, etc.).
- The city and the county were legally separate jurisdictions until the Act of Consolidation in 1854 merged them. For events before 1854, determine whether the event occurred in the city proper or in one of the surrounding townships, as records may be held under different jurisdictions.
- No boundary changes to the county itself during the 1780–1810 period have been confirmed by tool results.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Pennsylvania statewide registration began in 1906. No civil registration existed in Pennsylvania in 1793. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki, Philadelphia Genealogy, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records)
- **What exists:** No birth, marriage, or death certificates for the 1793 period. Church records are the only vital-record source.
- **Where held:** Church archives, Historical Society of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia City Archives
- **Gaps:** Total absence of civil vital records before 1906 statewide; the epidemic's heavy mortality created a surge in church burial registrations in late 1793 that may be incomplete given the volume of deaths
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism/burial registers, Mathew Carey's published list of epidemic dead, Committee minutes, Bush Hill hospital records, probate inventories, newspaper death notices

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Anglican/Episcopal (Christ Church, founded 1695), Swedish Lutheran (Gloria Dei/Old Swedes', founded 1642), Quaker (Philadelphia Yearly Meeting, founded 1681), Presbyterian, Lutheran, German Reformed, Catholic, Methodist, Baptist
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations; Quaker meeting minutes (which record births, marriages, and deaths of Friends)
- **Where held:** Individual church archives; many early registers transcribed and held by the Historical Society of Pennsylvania; Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania has compiled indexes to many Philadelphia church records (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records)
- **Epidemic-specific note:** Burial records from Christ Church and Gloria Dei (Old Swedes') are specifically cited as key genealogical sources for 1793 epidemic deaths (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793)
- **FamilySearch digitized volume:** Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes (1750–1800), image group 001188322, 145 images — browse-only, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable
- **Language:** English; some German Lutheran and German Reformed registers in German

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1790 federal census precedes the epidemic and covers Philadelphia; 1800 and 1810 federal censuses cover the post-epidemic period. These are name-indexed on Ancestry and FamilySearch.
- **State/provincial census:** Pennsylvania did not conduct a state census in this period.
- **Other enumerations:** Philadelphia City Directory series (began 1785) is an effective annual substitute; lists heads of household by address and occupation. Gaps in directory coverage are a known issue.
- **Access:** 1790, 1800, and 1810 federal censuses are indexed and freely available on FamilySearch and Ancestry.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, letters of administration, estate inventories, guardianship files, petitions
- **Epidemic relevance:** The 1793 epidemic produced a surge in estate filings; intestate administrations are especially common for those who died suddenly without time to prepare wills
- **Date range:** Philadelphia County probate records survive from the colonial period; Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683–1994 (collection 1999196) is on FamilySearch with 3,200,560 images but 0 name-indexed — browse-only
- **Where held:** Philadelphia City Archives (originals); FamilySearch collection 1999196 provides browse-only images

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Penn proprietorship)
- **Types:** Deeds, grants, patents, mortgages, ground rents (ground rent was a common Philadelphia tenure), tax records
- **Date range:** Philadelphia County deed records from the colonial era
- **Where held:** Philadelphia City Archives (Recorder of Deeds); Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) for proprietary land records; FamilySearch-specific land collection pages for Philadelphia were unavailable during this survey

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Revolutionary War (1775–1783) immediately precedes the period; War of 1812 falls at its close
- **Record types:** Revolutionary War service and pension records, bounty land warrants, War of 1812 service records
- **Where held:** National Archives and Records Administration (NARA, https://www.archives.gov/); Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) for digitized military records; Pennsylvania State Archives for state militia records
- **Epidemic note:** Some epidemic relief committee members and medical volunteers are named in committee minutes held at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Christ Church Burial Ground, Gloria Dei (Old Swedes') burial ground, Quaker burial grounds, St. Mary's Catholic churchyard, Methodist burial grounds
- **Epidemic context:** Epidemic burials in 1793 were sometimes hasty and not fully recorded; the Committee established a temporary burial site (Potter's Field area)
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has coverage for many Philadelphia historic cemeteries
- **Physical records:** Sexton's records where extant are held by individual churches or the Historical Society of Pennsylvania

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Dunlap's American Daily Advertiser (1791–), Philadelphia Gazette, Gazette of the United States — all published during the epidemic; they carried death notices, announcements of departure from the city, and business closures
- **Epidemic-specific:** Mathew Carey's pamphlet "A Short Account of the Malignant Fever" (1793) includes lists of the dead and is cited as a key genealogical source (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793)
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) for digitized papers; Library of Congress Chronicling America; American Antiquarian Society

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia was a major port of entry throughout this period
- **Record types:** Passenger lists (Philadelphia customs records), naturalization records (filed in Common Pleas Court, pre-1906)
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) holds Philadelphia customs passenger lists; FamilySearch and Ancestry have indexes
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Philadelphia County tax assessments
- **Date range:** Colonial-era tax lists survive and continue through the early national period; the 1798 Federal Direct Tax ("Glass Tax") is a valuable national enumeration
- **Where held:** Pennsylvania State Archives; some transcribed by the Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists substitute effectively for missing census years and can place a family in a specific ward or township

### Epidemic-specific records (unique to 1793 research)
- **Mathew Carey's list:** A published account including names of those who died; a key finding aid for locating epidemic deaths
- **Committee minutes:** Minutes and reports of the Committee appointed by the citizens of Philadelphia to attend to and alleviate the sufferings of the afflicted with the malignant fever — name both the dead and relief recipients; held at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania and Philadelphia City Archives (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793)
- **Bush Hill hospital records:** Records of the fever hospital established during the epidemic; named patients and staff; held at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683–1994 (collection 1999196, 3.2M browse-only images); Pennsylvania Civil Marriages 1677–1950 (collection 1571957, 312,045 records); Pennsylvania Compiled Marriages 1700–1900 (collection 1502909, 198,765 records); Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes 1750–1800 (vol 001188322, browse-only) | Pre-civil-registration vital events; Quaker records; probate | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | 1790, 1800, 1810 census; indexed search | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery Records (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Philadelphia historic burial grounds | Free |
| Fold3 | Military Records (https://www.fold3.com/) | Revolutionary War and War of 1812 service | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Newspapers (https://www.newspapers.com/) | 1793 death notices and epidemic coverage | Subscription |
| NARA | National Archives (https://www.archives.gov/) | Passenger lists, federal military, naturalization | Free/request |

**Coverage of this survey:** Volume_search returned 1 digitized volume matching Philadelphia for this period. This is the complete result set — no additional pages exist.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Philadelphia City Archives | City and county vital records, deeds, probate, Committee minutes, municipal records | In-person; some records available on request |
| Historical Society of Pennsylvania | Church register transcriptions, Mathew Carey's list, Committee minutes, Bush Hill hospital records, manuscript collections, city directories | In-person; some digitized |
| Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania | Compiled indexes to Philadelphia church records; published volumes of abstracts | In-person; interlibrary loan for publications |
| Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) | Proprietary land records, state militia, colonial-era records | In-person; some online |
| Individual church archives | Original baptism, marriage, and burial registers | Contact each denomination directly |

## Records NOT online
- Original church baptism, marriage, and burial registers for most Philadelphia congregations
- Original Philadelphia Committee minutes and Bush Hill hospital records (held at Historical Society of Pennsylvania and Philadelphia City Archives — physical access)
- Philadelphia County deed and mortgage books for 1780–1810
- Philadelphia City Directory volumes (most not digitized beyond library microfilm)
- Original Quaker meeting records beyond the 1750–1800 minutes volume on FamilySearch

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey identified specific record losses for Philadelphia County vital, church, or probate records in the 1780–1810 period. The 1793 epidemic's high mortality may have produced incomplete church burial registers given the volume of deaths in a compressed period (August–November 1793), but no tool result confirms a specific loss. Consult the Historical Society of Pennsylvania and Philadelphia City Archives directly to verify the completeness of any specific register.

## Research tips
- For epidemic deaths, start with Mathew Carey's published list of the dead and the minutes of the citizen Committee before turning to church registers — they were compiled specifically to document epidemic mortality and name many individuals who may have been buried without full church ceremony (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793).
- Church records are the only vital-record source for 1793; Pennsylvania statewide registration did not begin until 1906. Identify the decedent's or family's denomination before searching registers, as records are held church by church, not in a centralized repository (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records).
- The 1790 federal census (taken just before the epidemic) and the 1800 census (taken seven years after) together bracket the epidemic — a name absent from the 1800 census that appeared in 1790 may indicate an epidemic death or emigration from the city.
- Philadelphia City Directories beginning in 1785 list heads of household annually and can track a family's presence, departure, or disappearance across the epidemic years — particularly useful given the gap between federal censuses.
- The 1798 Federal Direct Tax ("Glass Tax") enumerates property owners in Philadelphia County and is an effective substitute census mid-way between the 1790 and 1800 federal enumerations.
- Probate records surged after the 1793 epidemic; search Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683–1994 (FamilySearch collection 1999196) by browsing the relevant Philadelphia County volumes for 1793–1795 — the images are not name-indexed and must be browsed page by page.
- FamilySearch specific wiki pages for Philadelphia vital records, church records, and land records all resolved to a generic page during this survey — verify current availability at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/ before treating their absence as confirmed.

FamilySearch specific wiki pages for Philadelphia County vital records, church records, and land records all resolved to a generic page during this survey — consult the FamilySearch Wiki directly for Philadelphia County before treating their absence as confirmed.
The Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania has compiled indexes to many Philadelphia church records; check their published works at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania or through interlibrary loan.
Philadelphia was the capital of the United States in 1793; some federal-level records (congressional proceedings, executive papers) may incidentally name Philadelphia residents.
added.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Philadelphia, Pennsylvania (1780–1810, with focus on the 1793 Yellow Fever Epidemic)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Philadelphia County established 1682; the city of Philadelphia chartered 1701
- **County seat / administrative center:** Philadelphia (city and county seat were the same location until 1854 consolidation)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States
- **Population during period:** Approximately 50,000 in 1793 (Wikipedia: Yellow fever epidemic of 1793, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow_fever_epidemic_of_1793)
- **Economy:** Dominant port city; commerce, shipping, artisan trades, printing; seat of the federal government until 1800
- **Ethnic composition:** English Quaker founding stock, significant German, Scots-Irish, Irish, and free Black communities; city was diverse even by 1793
- **Religious denominations:** Anglican/Episcopal (Christ Church), Lutheran, German Reformed, Presbyterian, Methodist, Catholic, Baptist, Jewish, Quaker (Friends), Swedish Lutheran (Gloria Dei/Old Swedes')
- **Key historical events:** 1793 yellow fever epidemic (August–November) killed approximately 5,000 residents; thousands fled the city; federal government temporarily relocated; Bush Hill established as a fever hospital

## Boundary changes
- In 1793 the city of Philadelphia occupied only the core of Philadelphia County — most of the county was made up of smaller townships (Germantown, Kensington, Northern Liberties, Southwark, etc.).
- The city and the county were legally separate jurisdictions until the Act of Consolidation in 1854 merged them. For events before 1854, determine whether the event occurred in the city proper or in one of the surrounding townships, as records may be held under different jurisdictions.
- No boundary changes to the county itself during the 1780–1810 period have been confirmed by tool results.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Pennsylvania statewide registration began in 1906. No civil registration existed in Pennsylvania in 1793. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki, Philadelphia Genealogy, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records)
- **What exists:** No birth, marriage, or death certificates for the 1793 period. Church records are the only vital-record source.
- **Where held:** Church archives, Historical Society of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia City Archives
- **Gaps:** Total absence of civil vital records before 1906 statewide; the epidemic's heavy mortality created a surge in church burial registrations in late 1793 that may be incomplete given the volume of deaths
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism/burial registers, Mathew Carey's published list of epidemic dead, Committee minutes, Bush Hill hospital records, probate inventories, newspaper death notices

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Anglican/Episcopal (Christ Church, founded 1695), Swedish Lutheran (Gloria Dei/Old Swedes', founded 1642), Quaker (Philadelphia Yearly Meeting, founded 1681), Presbyterian, Lutheran, German Reformed, Catholic, Methodist, Baptist
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations; Quaker meeting minutes (which record births, marriages, and deaths of Friends)
- **Where held:** Individual church archives; many early registers transcribed and held by the Historical Society of Pennsylvania; Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania has compiled indexes to many Philadelphia church records (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records)
- **Epidemic-specific note:** Burial records from Christ Church and Gloria Dei (Old Swedes') are specifically cited as key genealogical sources for 1793 epidemic deaths (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793)
- **FamilySearch digitized volume:** Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes (1750–1800), image group 001188322, 145 images — browse-only, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable
- **Language:** English; some German Lutheran and German Reformed registers in German

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1790 federal census precedes the epidemic and covers Philadelphia; 1800 and 1810 federal censuses cover the post-epidemic period. These are name-indexed on Ancestry and FamilySearch.
- **State/provincial census:** Pennsylvania did not conduct a state census in this period.
- **Other enumerations:** Philadelphia City Directory series (began 1785) is an effective annual substitute; lists heads of household by address and occupation. Gaps in directory coverage are a known issue.
- **Access:** 1790, 1800, and 1810 federal censuses are indexed and freely available on FamilySearch and Ancestry.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, letters of administration, estate inventories, guardianship files, petitions
- **Epidemic relevance:** The 1793 epidemic produced a surge in estate filings; intestate administrations are especially common for those who died suddenly without time to prepare wills
- **Date range:** Philadelphia County probate records survive from the colonial period; Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683–1994 (collection 1999196) is on FamilySearch with 3,200,560 images but 0 name-indexed — browse-only
- **Where held:** Philadelphia City Archives (originals); FamilySearch collection 1999196 provides browse-only images

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Penn proprietorship)
- **Types:** Deeds, grants, patents, mortgages, ground rents (ground rent was a common Philadelphia tenure), tax records
- **Date range:** Philadelphia County deed records from the colonial era
- **Where held:** Philadelphia City Archives (Recorder of Deeds); Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) for proprietary land records; FamilySearch-specific land collection pages for Philadelphia were unavailable during this survey

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Revolutionary War (1775–1783) immediately precedes the period; War of 1812 falls at its close
- **Record types:** Revolutionary War service and pension records, bounty land warrants, War of 1812 service records
- **Where held:** National Archives and Records Administration (NARA, https://www.archives.gov/); Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) for digitized military records; Pennsylvania State Archives for state militia records
- **Epidemic note:** Some epidemic relief committee members and medical volunteers are named in committee minutes held at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Christ Church Burial Ground, Gloria Dei (Old Swedes') burial ground, Quaker burial grounds, St. Mary's Catholic churchyard, Methodist burial grounds
- **Epidemic context:** Epidemic burials in 1793 were sometimes hasty and not fully recorded; the Committee established a temporary burial site (Potter's Field area)
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has coverage for many Philadelphia historic cemeteries
- **Physical records:** Sexton's records where extant are held by individual churches or the Historical Society of Pennsylvania

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Dunlap's American Daily Advertiser (1791–), Philadelphia Gazette, Gazette of the United States — all published during the epidemic; they carried death notices, announcements of departure from the city, and business closures
- **Epidemic-specific:** Mathew Carey's pamphlet "A Short Account of the Malignant Fever" (1793) includes lists of the dead and is cited as a key genealogical source (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793)
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) for digitized papers; Library of Congress Chronicling America; American Antiquarian Society

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia was a major port of entry throughout this period
- **Record types:** Passenger lists (Philadelphia customs records), naturalization records (filed in Common Pleas Court, pre-1906)
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) holds Philadelphia customs passenger lists; FamilySearch and Ancestry have indexes
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Philadelphia County tax assessments
- **Date range:** Colonial-era tax lists survive and continue through the early national period; the 1798 Federal Direct Tax ("Glass Tax") is a valuable national enumeration
- **Where held:** Pennsylvania State Archives; some transcribed by the Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists substitute effectively for missing census years and can place a family in a specific ward or township

### Epidemic-specific records (unique to 1793 research)
- **Mathew Carey's list:** A published account including names of those who died; a key finding aid for locating epidemic deaths
- **Committee minutes:** Minutes and reports of the Committee appointed by the citizens of Philadelphia to attend to and alleviate the sufferings of the afflicted with the malignant fever — name both the dead and relief recipients; held at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania and Philadelphia City Archives (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793)
- **Bush Hill hospital records:** Records of the fever hospital established during the epidemic; named patients and staff; held at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683–1994 (collection 1999196, 3.2M browse-only images); Pennsylvania Civil Marriages 1677–1950 (collection 1571957, 312,045 records); Pennsylvania Compiled Marriages 1700–1900 (collection 1502909, 198,765 records); Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes 1750–1800 (vol 001188322, browse-only) | Pre-civil-registration vital events; Quaker records; probate | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | 1790, 1800, 1810 census; indexed search | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery Records (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Philadelphia historic burial grounds | Free |
| Fold3 | Military Records (https://www.fold3.com/) | Revolutionary War and War of 1812 service | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Newspapers (https://www.newspapers.com/) | 1793 death notices and epidemic coverage | Subscription |
| NARA | National Archives (https://www.archives.gov/) | Passenger lists, federal military, naturalization | Free/request |

**Coverage of this survey:** Volume_search returned 1 digitized volume matching Philadelphia for this period. This is the complete result set — no additional pages exist.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Philadelphia City Archives | City and county vital records, deeds, probate, Committee minutes, municipal records | In-person; some records available on request |
| Historical Society of Pennsylvania | Church register transcriptions, Mathew Carey's list, Committee minutes, Bush Hill hospital records, manuscript collections, city directories | In-person; some digitized |
| Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania | Compiled indexes to Philadelphia church records; published volumes of abstracts | In-person; interlibrary loan for publications |
| Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) | Proprietary land records, state militia, colonial-era records | In-person; some online |
| Individual church archives | Original baptism, marriage, and burial registers | Contact each denomination directly |

## Records NOT online
- Original church baptism, marriage, and burial registers for most Philadelphia congregations
- Original Philadelphia Committee minutes and Bush Hill hospital records (held at Historical Society of Pennsylvania and Philadelphia City Archives — physical access)
- Philadelphia County deed and mortgage books for 1780–1810
- Philadelphia City Directory volumes (most not digitized beyond library microfilm)
- Original Quaker meeting records beyond the 1750–1800 minutes volume on FamilySearch

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey identified specific record losses for Philadelphia County vital, church, or probate records in the 1780–1810 period. The 1793 epidemic's high mortality may have produced incomplete church burial registers given the volume of deaths in a compressed period (August–November 1793), but no tool result confirms a specific loss. Consult the Historical Society of Pennsylvania and Philadelphia City Archives directly to verify the completeness of any specific register.

## Research tips
- For epidemic deaths, start with Mathew Carey's published list of the dead and the minutes of the citizen Committee before turning to church registers — they were compiled specifically to document epidemic mortality and name many individuals who may have been buried without full church ceremony (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793).
- Church records are the only vital-record source for 1793; Pennsylvania statewide registration did not begin until 1906. Identify the decedent's or family's denomination before searching registers, as records are held church by church, not in a centralized repository (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records).
- The 1790 federal census (taken just before the epidemic) and the 1800 census (taken seven years after) together bracket the epidemic — a name absent from the 1800 census that appeared in 1790 may indicate an epidemic death or emigration from the city.
- Philadelphia City Directories beginning in 1785 list heads of household annually and can track a family's presence, departure, or disappearance across the epidemic years — particularly useful given the gap between federal censuses.
- The 1798 Federal Direct Tax ("Glass Tax") enumerates property owners in Philadelphia County and is an effective substitute census mid-way between the 1790 and 1800 federal enumerations.
- Probate records surged after the 1793 epidemic; search Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683–1994 (FamilySearch collection 1999196) by browsing the relevant Philadelphia County volumes for 1793–1795 — the images are not name-indexed and must be browsed page by page.
- FamilySearch specific wiki pages for Philadelphia vital records, church records, and land records all resolved to a generic page during this survey — verify current availability at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/ before treating their absence as confirmed.
