Plymouth Colony was a separate entity founded 1620 and remained distinct until both merged into the Province of Massachusetts Bay in 1691.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Boston (Massachusetts Bay Colony); Plymouth (Plymouth Colony)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** English Crown; Province of Massachusetts Bay from 1691
- **Population during period:** Approximately 20,000 settlers in the Great Migration alone (1630–1640); no population figures returned by the tools surveyed for this exact period.
- **Economy:** Agriculture, fishing, trade, shipbuilding — these shaped record-keeping in that ships' logs, merchant ledgers, and town land grants supplemented civil registers.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English Puritan settlers; small numbers of other European backgrounds.
- **Religious denominations:** Congregational (Puritan) was the established church of the colony from the 1630s. Quakers arrived ca. 1650s and faced colonial persecution until the late 1670s. Baptists and a small Anglican presence also existed.
- **Key historical events:** Great Migration 1630–1640; Pequot War 1636–1638; King Philip's War 1675–1676 (destroyed several towns and their records); Salem witch trials 1692; merger of Plymouth Colony and Massachusetts Bay Colony in 1691.

## Boundary changes
- Plymouth Colony (1620–1691) operated entirely separately from Massachusetts Bay Colony (1628–1691). Their records are indexed and published separately; research prior to 1691 must establish which colony the ancestor lived in.
- In 1691 both colonies merged into the Province of Massachusetts Bay. Records from that date forward fall under the unified province.
- King Philip's War (1675–1676) resulted in the destruction of a number of towns in central and western Massachusetts; some earliest town records were lost in those events.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Town-level recording of births, marriages, and deaths was mandated by the colony starting in **1639** — at the **town level**, not county or statewide. ([Massachusetts Genealogy — Colonial Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records))
- **What exists:** Town clerk registers of births, marriages, and deaths from 1639 onward in surviving town books; compliance and survival vary significantly by town.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 2061550, "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890," approximately 3.4 million records, covers this period and is indexed. Town originals are held by each town clerk and by the Massachusetts Archives (Boston). The published "Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850" series (Tanner–Corbin series) abstracts town clerk records for over 200 Massachusetts towns and is widely held in research libraries.
- **Gaps:** No statewide civil registration existed during this period. Towns destroyed in King Philip's War (1675–1676) may have lost earliest records. Individual town diligence in recording varied.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Congregational church baptism, marriage, and burial records; probate records naming heirs and relationships; county court records.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Congregational (established church from the 1630s); Quakers (from ca. 1650s); Baptists; small Anglican presence.
- **Record types:** Congregational meeting records include membership rolls, baptisms, marriages, ecclesiastical disciplinary proceedings (trials, excommunications, admonishments), and burial records. ([Massachusetts Church Records — Congregational](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational))
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1921657, "Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920," approximately 987,654 records. - **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Town proprietors granted land within townships; the Massachusetts Bay Colony and Plymouth Colony governments granted townships. # Locality Guide: Oklahoma (1889–1910)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** The Land Run of April 22, 1889, opened the Unassigned Lands. Oklahoma Territory was formally created May 2, 1890, by the Organic Act; Oklahoma became the 46th state on November 16, 1907, when Oklahoma Territory and Indian Territory merged.
- **Administrative center:** Guthrie (territorial capital 1890–1907); Oklahoma City became state capital at statehood.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Federal (General Land Office) through the territorial period; Indian Territory governed eastern Oklahoma under tribal councils and federal oversight.
- **Population during period:** An estimated 50,000 participants entered the initial Land Run of 1889. No population figures were returned by the survey tool for this period.
- **Economy:** Subsistence homesteading and farming; cattle ranching; oil discovered near Bartlesville in 1897.
- **Ethnic composition:** Anglo-American settlers from Kansas, Texas, Missouri, and surrounding states; Five Civilized Tribes (Cherokee, Choctaw, Creek, Chickasaw, Seminole) in Indian Territory; freedmen communities on tribal rolls.
- **Religious denominations:** Methodist, Baptist, Presbyterian, and Catholic congregations formed rapidly from 1889; mission churches pre-dated settlement in Indian Territory.
- **Key historical events:** Land Run of April 22, 1889; subsequent land openings in 1891, 1892, 1893, and 1895; Organic Act 1890; Dawes Commission enrollment 1898–1906; statehood 1907.

## Boundary changes
- Before April 22, 1889, the area had no organized civil government for settlers — it was administered as Indian Territory.
- Oklahoma Territory created May 2, 1890, with organized county government beginning then; county boundaries continued shifting with each land opening through 1895.
- Indian Territory (eastern Oklahoma) remained separately governed until statehood in 1907.
- County boundaries were still forming through the territorial period — a research location's county in 1891 may differ from its county in 1907.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** A statewide vital registration start date for Oklahoma was not confirmed from a fetched FamilySearch Wiki page (all Oklahoma-specific pages returned only generic content in this survey). County-level marriage records at FamilySearch begin from 1890 per collection 2134789.
- **What exists:** County marriages from 1890, indexed at FamilySearch (collection 2134789, 456,789 records / 913,578 persons, 1890–1995). Birth and death civil registration during the territorial period was incomplete; specific start dates were not confirmed from a fetched wiki page.
- **Where held:** County clerk at the county courthouse for marriages; Oklahoma State Department of Health for later births and deaths.
- **Gaps:** Civil birth and death registration was inconsistent or absent for most of the territorial period 1889–1907.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Homestead final proof files (name wife and children as witnesses), church records (collection 1654321), Dawes Commission enrollment jackets for families of Native American descent.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Methodist, Baptist, Presbyterian, and Catholic congregations established from 1889 onwards; mission churches pre-dating settlement in Indian Territory.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1654321, "Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965" (123,456 records), at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1654321; denominational archives; Oklahoma Historical Society.
- **Gaps:** Most Protestant congregations were newly formed after 1889; systematic record-keeping may not begin until 1890–1895.
- **Language:** English.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** The 1890 federal census was destroyed by fire nationwide. Oklahoma Territory has a surviving 1890 special territorial census — described as one of the few surviving 1890 census records in the nation — held by the Oklahoma Historical Society (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run). The 1900 and 1910 federal censuses are available and indexed.
- **State/provincial census:** Territorial censuses were taken in 1890; county-level enumerations may exist for some counties in the 1890s.
- **Other enumerations:** County-level tax rolls from the 1890s help document early settlers (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts).
- **Access:** 1900 and 1910 federal censuses are indexed and searchable on FamilySearch and Ancestry. The 1890 territorial census at the Oklahoma Historical Society may require an in-person visit or mail request.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories; district court civil and criminal cases.
- **Date range:** From county organization, 1890 onwards; territorial district courts served 1890–1907.
- **Where held:** Territorial district court records 1890–1907 are at the National Archives at Fort Worth and the Oklahoma State Archives (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts). County-level probate records are at county courthouses.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Rectangular survey (township-range-section) — Oklahoma is a federal land state.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The General Land Office (federal) administered homestead claims; initial filings were at the land offices in Guthrie and Kingfisher (source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land_Run_of_1889). Patents are searchable at the BLM General Land Office Records website (glorecords.blm.gov).
- **Types:** Homestead applications, final certificates, land patents, rejected applications; Dawes allotment records for Indian Territory families.
- **Date range:** Land-entry case files from 1889 onwards.
- **Where held:**
  - imageGroup 005221388: 402 images, 74% name-indexed (indexed + images), "Land-entry case files / homestead final proofs," 1889–1907.
  - imageGroup 005221389: 176 images, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable (browse-only images), "Dawes Commission enrollment jackets," 1898–1910.
  - FamilySearch collection 1541872, "Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907" (234,567 records), https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1541872.
  - National Archives RG49 (General Land Office) for the full homestead file series; also accessible at glorecords.blm.gov (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run).

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Spanish-American War (1898); Civil War pension files for veteran settlers who participated in the Land Run.
- **Record types:** Service records and pension files at NARA; Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) for digitized military records.
- **Where held:** National Archives and Records Administration (https://www.archives.gov/).

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Town cemeteries established in boomtowns from 1889 onwards; many rural burial grounds associated with homestead claims.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/).
- **Physical records:** Sexton records where towns had organized cemeteries; many rural graves are unrecorded.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Newspapers established rapidly in boomtowns after 1889 — Guthrie and Kingfisher had papers within days of the Land Run; most towns had papers by 1890.
- **Where held:** Oklahoma Historical Society; digitized newspapers at Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/).
- **Content value:** Land claim notices, marriage notices, obituaries, legal notices.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Most Land Run settlers arrived overland from Kansas, Texas, and Missouri; ocean passenger lists are relevant only for those who immigrated to the U.S. before moving to Oklahoma.
- **Record types:** Naturalization records in territorial district court files (pre-1906 naturalizations can appear in any court of record); passenger lists at NARA for earlier trans-Atlantic arrivals.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) for naturalization records; National Archives at Fort Worth for territorial court records.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** County-level property and poll tax rolls.
- **Date range:** From county organization, 1890 onwards.
- **Where held:** County courthouse and Oklahoma State Archives.
- **Substitute value:** Tax rolls substitute for the destroyed 1890 federal census and fill the gap between the 1890 territorial census and the 1900 federal census.

### Other record types
- **Indian censuses and rolls:** FamilySearch collection 1987432, "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959" (567,890 records), https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987432. Essential for families with Native American ancestry or any family in Indian Territory.
- **Dawes Commission enrollment jackets:** imageGroup 005221389 (176 browse-only images, 1898–1910) — enrollment files for the Five Civilized Tribes, including family data, ages, and relationships. No name index; must be browsed image by image.
- **City directories:** Territorial-era directories exist for Guthrie, Oklahoma City, and larger towns from the mid-1890s; held at the Oklahoma Historical Society.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Collection 1541872: Early Land Records 1834–1907 (234,567 records); Collection 1987432: Indian Censuses and Rolls (567,890 records); Collection 2134789: County Marriages 1890–1995 (456,789 records); Collection 1654321: Mission and Church Records 1820–1965 (123,456 records) | Land run homestead filings; Indian Territory families; marriages from 1890; church records | Free |
| BLM General Land Office Records (glorecords.blm.gov) | Land patents and homestead files | Missing patent information not in county deed indexes | Free |
| Ancestry.com (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | U.S. Federal Census Collection | 1900 and 1910 censuses for territorial/early state settlers | Subscription |
| Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) | Military records | Service and pension records for veteran Land Run settlers | Subscription |
| FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Cemetery records | Rural and town burial grounds | Free |
| NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) | RG49 GLO records; territorial court records | Full homestead case files; naturalization and territorial court records | In-person / NARA Online |

**Coverage of this survey:** 2 digitized volumes matching Oklahoma 1889–1910 were found and both are detailed above (volume_search returned the complete result set with no further pages). The 4 FamilySearch collections above are the complete indexed set returned for Oklahoma.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Oklahoma Historical Society, Oklahoma City | 1890 territorial census; territorial newspapers; city directories; county records | In-person; some holdings digitized |
| Oklahoma State Archives, Oklahoma City | Territorial district court records; state agency records post-1907 | In-person; mail request |
| National Archives at Fort Worth, TX | Territorial court records 1890–1907; federal land office records | In-person; reproductions by mail |
| National Archives, Washington DC / College Park | RG49 General Land Office; military pension files | In-person; NARA Online |
| County courthouses | Deed books; probate records; marriage licenses | In-person / mail |

## Records NOT online
- 1890 special territorial census (held by Oklahoma Historical Society — not confirmed as fully digitized in this survey)
- County tax rolls and poll books from the 1890s
- Full homestead case files beyond what FamilySearch collection 1541872 covers
- Territorial district court civil and criminal case files at National Archives at Fort Worth
- City directory collections for territorial-era towns
- Dawes Commission enrollment jackets (imageGroup 005221389) are online but browse-only — no name index

## Known record losses
- The 1890 federal census was destroyed by fire nationwide. Oklahoma's special territorial census of 1890 survives at the Oklahoma Historical Society (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run). No other specific record losses for Oklahoma were stated by tool results in this survey.

## Research tips
- Start with homestead files. For any family that participated in the Land Run, the homestead final proof file is the richest single record — it names the applicant, often their spouse and children as witnesses, and includes residence affidavits that can confirm arrival dates and origins. Search FamilySearch collection 1541872, imageGroup 005221388, and glorecords.blm.gov. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run)
- Use the 1890 territorial census. Because the 1890 federal census was destroyed, Oklahoma's territorial census is irreplaceable for families who arrived in the first year of settlement. Contact the Oklahoma Historical Society.
- Trace origins before researching Oklahoma. Most Land Run settlers came from Kansas, Texas, and Missouri — once you document an Oklahoma homestead, search departure-state records (1880 census, departure-state vital records, church records) to identify parents and siblings. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts)
- Distinguish Oklahoma Territory from Indian Territory. Western Oklahoma was Oklahoma Territory (organized civil government from 1890); eastern Oklahoma was Indian Territory, governed by tribal councils until 1907. The record series differ substantially — Indian Territory families require collection 1987432 and imageGroup 005221389.
- County boundaries were still forming. Verify the county at each research date before searching courthouse records.
- Tax rolls substitute for the 1890s gap. County tax rolls survive and can pinpoint a settler in a specific township between the 1890 territorial census and the 1900 federal census. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts)

- **Indian censuses and rolls:** FamilySearch collection 1987432, "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959" (567,890 records), https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987432. Essential for families with Native American ancestry or any family in Indian Territory.
- **Dawes Commission enrollment jackets:** imageGroup 005221389 (176 browse-only images, 1898–1910) — enrollment files for the Five Civilized Tribes, including family data, ages, and relationships. No name index; must be browsed image by image.
- **City directories:** Territorial-era directories exist for Guthrie, Oklahoma City, and larger towns from the mid-1890s; held at the Oklahoma Historical Society.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Collection 1541872: Early Land Records 1834–1907 (234,567 records); Collection 1987432: Indian Censuses and Rolls (567,890 records); Collection 2134789: County Marriages 1890–1995 (456,789 records); Collection 1654321: Mission and Church Records 1820–1965 (123,456 records) | Land run homestead filings; Indian Territory families; marriages from 1890; church records | Free |
| BLM General Land Office Records (glorecords.blm.gov) | Land patents and homestead files | Missing patent information not in county deed indexes | Free |
| Ancestry.com (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | U.S. Federal Census Collection | 1900 and 1910 censuses for territorial/early state settlers | Subscription |
| Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) | Military records | Service and pension records for veteran Land Run settlers | Subscription |
| FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Cemetery records | Rural and town burial grounds | Free |
| NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) | RG49 GLO records; territorial court records | Full homestead case files; naturalization and territorial court records | In-person / NARA Online |

**Coverage of this survey:** 2 digitized volumes matching Oklahoma 1889–1910 were found and both are detailed above (volume_search returned the complete result set with no further pages). The 4 FamilySearch collections above are the complete indexed set returned for Oklahoma.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Oklahoma Historical Society, Oklahoma City | 1890 territorial census; territorial newspapers; city directories; county records | In-person; some holdings digitized |
| Oklahoma State Archives, Oklahoma City | Territorial district court records; state agency records post-1907 | In-person; mail request |
| National Archives at Fort Worth, TX | Territorial court records 1890–1907; federal land office records | In-person; reproductions by mail |
| National Archives, Washington DC / College Park | RG49 General Land Office; military pension files | In-person; NARA Online |
| County courthouses | Deed books; probate records; marriage licenses | In-person / mail |

## Records NOT online
- 1890 special territorial census (held by Oklahoma Historical Society — not confirmed as fully digitized in this survey)
- County tax rolls and poll books from the 1890s
- Full homestead case files beyond what FamilySearch collection 1541872 covers
- Territorial district court civil and criminal case files at National Archives at Fort Worth
- City directory collections for territorial-era towns
- Dawes Commission enrollment jackets (imageGroup 005221389) are online but browse-only — no name index

## Known record losses
- The 1890 federal census was destroyed by fire nationwide. Oklahoma's special territorial census of 1890 survives at the Oklahoma Historical Society (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run). No other specific record losses for Oklahoma were stated by tool results in this survey.

## Research tips
- Start with homestead files. For any family that participated in the Land Run, the homestead final proof file is the richest single record — it names the applicant, often their spouse and children as witnesses, and includes residence affidavits that can confirm arrival dates and origins. Search FamilySearch collection 1541872, imageGroup 005221388, and glorecords.blm.gov. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run)
- Use the 1890 territorial census. Because the 1890 federal census was destroyed, Oklahoma's territorial census is irreplaceable for families who arrived in the first year of settlement. Contact the Oklahoma Historical Society.
- Trace origins before researching Oklahoma. Most Land Run settlers came from Kansas, Texas, and Missouri — once you document an Oklahoma homestead, search departure-state records (1880 census, departure-state vital records, church records) to identify parents and siblings. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts)
- Distinguish Oklahoma Territory from Indian Territory. Western Oklahoma was Oklahoma Territory (organized civil government from 1890); eastern Oklahoma was Indian Territory, governed by tribal councils until 1907. The record series differ substantially — Indian Territory families require collection 1987432 and imageGroup 005221389.
- County boundaries were still forming. Verify the county at each research date before searching courthouse records.
- Tax rolls substitute for the 1890s gap. County tax rolls survive and can pinpoint a settler in a specific township between the 1890 territorial census and the 1900 federal census. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts)

Here is the locality research guide produced for **Alabama circa 1800** (pre-statehood):

---

## Alabama Region, c. 1780–1820 — Locality Research Guide

### Jurisdictional History (Critical Context)

The Alabama region changed hands rapidly before statehood, which directly affects where records are filed:

| Period | Governing Authority |
|---|---|
| Before 1798 | French, British, then **Spanish** colonial territory (Mobile area under Spain until 1813) |
| 1798–1817 | **Mississippi Territory** (eastern half) |
| 1817–1819 | **Alabama Territory** |
| 1819+ | State of Alabama |

> ⚠️ Pre-statehood records are filed under the jurisdiction that created them — not under "Alabama." Territorial records before 1817 must be searched under **Mississippi Territory**.

---

### European Colonial Records

For the Mobile coast and Gulf region before 1813:
- **Spanish records** → *Archivo General de Indias*, Seville (copies at the Library of Congress)
- **French records** → *Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer*, Aix-en-Provence (some microfilm at the Mobile Municipal Archives)

---

### Online / Indexed Collections on FamilySearch

| Collection | Date Range | Records |
|---|---|---|
| Alabama County Marriages | from 1809 | ~612,345 records |
| Alabama Probate Records | from 1809 | ~438,210 records |
| Census Substitutes Index | from 1810 | ~287,634 records *(index only, no images)* |
| Church Records | from 1803 | ~156,789 records |

---

### Digitized, Browsable Volumes?

**The direct answer to your specific question: none found on FamilySearch** for the Alabama 1780–1830 window. This is a genuine digitization gap, not a data error. The records that survive are largely in physical custody.

---

### Key Physical Repository — Alabama Dept. of Archives & History (ADAH), Montgomery

Holds the most important pre-statehood records:
- **Mississippi Territory census enumerations** for 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810 — the essential census *substitutes* for this period
- **Territorial tax lists** from 1798 onward
- **Land grant files**
- **Territorial court records**

None of these are currently on FamilySearch.

---

### Land Records — Best Free Online Resource

Alabama is a **federal land state**. The **BLM General Land Office** site ([glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov)) provides free access to federal patents and is the best tool for anchoring a settler to a specific county and date. Start here if you have a known ancestor in the region.

---

### Suggested Next Steps

1. **ADAH** for territorial census enumerations and tax lists (the best census substitutes for 1798–1817)
2. **BLM-GLO** for federal land patents
3. If your ancestor was near Mobile before 1813, pursue **Spanish colonial records** via the Library of Congress copies
4. Use **research-plan** to stage specific searches keyed to whoever in your tree was in this region around 1800

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Alabama Region (Pre-Statehood, ca. 1780–1820)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Alabama Territory organized 1817; statehood December 14, 1819
- **Administrative center:** St. Stephens (territorial capital); Cahawba (first state capital after 1820)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Mississippi Territory (1798–1817) → Alabama Territory (1817–1819) → State of Alabama (1819–)
- **Population during period:** Population data not returned by tools for this period. Wikipedia notes significant in-migration from the Carolinas, Virginia, and Georgia after the Creek War of 1813–1814.
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, early cotton cultivation, Mobile port commerce, trading with Creek and Cherokee nations
- **Ethnic composition:** Creek and Cherokee nations (major indigenous presence across interior); European-American settlers from southeastern states; free and enslaved African Americans; Spanish and French Creole community concentrated in Mobile
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic (Mobile, continuous from French and Spanish colonial periods); Methodist circuit riders (arriving ca. 1807); Baptist congregations (arriving with Georgia/Carolina settlers, organized ca. 1808–1815); Presbyterian missions
- **Key historical events:** Creek War (1813–1814) opened interior to American settlement; Spanish cession of Mobile (1813) brought the coastal district under full U.S. administration; rapid county formation 1809–1819

## Boundary changes
- **Before 1763:** French colonial territory (Mobile founded 1702)
- **1763–1780:** British West Florida
- **1780–1813:** Spanish West Florida (Mobile District)
- **1798:** Mississippi Territory organized; present-day Alabama became its eastern portion
- **1813:** United States seized Mobile from Spain; Mobile District came under American civil administration
- **1817:** When Mississippi achieved statehood, the eastern Mississippi Territory became the Alabama Territory
- **1819:** Alabama admitted to the Union, December 14

Records generated before 1798 are colonial records (French, British, or Spanish) and are not held in American territorial or state repositories. Records from 1798–1817 were created under Mississippi Territory authority; from 1817–1819, under Alabama Territory authority. County-level courts continued operating across the territorial transitions, so land and court records follow a generally continuous series.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No statewide civil registration existed during the pre-statehood period. The FamilySearch Wiki did not return Alabama-specific vital records start dates during this survey.
- **What exists:** Marriage records at county level from county formation (many Alabama counties formed 1809–1819). FamilySearch collection "Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950" (coll. 1598408; 612,345 records, 1,224,690 persons, 306,172 images) is the earliest accessible civil record series with an online presence. No birth or death registration existed during this period.
- **Where held:** County courthouses; FamilySearch (coll. 1598408, indexed with images)
- **Gaps:** Births and deaths were not registered. Counties not yet formed in 1800 have no marriage record series until their formation date.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism, marriage, and burial registers; estate inventories naming heirs; territorial census enumerations (see Census records below)

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Catholic (Mobile, continuous from colonial period); Methodist and Baptist (interior, organized ca. 1807–1815); Presbyterian (sparse before statehood)
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials (Catholic, Mobile); membership rolls, class lists, and minutes (Methodist, Baptist interior)
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950" (coll. 1986396; 156,789 records, 78,394 images) covers some denominations from 1803. Catholic records for Mobile from the colonial period are held at the Diocese of Mobile and on microfilm at the Mobile Municipal Archives.
- **Gaps:** Interior Alabama had very sparse organized church infrastructure before 1819. Methodist and Baptist congregations in the interior rarely maintained formal registers before the mid-19th century; coverage in the 1803–1819 window is likely thin. No tool result documented which specific interior congregations have surviving pre-1820 registers.
- **Language:** Spanish and French for pre-1813 Mobile Catholic records

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** The 1810 federal census (enumerated as Mississippi Territory) is the first federal enumeration including present-day Alabama residents. Alabama appears as a state from 1820 onward.
- **Territorial censuses:** Mississippi Territory conducted enumerations in 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810. Residents of present-day Alabama appear in these. They are held at the Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH), Montgomery — not in any FamilySearch digitized collection. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records)
- **Other enumerations:** Spanish colonial census returns for the Mobile District exist for the period of Spanish control (1780–1813), held at the Archivo General de Indias, Seville, with copies at the Library of Congress. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- **Access:** FamilySearch collection "Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890" (coll. 2016756; 287,634 records) is name-indexed with no images — it is an index only. The 1801, 1805, and 1808 territorial enumerations are physical documents at ADAH.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate administrations, guardianships, inventories, letters testamentary; territorial court records including land disputes and naturalization proceedings
- **Date range:** County probate courts date from county formation, mostly 1809 onward; Mississippi Territory court records go back to 1798
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985" (coll. 1537764; 438,210 records, 219,105 images) starts in 1809 — indexed with images. Territorial court records (pre-county) are held at ADAH.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Rectangular survey (federal land state; U.S. surveys began ca. 1803)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** U.S. federal government (Bureau of Land Management, General Land Office) for all U.S.-era grants. Spanish crown for Mobile District grants before 1813.
- **Types:** Federal land patents (original U.S. grants); Spanish land grants (Mobile area, pre-1813); county deed books (subsequent transfers); territorial and county tax digests
- **Date range:** U.S. federal land sales in present-day Alabama begin ca. 1803. Spanish land grants in the Mobile District predate this. County deed books date from county formation.
- **Where held:** BLM-GLO website (https://glorecords.blm.gov) for federal patents (online, free); ADAH for Spanish grant records and territorial land records; county courthouses for deed books. Land grants are cited as a core territorial record type at ADAH (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records).

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Creek War (1813–1814); War of 1812; territorial militia musters
- **Record types:** Territorial militia rolls; service records and pension files (War of 1812, Creek War) at NARA; bounty land warrants
- **Where held:** NARA holds federal service and pension records; ADAH holds territorial militia rolls; Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com) has War of 1812 records accessible by subscription

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Old Catholic cemeteries in Mobile (continuous from colonial period); small family and church cemeteries scattered through interior, many unmarked
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com) has listings for Alabama cemeteries; coverage for pre-1820 interior burials is sparse
- **Physical records:** Sexton records for Mobile Catholic parishes may predate statehood; interior cemeteries generally have no contemporaneous sexton records

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Mobile Centinel (est. ca. 1811) is among the earliest. Interior Alabama had no newspapers before statehood.

Locality guide written as loc_001.

---

The Alabama region around 1800 sat under three successive governments in quick succession: before 1798 it was French, then British, then Spanish colonial territory (with the Mobile area remaining under Spain until 1813); from 1798 to 1817 it was the eastern half of the Mississippi Territory; from 1817 to 1819 it was the Alabama Territory before statehood. Because of this layered history, the most important warning for a researcher is that pre-statehood records are filed under the jurisdiction that created them, not under "Alabama" — so territorial records before 1817 must be searched under Mississippi Territory, and anything touching the Mobile coast before 1813 is in European archives (Spanish records at the Archivo General de Indias in Seville with copies at the Library of Congress; French records at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer in Aix-en-Provence with some microfilm at the Mobile Municipal Archives). On the question of digitized browsable volumes specifically: the survey found zero digitized image volumes for Alabama in the 1780-1830 window on FamilySearch — that is a genuine digitization gap, not a data error. The records that survive are largely in physical custody at the Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH) in Montgomery, which holds the Mississippi Territory census enumerations for 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810 (the essential census substitutes for this period), territorial tax lists from 1798 onward, land grant files, and territorial court records — none of these are on FamilySearch. What is online and indexed consists of four FamilySearch collections: county marriages starting 1809 (612,345 records), probate records starting 1809 (438,210 records), a census substitutes index starting 1810 (287,634 records, index only with no images), and church records starting 1803 (156,789 records). For original land grants, Alabama is a federal land state and the BLM General Land Office website (glorecords.blm.gov) provides free access to federal patents and is the best tool for anchoring a settler to a specific county and date. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Alabama returned only generic content during this survey, so the guide was built from wiki search results and collections data rather than the Alabama-specific wiki articles; re-running the locality guide when the wiki is accessible will add further detail.

# Locality Guide: Alabama Region (Pre-Statehood, ca. 1780–1820)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Alabama Territory organized 1817; statehood December 14, 1819
- **Administrative center:** St. Stephens (territorial capital); Cahawba (first state capital after 1820)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Mississippi Territory (1798–1817) → Alabama Territory (1817–1819) → State of Alabama (1819–)
- **Population during period:** Population data not returned by tools for this period. Wikipedia notes significant in-migration from the Carolinas, Virginia, and Georgia after the Creek War of 1813–1814.
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, early cotton cultivation, Mobile port commerce, trading with Creek and Cherokee nations
- **Ethnic composition:** Creek and Cherokee nations (major indigenous presence across interior); European-American settlers from southeastern states; free and enslaved African Americans; Spanish and French Creole community concentrated in Mobile
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic (Mobile, continuous from French and Spanish colonial periods); Methodist circuit riders (arriving ca. 1807); Baptist congregations (arriving with Georgia/Carolina settlers, organized ca. 1808–1815); Presbyterian missions
- **Key historical events:** Creek War (1813–1814) opened interior to American settlement; Spanish cession of Mobile (1813) brought the coastal district under full U.S. administration; rapid county formation 1809–1819

## Boundary changes
- **Before 1763:** French colonial territory (Mobile founded 1702)
- **1763–1780:** British West Florida
- **1780–1813:** Spanish West Florida (Mobile District)
- **1798:** Mississippi Territory organized; present-day Alabama became its eastern portion
- **1813:** United States seized Mobile from Spain; Mobile District came under American civil administration
- **1817:** When Mississippi achieved statehood, the eastern Mississippi Territory became the Alabama Territory
- **1819:** Alabama admitted to the Union, December 14

Records generated before 1798 are colonial records (French, British, or Spanish) and are not held in American territorial or state repositories. Records from 1798–1817 were created under Mississippi Territory authority; from 1817–1819, under Alabama Territory authority. County-level courts continued operating across the territorial transitions, so land and court records follow a generally continuous series.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No statewide civil registration existed during the pre-statehood period. The FamilySearch Wiki did not return Alabama-specific vital records start dates during this survey.
- **What exists:** Marriage records at county level from county formation (many Alabama counties formed 1809–1819). FamilySearch collection "Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950" (coll. 1598408; 612,345 records, 1,224,690 persons, 306,172 images) is the earliest accessible civil record series with an online presence. No birth or death registration existed during this period.
- **Where held:** County courthouses; FamilySearch (coll. 1598408, indexed with images)
- **Gaps:** Births and deaths were not registered. Counties not yet formed in 1800 have no marriage record series until their formation date.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism, marriage, and burial registers; estate inventories naming heirs; territorial census enumerations (see Census records below)

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Catholic (Mobile, continuous from colonial period); Methodist and Baptist (interior, organized ca. 1807–1815); Presbyterian (sparse before statehood)
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials (Catholic, Mobile); membership rolls, class lists, and minutes (Methodist, Baptist interior)
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950" (coll. 1986396; 156,789 records, 78,394 images) covers some denominations from 1803. Catholic records for Mobile from the colonial period are held at the Diocese of Mobile and on microfilm at the Mobile Municipal Archives.
- **Gaps:** Interior Alabama had very sparse organized church infrastructure before 1819. Methodist and Baptist congregations in the interior rarely maintained formal registers before the mid-19th century; coverage in the 1803–1819 window is likely thin. No tool result documented which specific interior congregations have surviving pre-1820 registers.
- **Language:** Spanish and French for pre-1813 Mobile Catholic records

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** The 1810 federal census (enumerated as Mississippi Territory) is the first federal enumeration including present-day Alabama residents. Alabama appears as a state from 1820 onward.
- **Territorial censuses:** Mississippi Territory conducted enumerations in 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810. Residents of present-day Alabama appear in these. They are held at the Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH), Montgomery — not in any FamilySearch digitized collection. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records)
- **Other enumerations:** Spanish colonial census returns for the Mobile District exist for the period of Spanish control (1780–1813), held at the Archivo General de Indias, Seville, with copies at the Library of Congress. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- **Access:** FamilySearch collection "Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890" (coll. 2016756; 287,634 records) is name-indexed with no images — it is an index only. The 1801, 1805, and 1808 territorial enumerations are physical documents at ADAH.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate administrations, guardianships, inventories, letters testamentary; territorial court records including land disputes and naturalization proceedings
- **Date range:** County probate courts date from county formation, mostly 1809 onward; Mississippi Territory court records go back to 1798
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985" (coll. 1537764; 438,210 records, 219,105 images) starts in 1809 — indexed with images. Territorial court records (pre-county) are held at ADAH.

- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** U.S. federal government (Bureau of Land Management, General Land Office) for all U.S.-era grants. Spanish crown for Mobile District grants before 1813.
- **Types:** Federal land patents (original U.S. grants); Spanish land grants (Mobile area, pre-1813); county deed books (subsequent transfers); territorial and county tax digests
- **Date range:** U.S. federal land sales in present-day Alabama begin ca. 1803. Spanish land grants in the Mobile District predate this. County deed books date from county formation.
- **Where held:** BLM-GLO website (https://glorecords.blm.gov) for federal patents (online, free); ADAH for Spanish grant records and territorial land records; county courthouses for deed books. ---

## Pennsylvania Anthracite Coal Region — Locality Research Guide (1860–1890)

### Core County: Schuylkill County, PA
The heart of the anthracite field, with large Irish immigrant communities settled in patch towns surrounding Pottsville.

---

### Specialized Coal-Region Resources (from the FamilySearch Wiki)
Three sources unique to the anthracite region were identified:

1. **Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index** — Names approximately 41,000 colliery workers with occupation and parish of origin, drawn from company payroll books. High value for Irish immigrants.
2. **Pennsylvania Triennial Tax Assessments** — Ran every three years from 1853; sometimes recorded nativity, useful for pinpointing origin.
3. **Mine-Inspection Reports** — Organized by colliery; can confirm employment and place within the coal patch system.

---

### Catholic / Church Records
- All Schuylkill County parishes fell under the **Diocese of Philadelphia** for the entire 1860–1890 period.
- Request baptism and marriage registers from the **Diocese of Philadelphia Archives** (not the Diocese of Allentown, which wasn't erected until 1961).
- Five digitized FamilySearch volumes exist for this county/period but are **almost entirely browse-only** (no name index), including:
  - Naturalization records 1849–1915 (298 images)
  - Church records 1842–1895 (187 images, English and German)

---

### Civil Registration Gaps
- Pennsylvania had **no statewide death registration until 1906** and **no county marriage registration until ~1885**.
- Church registers are the **primary source** for births, marriages, and deaths throughout most of the 1860–1890 window.

---

### Neighboring Anthracite Counties (each needs its own guide)
- **Luzerne County**
- **Lackawanna County** (formed from Luzerne in 1878)
- **Northumberland County**
- **Carbon County**

---

### Recommended Next Steps
1. Open a research question for your ancestor.
2. Plan first searches starting with:
   - **Diocese of Philadelphia Archives** for Catholic parish registers
   - **Browse-only Schuylkill County naturalization volume** on FamilySearch (298 images, 1849–1915)
   - The **Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index** for colliery employment records

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania — Anthracite Coal Region (1860–1890)

**Scope note:** This guide surveys Schuylkill County as the representative county of the Pennsylvania anthracite coal region. The other anthracite counties — Luzerne, Lackawanna (carved from Luzerne in 1878), Northumberland, and Carbon — each need their own locality survey.

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties
- **County seat:** Pottsville
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania
- **Population during period:** 89,510 (1860), 116,428 (1870), 129,974 (1880)
- **Economy:** Anthracite coal extraction dominated every borough and township; associated iron-furnace, railroad, and canal industries shaped who kept records
- **Ethnic composition:** Large Irish immigrant community concentrated in mining patches; German, Welsh, and (later in the period) Eastern European miners alongside
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (dominant among Irish), German Lutheran and Reformed, Welsh Calvinist Methodist, Episcopal
- **Key historical events:** Civil War draft and enlistment 1861–1865; Molly Maguires trials 1875–1877 generated extensive court records naming Irish miners by name, employer, and patch town

## Boundary changes
- Schuylkill County boundaries were stable throughout the 1860–1890 target period.
- Lackawanna County (northeast of Schuylkill) was carved from Luzerne County in 1878 — not a Schuylkill boundary change, but essential context if research extends to the northern field.

## Specialized coal-region indexes

The FamilySearch Wiki page **Pennsylvania Coal Region Records** (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records) documents three classes of source unique to the anthracite field:

### Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index, 1855–1898
- Names approximately 41,000 colliery workers across the lower anthracite field, drawn from company payroll books that survived a 1903 records consolidation
- Each entry states occupation (loader, breaker boy, mule driver), wage rate, and parish of origin where stated
- Coverage is centered on Luzerne and Lackawanna counties (the lower field); Schuylkill County is the southern/middle field and may appear less fully, but workers employed across the field may be listed
- Payroll-derived indexes are the most direct finding aid for immigrant miners whose names were inconsistently indexed in census records

### Pennsylvania triennial tax assessments
- State assessors enumerated coal-region residents every three years from 1853
- Assessment ledgers record householder name, real estate value, occupation, and sometimes nativity
- Covers every third year of the target period (1860, 1863, 1866, 1869, 1872, 1875, 1878, 1881, 1884, 1887, 1890) — directly filling census gap years
- Held at the Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg

### Mine-inspection and accident reports
- Organized by colliery rather than by person — less useful as a genealogical finding aid than the payroll index, but document fatal accidents and name decedents

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start dates:** The FamilySearch Wiki page for Pennsylvania Vital Records returned only generic content and gave no specific registration dates. The FamilySearch collection "Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906–1968" (collection 2255317, 4,218,763 indexed records) starts in 1906, indicating statewide death registration was not in place during the 1860–1890 target period. County-level marriage registration, reflected in collection 1921317 ("Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885–1950"), covers the last five years of the target period only.
- **What exists:** Statewide death certificates: post-period (1906+). Statewide indexed marriages from ca. 1885 (collection 1921317, 524,189 records, indexed + images). Civil marriages 1677–1950 (collection 1571957, 312,045 records, indexed + images). Compiled marriages 1700–1900 (collection 1502909, 198,765 records, no images).
- **Where held:** Online at FamilySearch (see collections above). Physical originals at county courthouse and Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **Gaps:** Births and deaths in 1860–1890 have no statewide civil registration — church records are the primary substitute. Marriages 1860–1884 are covered only by church registers and compiled collections.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Catholic, Lutheran, and Methodist parish registers; coroner's inquests; newspaper death notices

### Church records
- **CRITICAL for Irish Catholic ancestors in Schuylkill County**
- **Diocesan jurisdiction:** Before 1868, all five anthracite counties fell under the Diocese of Philadelphia. From 1868, Luzerne and Lackawanna transferred to the Diocese of Scranton and Northumberland to the Diocese of Harrisburg; Schuylkill and Carbon remained under Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. For the entire 1860–1890 target period, Schuylkill Catholic parish registers are held under the Diocese of Philadelphia. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records)
- **Founding dates:** Many Catholic parishes in the coal region were established between 1840 and 1870 specifically to serve Irish and Eastern European immigrant communities
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations
- **Digitized volumes:** 1 volume of Schuylkill County Church Records 1842–1895 (image group 007936751, 187 images). **Browse-only: 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable — must be browsed image by image.** Records are in English and German.
- **Gaps:** Only 187 images are digitized — most parish registers have not been microfilmed by FamilySearch and are held physically by the Diocese of Philadelphia Archives or at the individual parish.
- **Language:** English and German in the digitized volume; individual Irish Catholic parish registers are typically in Latin or English
- **Note on SYNTH-PA-CHURCH:** The collections tool returned an entry titled "Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records (synthetic test fixture)" — the label "synthetic test fixture" indicates this is not a live research collection. Do not use it for actual searches.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1860, 1870, and 1880 all fall within the target period and are indexed and online
- **Mortality schedules:** 1860, 1870, and 1880 mortality schedules record deaths in the year preceding each census — an important substitute for missing death records
- **State census:** No Pennsylvania state census was taken during this period
- **1850 Schuylkill County census** is available on Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/1276/) — useful for establishing families in the decade before the target period
- **Access:** Federal census images and indexes are free on FamilySearch and subscription on Ancestry

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, letters of administration, guardianship files
- **Digitized volumes:** 1 volume, Probate Records 1851–1930 (image group 007936749, 412 images). **Browse-only: 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable.**
- **Statewide collection:** "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994" (collection 1999196), 3,200,560 images, browse-only (0 indexed records)
- **Filed at:** County level — Schuylkill County Orphans' Court and Court of Common Pleas, Pottsville
- **Value for Irish families:** Intestate administrations name next of kin and heirs; guardianship petitions name minor children and their relationships; both establish family structure where vital records are absent

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Pennsylvania is not a rectangular-survey state)
- **Digitized volumes:** 1 volume, Deed Records 1815–1900 (image group 007936752, 543 images, 22% name-indexed — partially searchable by name, partially browse-only)
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages; mining-company leases and company-town property records may appear in deed books
- **Filed at:** Schuylkill County Recorder of Deeds, Pottsville; Pennsylvania State Archives for some earlier grants
- **Note:** The FamilySearch Wiki page for Pennsylvania Land and Property returned only generic content; specific repository details for originals were not confirmed

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865) — Schuylkill County contributed heavily, including the 48th Pennsylvania Infantry with many Irish and coal-miner enlistees
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants (at NARA); Pennsylvania Adjutant General records (at Pennsylvania State Archives); draft registrations 1863–1865
- **Value:** Pension files name widow, children, and sometimes parents; they frequently document Irish birthplace and immigration date
- **Where held:** NARA Philadelphia region; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg

### Marriage records
- **Digitized volumes:** 1 volume, Marriage Records 1870–1910 (image group 007936753, 94 images). **Browse-only: 0% name-indexed — must be browsed image by image.**
- **Indexed collections:** County Marriages 1885–1950 (collection 1921317, 524,189 records, indexed + images); Civil Marriages 1677–1950 (collection 1571957, 312,045 records, indexed + images); Compiled Marriages 1700–1900 (collection 1502909, 198,765 records, no images)
- **Gap:** Marriages 1860–1884 are not covered by county civil registration; church records are the primary source

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Not enumerated in tool results for this county specifically
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave and BillionGraves cover Pennsylvania broadly; both are worth searching for Schuylkill County
- **Physical records:** Sexton records may survive at individual cemeteries; the Historical Society of Schuylkill County (Pottsville) may hold transcriptions

### Naturalization records
- **Digitized volumes:** 1 volume, Naturalization Records 1849–1915 (image group 007936750, 298 images). **Browse-only: 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable — must be browsed image by image.**
- **Critical for Irish ancestors:** Declarations of intention (first papers) and petitions for naturalization name the applicant's county and country of birth, date and port of arrival, and witness names — often the only document linking an immigrant to a specific Irish townland
- **Court of record:** Pre-1906, any court of record could grant naturalization; in Schuylkill County this includes the Court of Common Pleas, the Quarter Sessions, and federal circuit courts — search all
- **Filed at:** Schuylkill County Courthouse (originals); NARA Philadelphia for federal-court naturalizations

### Tax records
- **Pennsylvania triennial assessments from 1853:** See Specialized coal-region indexes above
- **Ancestry collection:** "Pennsylvania, U.S., Tax and Exoneration Lists, 1768–1801" (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/7667/) — pre-period, not applicable to 1860–1890
- **Value as substitute:** Triennial assessments document presence and occupation in years between federal censuses; nativity entries help connect an Irish surname to the immigrant generation

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Nearest ports:** Philadelphia and New York (Castle Garden / Ellis Island)
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival manifests at NARA; naturalization records (above) often note port and date
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents — examine the full manifest for all family members
- **Declarations of intention** filed in Schuylkill County courts often record arrival date and port, supplying a bridge to the passenger list

### Other record types
- **Molly Maguires court records (1875–1877):** Trials in Schuylkill County generated extensive testimony naming Irish miners, their employers, patch towns, and associations — an unusually rich source for Irish genealogical data
- **Company records:** Mine company payroll books and employment ledgers where they survive (some at the Historical Society of Schuylkill County; others held by coal-company successor archives)
- **Newspapers:** The Miners' Journal (Pottsville, 1825–present) published birth, marriage, and death notices; available on microfilm and partially digitized

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Collection 1921317 (County Marriages 1885–1950, 524K records); collection 1999196 (Probate Records 1683–1994, 3.2M images browse-only); collection 2255317 (Death Certificates 1906–1968, 4.2M indexed); collection 1571957 (Civil Marriages 1677–1950, 312K records); collection 1502909 (Compiled Marriages 1700–1900, 199K records); 5 digitized browse-only volumes | Marriages, probate, post-1906 deaths | Free |
| Ancestry | 1850 Schuylkill County Federal Census (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/1276/); Tax and Exoneration Lists 1768–1801 (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/7667/) | 1850 census (pre-period baseline) | Subscription |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned all 5 matching digitized volumes for Schuylkill County within this period — the result set is complete (totalResults = 5, all 5 detailed above).

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Schuylkill County Courthouse, Pottsville | Deeds, court records, naturalization papers (pre-1906), marriage licenses | In-person |
| Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg | State-level records, militia/military records, triennial tax assessments | In-person / written request |
| Diocese of Philadelphia Archives | Catholic baptism and marriage registers for all Schuylkill County parishes, 1860–1890 | Contact archives directly |
| Historical Society of Schuylkill County, Pottsville | Local histories, newspaper microfilm (Miners' Journal), transcribed cemetery records, company records | In-person |
| NARA, Philadelphia | Civil War pension and service records; federal-court naturalization petitions | In-person / online request |

## Records NOT online
- Pennsylvania triennial tax assessment ledgers (1853 onward) — physical at Pennsylvania State Archives
- Molly Maguires trial transcripts and court papers — physical at Schuylkill County Courthouse and state archives
- Mine company payroll books (where surviving) — Historical Society of Schuylkill County and coal-company successor archives
- Catholic parish baptism and marriage registers not yet digitized by FamilySearch — Diocese of Philadelphia Archives
- Miners' Journal obituaries and vital notices beyond any partially digitized run — microfilm at the Historical Society of Schuylkill County

## Known record losses
No specific record losses for Schuylkill County were confirmed by tool results during this survey. The FamilySearch Wiki county home page returned only generic content and could not be queried for specific courthouse losses. If a record class appears absent, treat the gap as a possible digitization gap rather than a confirmed loss until the county courthouse is queried directly.

## Research tips
- Begin with the Catholic parish registers under the Diocese of Philadelphia — the governing diocese for all Schuylkill County parishes throughout 1860–1890 — before searching civil records that largely do not exist for this period. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records)
- Consult the **Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index, 1855–1898** for colliery employment, occupation, wage rate, and parish of origin; it names ~41,000 workers and is the most direct genealogical finding aid for immigrant miners not easily found in census indexes. See the full page at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records.
- Pennsylvania triennial tax assessments from 1853 list occupation and sometimes nativity and run every three years through the target period — an essential substitute for the absence of civil vital registration and a way to establish year-by-year residence in a patch town.
- The Schuylkill County naturalization volume (image group 007936750, 1849–1915, 298 images) is entirely browse-only — plan to work through all images. First papers filed before 1860 may still be in this volume, so browse the full run rather than only the 1860–1890 images.
- Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record; search the Common Pleas, Quarter Sessions, and federal court records as separate series — a declaration filed in one court does not always appear in the same index as the final petition.
- The FamilySearch Wiki place-specific pages for Schuylkill County (home), Pennsylvania getting-started, online-records, and research-tips all returned only generic content during this survey; consult those pages directly at familysearch.org/wiki to check for guidance added since this guide was built.
