# Locality Guide: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania — Anthracite Coal Region (1860–1890)

**Scope note:** This guide surveys Schuylkill County as the representative county of the Pennsylvania anthracite coal region. The other anthracite counties — Luzerne, Lackawanna (carved from Luzerne in 1878), Northumberland, and Carbon — each need their own locality survey.

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties
- **County seat:** Pottsville
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania
- **Population during period:** 89,510 (1860), 116,428 (1870), 129,974 (1880)
- **Economy:** Anthracite coal extraction dominated every borough and township; associated iron-furnace, railroad, and canal industries shaped who kept records
- **Ethnic composition:** Large Irish immigrant community concentrated in mining patches; German, Welsh, and (later in the period) Eastern European miners alongside
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (dominant among Irish), German Lutheran and Reformed, Welsh Calvinist Methodist, Episcopal
- **Key historical events:** Civil War draft and enlistment 1861–1865; Molly Maguires trials 1875–1877 generated extensive court records naming Irish miners by name, employer, and patch town

## Boundary changes
- Schuylkill County boundaries were stable throughout the 1860–1890 target period.
- Lackawanna County (northeast of Schuylkill) was carved from Luzerne County in 1878 — not a Schuylkill boundary change, but essential context if research extends to the northern field.

## Specialized coal-region indexes

The FamilySearch Wiki page **Pennsylvania Coal Region Records** (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records) documents three classes of source unique to the anthracite field:

### Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index, 1855–1898
- Names approximately 41,000 colliery workers across the lower anthracite field, drawn from company payroll books that survived a 1903 records consolidation
- Each entry states occupation (loader, breaker boy, mule driver), wage rate, and parish of origin where stated
- Coverage is centered on Luzerne and Lackawanna counties (the lower field); Schuylkill County is the southern/middle field and may appear less fully, but workers employed across the field may be listed
- Payroll-derived indexes are the most direct finding aid for immigrant miners whose names were inconsistently indexed in census records

### Pennsylvania triennial tax assessments
- State assessors enumerated coal-region residents every three years from 1853
- Assessment ledgers record householder name, real estate value, occupation, and sometimes nativity
- Covers every third year of the target period (1860, 1863, 1866, 1869, 1872, 1875, 1878, 1881, 1884, 1887, 1890) — directly filling census gap years
- Held at the Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg

### Mine-inspection and accident reports
- Organized by colliery rather than by person — less useful as a genealogical finding aid than the payroll index, but document fatal accidents and name decedents

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start dates:** The FamilySearch Wiki page for Pennsylvania Vital Records returned only generic content and gave no specific registration dates. The FamilySearch collection "Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906–1968" (collection 2255317, 4,218,763 indexed records) starts in 1906, indicating statewide death registration was not in place during the 1860–1890 target period. County-level marriage registration, reflected in collection 1921317 ("Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885–1950"), covers the last five years of the target period only.
- **What exists:** Statewide death certificates: post-period (1906+). Statewide indexed marriages from ca. 1885 (collection 1921317, 524,189 records, indexed + images). Civil marriages 1677–1950 (collection 1571957, 312,045 records, indexed + images). Compiled marriages 1700–1900 (collection 1502909, 198,765 records, no images).
- **Where held:** Online at FamilySearch (see collections above). Physical originals at county courthouse and Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **Gaps:** Births and deaths in 1860–1890 have no statewide civil registration — church records are the primary substitute. Marriages 1860–1884 are covered only by church registers and compiled collections.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Catholic, Lutheran, and Methodist parish registers; coroner's inquests; newspaper death notices

### Church records
- **CRITICAL for Irish Catholic ancestors in Schuylkill County**
- **Diocesan jurisdiction:** Before 1868, all five anthracite counties fell under the Diocese of Philadelphia. From 1868, Luzerne and Lackawanna transferred to the Diocese of Scranton and Northumberland to the Diocese of Harrisburg; Schuylkill and Carbon remained under Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. For the entire 1860–1890 target period, Schuylkill Catholic parish registers are held under the Diocese of Philadelphia. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records)
- **Founding dates:** Many Catholic parishes in the coal region were established between 1840 and 1870 specifically to serve Irish and Eastern European immigrant communities
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations
- **Digitized volumes:** 1 volume of Schuylkill County Church Records 1842–1895 (image group 007936751, 187 images). **Browse-only: 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable — must be browsed image by image.** Records are in English and German.
- **Gaps:** Only 187 images are digitized — most parish registers have not been microfilmed by FamilySearch and are held physically by the Diocese of Philadelphia Archives or at the individual parish.
- **Language:** English and German in the digitized volume; individual Irish Catholic parish registers are typically in Latin or English
- **Note on SYNTH-PA-CHURCH:** The collections tool returned an entry titled "Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records (synthetic test fixture)" — the label "synthetic test fixture" indicates this is not a live research collection. Do not use it for actual searches.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1860, 1870, and 1880 all fall within the target period and are indexed and online
- **Mortality schedules:** 1860, 1870, and 1880 mortality schedules record deaths in the year preceding each census — an important substitute for missing death records
- **State census:** No Pennsylvania state census was taken during this period
- **1850 Schuylkill County census** is available on Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/1276/) — useful for establishing families in the decade before the target period
- **Access:** Federal census images and indexes are free on FamilySearch and subscription on Ancestry

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, letters of administration, guardianship files
- **Digitized volumes:** 1 volume, Probate Records 1851–1930 (image group 007936749, 412 images). **Browse-only: 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable.**
- **Statewide collection:** "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994" (collection 1999196), 3,200,560 images, browse-only (0 indexed records)
- **Filed at:** County level — Schuylkill County Orphans' Court and Court of Common Pleas, Pottsville
- **Value for Irish families:** Intestate administrations name next of kin and heirs; guardianship petitions name minor children and their relationships; both establish family structure where vital records are absent

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Pennsylvania is not a rectangular-survey state)
- **Digitized volumes:** 1 volume, Deed Records 1815–1900 (image group 007936752, 543 images, 22% name-indexed — partially searchable by name, partially browse-only)
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages; mining-company leases and company-town property records may appear in deed books
- **Filed at:** Schuylkill County Recorder of Deeds, Pottsville; Pennsylvania State Archives for some earlier grants
- **Note:** The FamilySearch Wiki page for Pennsylvania Land and Property returned only generic content; specific repository details for originals were not confirmed

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865) — Schuylkill County contributed heavily, including the 48th Pennsylvania Infantry with many Irish and coal-miner enlistees
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants (at NARA); Pennsylvania Adjutant General records (at Pennsylvania State Archives); draft registrations 1863–1865
- **Value:** Pension files name widow, children, and sometimes parents; they frequently document Irish birthplace and immigration date
- **Where held:** NARA Philadelphia region; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg

### Marriage records
- **Digitized volumes:** 1 volume, Marriage Records 1870–1910 (image group 007936753, 94 images). **Browse-only: 0% name-indexed — must be browsed image by image.**
- **Indexed collections:** County Marriages 1885–1950 (collection 1921317, 524,189 records, indexed + images); Civil Marriages 1677–1950 (collection 1571957, 312,045 records, indexed + images); Compiled Marriages 1700–1900 (collection 1502909, 198,765 records, no images)
- **Gap:** Marriages 1860–1884 are not covered by county civil registration; church records are the primary source

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Not enumerated in tool results for this county specifically
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave and BillionGraves cover Pennsylvania broadly; both are worth searching for Schuylkill County
- **Physical records:** Sexton records may survive at individual cemeteries; the Historical Society of Schuylkill County (Pottsville) may hold transcriptions

### Naturalization records
- **Digitized volumes:** 1 volume, Naturalization Records 1849–1915 (image group 007936750, 298 images). **Browse-only: 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable — must be browsed image by image.**
- **Critical for Irish ancestors:** Declarations of intention (first papers) and petitions for naturalization name the applicant's county and country of birth, date and port of arrival, and witness names — often the only document linking an immigrant to a specific Irish townland
- **Court of record:** Pre-1906, any court of record could grant naturalization; in Schuylkill County this includes the Court of Common Pleas, the Quarter Sessions, and federal circuit courts — search all
- **Filed at:** Schuylkill County Courthouse (originals); NARA Philadelphia for federal-court naturalizations

### Tax records
- **Pennsylvania triennial assessments from 1853:** See Specialized coal-region indexes above
- **Ancestry collection:** "Pennsylvania, U.S., Tax and Exoneration Lists, 1768–1801" (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/7667/) — pre-period, not applicable to 1860–1890
- **Value as substitute:** Triennial assessments document presence and occupation in years between federal censuses; nativity entries help connect an Irish surname to the immigrant generation

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Nearest ports:** Philadelphia and New York (Castle Garden / Ellis Island)
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival manifests at NARA; naturalization records (above) often note port and date
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents — examine the full manifest for all family members
- **Declarations of intention** filed in Schuylkill County courts often record arrival date and port, supplying a bridge to the passenger list

### Other record types
- **Molly Maguires court records (1875–1877):** Trials in Schuylkill County generated extensive testimony naming Irish miners, their employers, patch towns, and associations — an unusually rich source for Irish genealogical data
- **Company records:** Mine company payroll books and employment ledgers where they survive (some at the Historical Society of Schuylkill County; others held by coal-company successor archives)
- **Newspapers:** The Miners' Journal (Pottsville, 1825–present) published birth, marriage, and death notices; available on microfilm and partially digitized

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Collection 1921317 (County Marriages 1885–1950, 524K records); collection 1999196 (Probate Records 1683–1994, 3.2M images browse-only); collection 2255317 (Death Certificates 1906–1968, 4.2M indexed); collection 1571957 (Civil Marriages 1677–1950, 312K records); collection 1502909 (Compiled Marriages 1700–1900, 199K records); 5 digitized browse-only volumes | Marriages, probate, post-1906 deaths | Free |
| Ancestry | 1850 Schuylkill County Federal Census (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/1276/); Tax and Exoneration Lists 1768–1801 (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/7667/) | 1850 census (pre-period baseline) | Subscription |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned all 5 matching digitized volumes for Schuylkill County within this period — the result set is complete (totalResults = 5, all 5 detailed above).

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Schuylkill County Courthouse, Pottsville | Deeds, court records, naturalization papers (pre-1906), marriage licenses | In-person |
| Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg | State-level records, militia/military records, triennial tax assessments | In-person / written request |
| Diocese of Philadelphia Archives | Catholic baptism and marriage registers for all Schuylkill County parishes, 1860–1890 | Contact archives directly |
| Historical Society of Schuylkill County, Pottsville | Local histories, newspaper microfilm (Miners' Journal), transcribed cemetery records, company records | In-person |
| NARA, Philadelphia | Civil War pension and service records; federal-court naturalization petitions | In-person / online request |

## Records NOT online
- Pennsylvania triennial tax assessment ledgers (1853 onward) — physical at Pennsylvania State Archives
- Molly Maguires trial transcripts and court papers — physical at Schuylkill County Courthouse and state archives
- Mine company payroll books (where surviving) — Historical Society of Schuylkill County and coal-company successor archives
- Catholic parish baptism and marriage registers not yet digitized by FamilySearch — Diocese of Philadelphia Archives
- Miners' Journal obituaries and vital notices beyond any partially digitized run — microfilm at the Historical Society of Schuylkill County

## Known record losses
No specific record losses for Schuylkill County were confirmed by tool results during this survey. The FamilySearch Wiki county home page returned only generic content and could not be queried for specific courthouse losses. If a record class appears absent, treat the gap as a possible digitization gap rather than a confirmed loss until the county courthouse is queried directly.

## Research tips
- Begin with the Catholic parish registers under the Diocese of Philadelphia — the governing diocese for all Schuylkill County parishes throughout 1860–1890 — before searching civil records that largely do not exist for this period. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records)
- Consult the **Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index, 1855–1898** for colliery employment, occupation, wage rate, and parish of origin; it names ~41,000 workers and is the most direct genealogical finding aid for immigrant miners not easily found in census indexes. See the full page at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records.
- Pennsylvania triennial tax assessments from 1853 list occupation and sometimes nativity and run every three years through the target period — an essential substitute for the absence of civil vital registration and a way to establish year-by-year residence in a patch town.
- The Schuylkill County naturalization volume (image group 007936750, 1849–1915, 298 images) is entirely browse-only — plan to work through all images. First papers filed before 1860 may still be in this volume, so browse the full run rather than only the 1860–1890 images.
- Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record; search the Common Pleas, Quarter Sessions, and federal court records as separate series — a declaration filed in one court does not always appear in the same index as the final petition.
- The FamilySearch Wiki place-specific pages for Schuylkill County (home), Pennsylvania getting-started, online-records, and research-tips all returned only generic content during this survey; consult those pages directly at familysearch.org/wiki to check for guidance added since this guide was built.
- The other anthracite coal counties — Luzerne, Lackawanna (from 1878), Northumberland, and Carbon — still need their own locality surveys. Any ancestor who moved between patch towns may have left records in more than one county.

# Locality Guide: Vermont (pre-statehood, ca. 1760–1791)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Status during target period:** Contested colonial territory (claimed by both New Hampshire and New York), then the independent Republic of Vermont (1777–1791), then admitted as the 14th U.S. state in 1791.
- **Administrative structure:** Town-based government throughout the period. Each town had its own selectmen, proprietors' meetings, and town clerk. No centralized colonial capital; Montpelier became the capital after statehood.
- **Population during period:** No tool result returned population figures for this specific window.
- **Economy:** Primarily agrarian; timber, milling, and small-scale trade along river valleys.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English-descended settlers from Connecticut, Massachusetts, and other New England colonies; small numbers of French Canadians in the north.
- **Religious denominations:** Congregationalist predominant among original settlers; Baptist and Methodist congregations grew during and after the Revolutionary period. Exact congregation presence varies by town and date.
- **Key historical events:** French and Indian War (1754–1763) shaped early settlement; American Revolutionary War (1775–1783) produced major military records; Battle of Bennington (1777) was fought in Vermont territory. The land-grant dispute between New Hampshire and New York ran throughout the 1760s–1770s and directly shaped which records were created and by whom.

## Boundary changes
- Before the target period, New Hampshire issued town grants in the Vermont territory beginning in 1749 (the "New Hampshire Grants"). New York disputed these and claimed sovereignty. The Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule — described in the FamilySearch Vermont Genealogy wiki page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy) — was prepared under New York colonial authority and enumerates approximately 1,800 grantees of New Hampshire grants that New York refused to recognise.
- Vermont declared independence from both colonies as the Republic of Vermont in 1777, operating its own courts and land records until admission to the Union in 1791.
- Because both New Hampshire and New York claimed jurisdiction, records from the 1760s–1777 period may appear under either colony's archives. After 1777, records are held under the Republic of Vermont and subsequently the State of Vermont.

## Available record types

For each record type, note that Vermont's pre-statehood period (to 1791) predates nearly all civil registration — the town clerk is the primary civil record-keeper for vital events, and even those records are uneven in survival.

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Statewide civil registration of births, marriages, and deaths began in 1857 (stated at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy). No statewide civil vital records exist for the 1760–1791 period.
- **What exists:** Earlier town clerk records survive for some towns, with some going back to the 1770s, but survival is uneven. These are not a uniform statewide series.
- **Where held:** Individual town clerk offices. The Vermont State Archives in Montpelier holds some early records. No consolidated online database covers the pre-statehood period.
- **Gaps:** The entire pre-statehood period is a gap in civil registration. Town-level records vary town by town; some towns have no surviving pre-1791 vital entries at all.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism, marriage, and burial registers; family bibles; proprietors' meeting records; cemetery records; town histories.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Congregationalist (the dominant denomination among early New England settlers), Baptist, and Methodist congregations are documented for the Vermont territory in this period. Exact founding dates for individual congregations vary by town.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials; some confirmation and membership records.
- **Where held:** Individual churches and denominational archives. The Vermont State Archives and Vermont Historical Society hold some transcribed or deposited church records. The FamilySearch Wiki specific page for Vermont Church Records resolved to a generic article rather than Vermont-specific content — consult the Vermont State Archives directly for a register of surviving church record deposits.
- **Gaps:** Many early congregations were small and itinerant; not all kept formal registers in the 1760s–1780s. Many registers that were kept have not been digitized.
- **Language:** English.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** The first federal census (1790) is the earliest national enumeration and covers Vermont just after statehood. It is the only federal census within or immediately following the target period.
- **State/provincial census:** None during the pre-statehood period.
- **Other enumerations:** Town tax lists and proprietors' meeting records serve as population substitutes for years before 1790. Some towns made local enumerations for military purposes during the Revolutionary War period.
- **Access:** The 1790 federal census is indexed and available via Ancestry.com (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) and FamilySearch. Town tax lists are physical records held by town clerks and the Vermont State Archives.
- **Note:** The FamilySearch Wiki specific page for Vermont Census resolved to a generic article; Vermont-specific census guidance was not returned by tools.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, letters of administration, guardianship files. The Republic of Vermont established its own courts beginning in 1777; county probate courts followed at statehood.
- **Date range:** The earliest Republic of Vermont probate records date from 1777. Pre-1777 probate for Vermont territory residents would have been filed under New York or New Hampshire colonial courts.
- **Where held:** Vermont State Archives (Montpelier) for early records; county probate courts for county-level records from their formation. The FamilySearch Wiki specific page for Vermont Probate Records resolved to a generic article; Vermont-specific probate guidance was not returned by tools.
- **Online access:** No indexed collections or digitized volumes for Vermont probate in this period were returned by FamilySearch's collections_search or volume_search tools.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds, following New England practice.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Dual-authority situation. New Hampshire issued grants from 1749; New York disputed these and issued competing grants. After 1777, the Republic of Vermont and then the State of Vermont controlled land distribution. The Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule — described in the Vermont Genealogy wiki page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy) — enumerates approximately 1,800 grantees of New Hampshire grants, with grantee name, township, grant date, acreage, and disputed-claim status. This is the earliest systematic landowner record for the future state.
- **Types:** Town proprietors' meeting records (land divisions, lot assignments), deeds, New Hampshire grants, New York grants, Republic of Vermont and state land records.
- **Where held:** Individual town clerk offices hold town proprietors' records and deed books. The Vermont State Archives holds Republic of Vermont land records. New Hampshire State Archives (Concord) and New York State Archives (Albany) hold the colonial-period grant records for each colony. The FamilySearch Wiki specific page for Vermont Land and Property resolved to a generic article.
- **Online access:** No digitized volumes for Vermont land records in this period were returned by FamilySearch's volume_search tool.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** French and Indian War (1754–1763) and American Revolutionary War (1775–1783) both directly affected Vermont territory.
- **Record types:** Revolutionary War service records, pension files, and bounty land warrants are held at NARA (https://www.archives.gov/). State-level muster rolls and militia records for the Vermont militia are held at the Vermont State Archives.
- **Where held:** NARA for federal records; Vermont State Archives for state militia records. Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) holds some digitized military records for this period.
- **Note:** Vermont residents who served before 1777 may appear in Connecticut, Massachusetts, or New York militia records.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Town burial grounds and church cemeteries were established throughout the Vermont territory beginning in the 1760s–1770s. Many are small, rural, and without formal sexton records for the pre-statehood period.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) is the primary online cemetery index; coverage for small pre-statehood Vermont cemeteries is incomplete.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records where they exist are held by individual towns or churches. Town histories frequently include cemetery transcriptions.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Vermont's first newspapers were established in the 1780s (e.g., the Vermont Gazette, 1783). Coverage for the earliest part of the target period (1760s–early 1780s) is minimal or absent.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) provides access to some historical Vermont newspapers. Physical holdings are at the Vermont Historical Society and Vermont State Library.
- **Content value:** Marriage and death notices appear in later years of the period; legal notices (land sales, estate settlements) are valuable.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Context:** Pre-statehood Vermont settlers arrived overwhelmingly from other New England colonies (Connecticut, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, Rhode Island), not from overseas ports. Overseas immigration to Vermont in this period was rare.
- **Record types:** Declarations of intention and naturalizations were filed in courts of record after statehood (1791). For the pre-statehood period, track migration through Connecticut, Massachusetts, and other originating colony records.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) for federal immigration and naturalization records post-1791. Originating-state archives for earlier migration trails.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Town property tax and poll tax lists; town grand lists (the Vermont term for annual tax valuation rolls).
- **Date range:** Some town grand lists survive from the 1770s and 1780s, though survival varies by town.
- **Where held:** Individual town clerk offices and the Vermont State Archives.
- **Substitute value:** Town grand lists are the primary substitute for the absence of census records before 1790 and can establish residence, approximate wealth, and household composition.

### Other record types
- **Town proprietors' records:** Minutes of proprietors' meetings record lot assignments, boundary disputes, and early land divisions — a critical source for identifying pre-statehood residents.
- **Town histories:** 19th-century town histories (most published 1860–1900) frequently reprint colonial-era proprietors' records that are otherwise not easily accessible, as stated in the Vermont Genealogy wiki page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy). These are a major research resource for the pre-statehood period.
- **Republic of Vermont records:** Court, legislative, and administrative records of the Republic of Vermont (1777–1791) are held at the Vermont State Archives.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch Vermont Genealogy wiki | Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule description; general guidance | Pre-statehood land grantees; research orientation | Free — https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census Collection | 1790 census (earliest national enumeration, taken just after statehood) | Subscription — https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/ |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records | Burial information before vital registration | Free — https://www.findagrave.com/ |
| Fold3 | Military records | Revolutionary War service records and pension files | Subscription — https://www.fold3.com/ |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers | Death and marriage notices from the 1780s onward | Subscription — https://www.newspapers.com/ |
| NARA | Federal records, military, immigration | Revolutionary War records; 1790 census originals | In-person / some online — https://www.archives.gov/ |

**Coverage of this survey:** FamilySearch's collections_search and volume_search tools returned zero indexed collections and zero digitized volumes for Vermont in the 1760–1800 period. This is a digitization and indexing coverage gap — it reflects what FamilySearch has currently indexed for this era, not the totality of surviving records. Undigitized pre-statehood Vermont records require contacting physical repositories.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Vermont State Archives (Montpelier) | Republic of Vermont records (1777–1791); early state records; some land and court records | In-person / written request; see vermont.gov |
| Individual town clerk offices (each Vermont town) | Town vital records (where surviving, some from 1770s); town meeting records; grand lists; deed books; proprietors' records | Contact each town clerk directly |
| Vermont Historical Society (Montpelier) | Town histories; genealogical collections; early newspapers; manuscript collections | In-person; some digitized holdings online |
| New Hampshire State Archives (Concord, NH) | New Hampshire colonial grants for Vermont territory (pre-1777) | In-person / written request |
| New York State Archives (Albany, NY) | New York colonial records disputing NH grants; New York's own Vermont-territory grants | In-person / written request |
| County probate courts (each Vermont county) | Probate records from county formation forward | In-person |

## Records NOT online
- Pre-statehood town clerk records (vital records, town meeting minutes, town grand lists/tax lists) for the 1760s–1791 period
- Early church baptism, marriage, and burial registers for most Vermont denominations
- Town proprietors' meeting records and lot-assignment books
- Republic of Vermont court and administrative records (most not digitized)
- County probate court records from formation through the early 19th century
- Local cemetery sexton records (most towns had none in the pre-statehood period)

## Known record losses
No tool result returned a statement about specific documented record losses for Vermont in this period. The Vermont Genealogy wiki page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy) describes the survival of pre-statehood town records as "uneven" — this reflects scattered custody and incomplete survival rather than a known catastrophic loss event. The researcher should contact individual town clerks and the Vermont State Archives to determine what survives for a specific town before concluding a record is gone.

## Research tips
- The Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule is the earliest systematic resident list for the future state, predating any civil registration. It is the first record to check for pre-statehood landholders and their disputed New Hampshire grants. See the Vermont Genealogy page at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy.

- Town clerk records from the 1770s onward survive for some towns but not others. Each town must be checked individually — there is no consolidated pre-statehood vital record series. The town clerk is both the vital record-keeper and the land record custodian. See https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy.
- The territory was claimed by both New Hampshire and New York before 1777. A person who received a New Hampshire grant may appear in New Hampshire colonial records; someone who received a New York competing grant will appear in New York records. Search both colonies' archives for land-related evidence in the 1760s–1770s.
- 19th-century Vermont town histories (most published 1860–1900) are a major research resource: they frequently reprint colonial-era proprietors' records, cemetery transcriptions, and early settler lists that are otherwise very difficult to access. The Vermont Historical Society holds the most comprehensive collection. See https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy.
- The 1790 federal census is the earliest national enumeration and covers Vermont. It is indexed and available through Ancestry.com and FamilySearch. Work backwards from this record to establish household composition just after statehood, then use town records to extend the trail into the pre-statehood years.

- **Relevant conflicts:** French and Indian War (1754–1763) and American Revolutionary War (1775–1783) both directly affected Vermont territory.
- **Record types:** Revolutionary War service records, pension files, and bounty land warrants are held at NARA (https://www.archives.gov/). State-level muster rolls and militia records for the Vermont militia are held at the Vermont State Archives.
- **Where held:** NARA for federal records; Vermont State Archives for state militia records. Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) holds some digitized military records for this period.
- **Note:** Vermont residents who served before 1777 may appear in Connecticut, Massachusetts, or New York militia records.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Town burial grounds and church cemeteries were established throughout the Vermont territory beginning in the 1760s–1770s. Many are small, rural, and without formal sexton records for the pre-statehood period.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) is the primary online cemetery index; coverage for small pre-statehood Vermont cemeteries is incomplete.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records where they exist are held by individual towns or churches. Town histories frequently include cemetery transcriptions.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Vermont's first newspapers were established in the 1780s (e.g., the Vermont Gazette, 1783). Coverage for the earliest part of the target period (1760s–early 1780s) is minimal or absent.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) provides access to some historical Vermont newspapers. Physical holdings are at the Vermont Historical Society and Vermont State Library.
- **Content value:** Marriage and death notices appear in later years of the period; legal notices (land sales, estate settlements) are valuable.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Context:** Pre-statehood Vermont settlers arrived overwhelmingly from other New England colonies (Connecticut, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, Rhode Island), not from overseas ports. Overseas immigration to Vermont in this period was rare.
- **Record types:** Declarations of intention and naturalizations were filed in courts of record after statehood (1791). For the pre-statehood period, track migration through Connecticut, Massachusetts, and other originating colony records.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) for federal immigration and naturalization records post-1791. Originating-state archives for earlier migration trails.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Town property tax and poll tax lists; town grand lists (the Vermont term for annual tax valuation rolls).
- **Date range:** Some town grand lists survive from the 1770s and 1780s, though survival varies by town.
- **Where held:** Individual town clerk offices and the Vermont State Archives.
- **Substitute value:** Town grand lists are the primary substitute for the absence of census records before 1790 and can establish residence, approximate wealth, and household composition.

### Other record types
- **Town proprietors' records:** Minutes of proprietors' meetings record lot assignments, boundary disputes, and early land divisions — a critical source for identifying pre-statehood residents.
- **Town histories:** 19th-century town histories (most published 1860–1900) frequently reprint colonial-era proprietors' records that are otherwise not easily accessible, as stated in the Vermont Genealogy wiki page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy). These are a major research resource for the pre-statehood period.
- **Republic of Vermont records:** Court, legislative, and administrative records of the Republic of Vermont (1777–1791) are held at the Vermont State Archives.

No tool result returned a statement about specific documented record losses for Vermont in this period. The Vermont Genealogy wiki page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy) describes the survival of pre-statehood town records as "uneven" — this reflects scattered custody and incomplete survival rather than a known catastrophic loss event. The researcher should contact individual town clerks and the Vermont State Archives to determine what survives for a specific town before concluding a record is gone.

- The Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule is the earliest systematic resident list for the future state, predating any civil registration. It is the first record to check for pre-statehood landholders and their disputed New Hampshire grants. See the Vermont Genealogy page at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy.
- Statewide civil registration did not begin until 1857 — for the 1760s–1791 period, church registers, town records, and family bibles are the primary vital sources. Do not expect to find birth or death certificates for this period.
- Town clerk records from the 1770s onward survive for some towns but not others. Each town must be checked individually — there is no consolidated pre-statehood vital record series. The town clerk is both the vital record-keeper and the land record custodian. See https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy.
- The territory was claimed by both New Hampshire and New York before 1777. A person who received a New Hampshire grant may appear in New Hampshire colonial records; someone who received a New York competing grant will appear in New York records. Search both colonies' archives for land-related evidence in the 1760s–1770s.
- 19th-century Vermont town histories (most published 1860–1900) are a major research resource: they frequently reprint colonial-era proprietors' records, cemetery transcriptions, and early settler lists that are otherwise very difficult to access. The Vermont Historical Society holds the most comprehensive collection. See https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy.
- The 1790 federal census is the earliest national enumeration and covers Vermont. It is indexed and available through Ancestry.com and FamilySearch. Work backwards from this record to establish household composition just after statehood, then use town records to extend the trail into the pre-statehood years.

## Yorkshire, England — Death Records Locality Guide (1851)

### Civil Registration (Primary Source)
Yorkshire in 1851 falls squarely within the era of **English civil registration**, which began on **1 July 1837** for all of England and Wales under the Registration Act 1836.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Yorkshire, England (1851)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **County:** Yorkshire — a historic county in northern England, the largest county in England by area
- **Administrative subdivisions in 1851:** Three ridings — East Riding (administrative center Beverley), West Riding (various; Leeds was the largest town), and North Riding (Northallerton area). The City of York was administered separately as a county borough.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** England and Wales for civil registration purposes; England (Church of England dioceses of York and Ripon) for church records
- **Economy:** Textile manufacturing dominated the West Riding (wool and later cotton mills in Leeds, Bradford, Halifax, Huddersfield); agriculture in the East and North Ridings; coal mining emerging in West Riding
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English; Irish immigration increasing after the 1845–1852 famine, particularly in mill towns
- **Religious denominations:** Church of England (dominant); strong Nonconformist presence — Methodism was particularly strong in Yorkshire; also Baptists, Quakers, Roman Catholics
- **Key historical events:** 1851 is a Great Exhibition year; the period saw rapid industrialization in West Riding towns affecting population movement and record-keeping

## Boundary changes

- Yorkshire's three-riding structure was ancient and unchanged in 1851.
- Civil registration districts (the units used for GRO death indexes) did not align precisely with riding boundaries — they were newly created administrative districts established under the Registration Act 1836.
- No significant boundary changes affecting Yorkshire as a whole county occurred in this period.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date:** 1 July 1837 — national level for England and Wales, established by the Registration Act 1836, administered by the General Register Office (GRO). Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/England_Civil_Registration
- **What exists:** Deaths, births, and marriages registered in quarterly GRO registration districts from 1 July 1837. Death certificates record name, date, place, age, occupation, cause of death, and the informant who reported the death.
- **Where held:** Certified copies of original certificates are held by the GRO. The quarterly death index is the finding aid — it gives the registration district and volume/page number needed to order the certificate.
- **Critical limitation for 1851:** Early civil registration (1837–1875) was incomplete. Enforcement was weak, and many deaths in this period — including 1851 — were never registered. A civil death registration may simply not exist for a death that occurred. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/England_Civil_Registration
- **Finding the index (free):**
  - FreeBMD (freebmd.org.uk) — volunteer-transcribed quarterly indexes
  - GRO Historical Indexes (gro.gov.uk) — free for deaths 1837–1957; can order certified certificates online for a fee
- **Finding the index (subscription):**
  - Findmypast (findmypast.co.uk)
  - Ancestry (ancestry.com)

### Church records

- **Denominations present:** Church of England (Anglican); Methodist (Wesleyan and other branches); Baptist; Quaker (Society of Friends); Roman Catholic; others
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, and burials in Anglican registers; baptism, marriage, and burial registers for Nonconformist congregations
- **Where held:** Anglican registers are held at the relevant diocesan record offices — Borthwick Institute for Archives (University of York) for the Diocese of York; West Yorkshire Archive Service for many West Riding parishes. Nonconformist registers collected at the GRO in 1837 are now at The National Archives in class RG 4–8. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/England_Civil_Registration
- **Relationship to 1851 death search:** Because civil registration enforcement was weak, Anglican burial records are an essential parallel source. If a 1851 death was not civilly registered, the burial register may be the only surviving record.
- **Language:** English

### Census records

- **National census:** The 1851 census was taken on 30 March 1851. It records every person in a household on that night, with name, age, relationship to head, occupation, and birthplace.
- **Search strategy:** If the ancestor died after 30 March 1851, they should appear on the 1851 census — use it to confirm identity and age before searching the death index. If they died before 30 March 1851, check the 1841 census instead.
- **Access:** The 1851 census for England is indexed and available on Ancestry (subscription) and Findmypast (subscription); FamilySearch also holds census records for England.

### Probate and court records

- **Types:** Wills and administrations for 1851 were proved in ecclesiastical courts — the Prerogative Court of York had jurisdiction over larger estates in Yorkshire and northern England. The Court of Probate Act 1857 (effective 1858) transferred probate to a civil system; for 1851, ecclesiastical probate applies.
- **Where held:** Borthwick Institute for Archives, University of York, holds the records of the Prerogative Court of York.
- **Value:** A probate record may name surviving family members and give the date and approximate place of death.

### Land records

- **Types:** Tithe maps and apportionments (produced from c.1836–1850 under the Tithe Commutation Act 1836); enclosure awards; rate books; deeds
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Land registration was decentralized in 1851 — deeds were held locally; there was no national land registry until 1862 and it was not comprehensive until much later.
- **Where held:** County and riding record offices (West Yorkshire Archive Service, North Yorkshire County Record Office, East Riding of Yorkshire Archives)

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** The Crimean War began 1853 — not yet relevant in 1851. Some individuals may have prior service in earlier conflicts (Napoleonic era veterans were still alive).

# Locality Guide: Yorkshire, England (1851)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Economy:** Textile manufacturing dominated the West Riding (wool and later cotton mills in Leeds, Bradford, Halifax, Huddersfield); agriculture in the East and North Ridings; coal mining emerging in the West Riding
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English; Irish immigration increasing after the 1845–1852 famine, particularly in mill towns
- **Religious denominations:** Church of England (dominant); strong Nonconformist presence — Methodism was particularly strong in Yorkshire; also Baptists, Quakers, Roman Catholics
- **Key historical events:** 1851 is a Great Exhibition year; rapid industrialization in West Riding towns affecting population movement and record-keeping

## Boundary changes

- Yorkshire's three-riding structure was ancient and unchanged in 1851.

- Many parish burial registers: not all are digitized; check with the relevant diocesan record office.
- Coroner's records (inquisitions): physical only, held at county record offices; can provide detailed cause-of-death information.
- Quarter sessions records: physical only, relevant riding record office.
- Rate books and poor law records: physical only, relevant record office.

## Known record losses

No specific record losses for Yorkshire civil registration records in 1851 were identified in the tool results of this survey. The key limitation for 1851 is structural, not a loss: civil registration enforcement was weak before 1875, so some deaths were simply never registered. The England Civil Registration wiki page states this explicitly (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/England_Civil_Registration). Anglican burial registers are the main substitute source for unregistered deaths.

## Research tips

- Search all four quarters of the 1851 GRO death index (not just the one you expect), since civil registration of a death was often delayed by weeks or months. FreeBMD (freebmd.org.uk) and the GRO Historical Indexes (gro.gov.uk) are both free starting points. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/England_Civil_Registration
- If the GRO index has no entry, go immediately to the Anglican burial register for the parish where the person lived — many 1851 deaths were recorded in parish burial registers but never civilly registered, because registration was not compulsory until 1875. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/England_Civil_Registration
- Yorkshire is large; identify the riding (East, West, or North) before searching physical repositories, as each riding has its own county archive. The registration district in a GRO index entry will also indicate the area.
- Use the 1851 census (30 March 1851) as a companion record: it shows the ancestor's age and birthplace, which helps confirm the right GRO index entry.
- Once you have the GRO index reference (registration district, volume, and page number), order the certified copy of the death certificate from the GRO at gro.gov.uk. The certificate gives the informant's name and address, the cause of death, and other details not in the index.
- Check local Yorkshire newspapers for an obituary or inquest report — the British Newspaper Archive at britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk holds digitized Yorkshire papers and may give richer cause-of-death and family details than the death registration alone.
